Hon. N. W. Rowell (President of the Privy Council) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 37, respecting the Department of Health.
Explain.

This Bill is to provide for the creation of a Department of Health, to be presided over by a minister of the Crown to be named by the Governor in Council. It also contains the usual provision for the appointment of a deputy minister, to be the deputy head of the department, and for the necessary officers, clerks and employees. The powers of the minister administering the department extend to and include all matters and questions relating to the promotion or preservation of the health and social welfare of the people of Canada over which the Parliament of Canada has jurisdiction; that is the general definition of the powers of the minister. Certain particular powers are mentioned in detail covering co-operation with the provincial, territorial and other health authorities, with a view to the coordination of efforts proposed or made for preserving public health. The department is also authorized to deal with questions relating to the conservation of child life and child welfare generally; the inspection and medical care of immigrants; the supervision, as regards the public health, of railways, boats, ships and all methods of transportation; the supervision of federal public buildings and offices with regard to the health of civil servants and other Government employees therein;
the enforcement of the regulations of the International Joint Commission promulgated pursuant to the treaty between the United States and Great Britain for the prevention of the pollution of boundary waters; and the administration of certain statutes mentioned in the schedule now being administered by other departments. Provision is also made for the appointment of a Dominion Council of Health, of which the Deputy Minister of Public Health is to be chairman; the council to be composed of the chief executive officers of the Provincial Health Departments and three other persons to be named by the Governor in Council.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

On 30th July, 1918, the department, in order to build up an organization to carry on the Victory Loan campaign, 1918, without having to lean too heavily on the department proper, wrote the Civil Service Commission to secure the services of a first class executive head and four or five accountants. The department emphasized the necessity of the immediate employment of these officials, because they must obtain a working knowledge of the arrangements to be made for the flotation of the loan.
The 1918 Victory Loan was to be issued on a very different basis from previous issues. The bonds were to be printed and furnished to all branches of the various banks before the campaign opened so that immediately on full payment of subscriptions the coupon bonds could be handed out at once to the subscribers and the fully registered bonds as soon as the required registration could be made in the books of the Finance Department.
The Civil Service Commission advertised for applications for above mentioned positions in the Canada Gazette of August 8, 1918, calling for the filing of applications not later than September 12 next but extending the time for one week for candidates from British Columbia, thus fixing the date for closing the lists as September 19. 1918. _
It became necessary for the department to take very prompt action in the direction of making all preparations for the issue of a very extensive loan, the plans of the Dominion Executive Committee being so far advanced as to require a conference arranged for the 20th August between the subcommittee and officers of the department to effect final arrangements of all details. As the commission was not in a position, until after the 19th of September, to furnish officials required for this work the services of the officers of the department who directed the work of previous loans wrere utilized. It was eventually deemed more advisable to delegate one of these officials to take complete charge of the carrying out of such arrangements rather than rely at such a late date on the services of a new and untried appointee. To assist him in this work, the department availed themselves of the services of four expert men loaned by the Victory Loan organizations in Toronto and
Montreal to, as it were, represent them in the work. These officers, whose names are as follows, were loaned to us from the organizations from the dates mentioned: Arthur Paterson, October 16, 1918; Thomas Holloway, October 16,	1918; James R.
Adams, October 16, 1918; George E. Elliott, October 24, 1918.
Their services will be required until the final adjustment of the loan. They receive remuneration from the department at the rate of $2,500 per annum each, being the amount of remuneration offered for assistants in the advertisement of the Civil Service Commission.
On the 5th December, 1918, the Deputy Minister of Finance wrote the Civil Service Commission in connection with the employment of the above and asked for certificates for such employment which were issued by the commission and forwarded to the department.

That, in the opinion of this House, the amount of $5,000 received by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick for the fiscal years 1915-16 and 1916-17 to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, should1 be returned by the said Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to the Treasury of Canada forthwith.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted to recall the circumstances to the minds of hon. gentlemen who were present last session when a discussion took place on this subject? The circumstances in connection with this motion, the payment of $2,500 to cover the expenses of the Chief Justice of Canada in connection with attending meetings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, dates back to 1897, I think, when, at the suggestion of the then Minister of Justice (the late Sir Oliver Mowat) that amount of money was placed in the Estimates for the specific purpose of meeting the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice when performing the journeys referred to. From 1897 until a few years ago the item always appeared in the Estimates in exactly the language which I have stated. No variation was made in that language until the fiscal year 1915-16, when the wording was somewhat changed. Previously the vote had invariably read " Travelling expenses attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy 'Council." In the fiscal year 1915-16 the wording of the vote was made " Special allowance to Sir Charles' Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council." I am aware that apologists for the respectable raid which has been made on the treasury to the extent of $5,000 will find in the wording of the vote-in its technical or legal phraseology-a loophole for an excuse for the payment of this money. I submit, however, that there can be no doubt that the express object for which this money was granted was to cover the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice when atr tending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. If the Chief Justice did not attend these sittings he would incur no travelling expenses, and there would be no justification for his taking advantage of this vote. The Chief Justice rather seems to have held that view himself at one time. When I first brought this matter up in the House on 13th May, 1918, the Ottawa papers the next morning contained an interview in which Sir 'Charles Fitzpatrick characterized my statement that he had received this money when he did 
not go overseas as absolutely untrue. In the interview in question that gentleman used these words, as reported in the press:
When I do not go to Dondon of course I do not receive the money.
I proceeded then to show from the Auditor General's Report that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had received money for travelling expenses, although he had not gone overseas in the two years referred to. On the 15th May, 1918, the Prime Minister without comment read to the House a statement which he announced had been placed in his hands by iSir Charles Fitzpatrick. The statement drew attention to the fact that the wording of the vote in the fiscal years 1915-16 and 1916-17 had been changed to "Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council," instead of reading as formerly "Travelling expenses for attending sittings of the Judicial lOommittee of the Privy Council." I hold myself responsible, as a member of this House, for allowing this vote for this purpose to pass for the two years in question. In common with very many other members of the House I was present at that time, but I excuse myself for not raising objection to the vote on the ground that ever since 1897 this money had been voted without dispute, and the purpose of the vote was taken for granted. But, Sir, after I found out that the gentleman concerned had not gone overseas and had not performed the service for which the money was undoubtedly voted, after I found out that we had made a mistake in passing this vote in those terms, I do not feel like adding to my mistake an offence; because if I were to allow Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to retain, without question on my part, money for which he had given no service whatever to the country, I should be condoning what I regard as absolutely wrong. I do not propose to do that, consequently, I am making the present motion.
But, Sir, I did not think it would be necessary to bring this matter up in this House at all after what transpired last session. When we were in Committee of Supply, as will be found by reference to page 2507 of last year's Hansard, I asked if the Chief Justice had repaid, or would do so, this $5,000. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George E. Foster) who was overseeing the Estimates, said that an answer would be given later in the evening, and for the time being the item was allowed to stand. Later on the same evening the Minister of Trade and Commerce

brought the item forward again, but at my request allowed it to stand until the statement which he had promised was produced. I said in explanation of my request:
But the fact that, in my judgment, five thousand dollars of the money of Canada has heen taken out of the treasury by a man who happens to be Chief Justice of the Dominion of Canada, warrants me in saying that I will not consent to the passage of another item of $2,500 to that gentleman until I know that the money-
-that is, the $5,000 in question-
-will be refunded.
Again the item stood, and when we came back to it a little later the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a summary of the statement which he had promised earlier in the evening to give, and which I take it from reading Hansard he was authorized by the Chief Justice to give. I commend to your consideration a portion of that statement, the full text of which will be found on page 2536 of Hansard. The Minister of Trade and Commerce said:
Sir Charles Fitzpatrick contends that he was entirely justified under the circumstances in accepting the allowance for the two years during which he visited London.
That is entirely true.
But with reference to the last two years-
That is, the fiscal years 1916 and 1917.
-as it appears to be the wish of the House that these amounts should be returned, he says

That is, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick says,
-that he is quite willing to return them.
I thought, Sir,when I had that statement from the Minister of Trade and Commerce expressing the words of the then Chief Justice of Canada, that I had an assurance which would make it unnecessary for me to refer to this matter again.
As soon as I received that assurance from the Minister of Trade and Commerce I withdrew any objection to the voting of the $2,500 for the next fiscal year. That is to say, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, having given the assurance of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick that this $5,000 would, be returned, obtained $2,500 from this House for the purpose of paying the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice when he went overseas. Now, Sir, I am informed that that $5,000 has not been returned.
I am not a lawyer, Sir, and therefore am at a great disadvantage in arguing a case of this kind where a lawyer is concerned; but I think I have heard of such a thing as
getting money under false pretences, and I do not know but what I will have the right to have the Minister of Trade and Commerce arrested for obtaining money under false pretences, because the committee did not consent to the $2,500 being voted until he had given the assurance from the mouth of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick himself that the $5,000 would be returned.
Now, Sir, the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in discussing this matter in the House on that occasion used these words:
This item goes back to 1897. It was for travelling expenses. It appeared in the Estimates in that form until 1915 or 1916, when the item w>as changed from "travelling expenses" to "special allowances." Under this the Chief Justice received his travelling expenses to attend the court, when, in fact, he had not attended the court.
Of course, we are all aware of the fact that about the time that wording was changed it was not quite so healthy to travel across the seas as it had formerly been; the submarine menace was growing all the time. I do not know whether the former Chief Justice of Canada was a good swimmer or not, but at all events he apparently found it safer to stay on this side of the water-and he did stay on this side of the water. My contention is that, having stayed on this side of the water, he should not have drawn the $5,000 which he did draw, and which I say this House voted with the intention that it was to cover his expenses when he went overseas.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to use any strong language in referring to this matter; perhaps if I did Bourinot would step in and guarantee immunity to the gentleman to whom I refer. Bourinot does step in as a guarantor of immunity to certain men when they happen to occupy exalted positions in this country. There is more in this matter, Mr. Speaker, than the sum of $5,000. If there was one person more than another in the Dominion of Canada whose every action should have been beyond the slightest question, that person was the one holding the highest judicial position in the gift of the Dominion of Canada. I regret very much that the former Chief Justice of Canada has not lived up to his intention of last session as announced to this House by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I do not know why he has not done so, but I can only come to this conclusion, that he must be in some doubt as to whether the members of this House think he should hand this money back, and the only way that I know of to remove that doubt is to get an ex-

pression of opinion from the members of the House on this motion, and that is what I propose to do this afternoon.
How can we as representatives of the people go back to our constituents and say that we have acted here in their interests in endeavouring to put down corruption or graft of whatever form or from whatever source, if we allow a man who occupies an exalted position in the country to pocket $5,000 for which he has never given one dollar's worth of service.
A short time ago we ,were told in this House that the prison doors were yawning to receive the profiteers and grafters of Canada. Yawning precedes sleep, and I suppose that this yawning is the physical manifestation preceding a somnolent condition. We must be asleep when our money is taken improperly by some one holding a high position. We have to answer for this to our constituents. Whether a man be the Chief Justice of Canada or a peasant, he has no right to receive money for which he has given no service. What service has Sir Charles Fitzpatrick rendered to Canada for the 85,000 which he received in those two years? Some members of the Government may deem it their duty to attempt to justify the receiving of this money by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick on the ground that it was voted by Parliament. I do not think that that would be good ground for the Government to take. Why not be fair with the general public? One does not add to his status as a man by refusing to acknowledge a mistake after he has made it; he certainly does not improve his position if he converts that mistake into an offence, and that is what I would feel I was doing if I permitted this gentleman to retain $5,000 for which he has given no service to the country.
This money was voted year after year for the purpose of paying the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice of Canada when he attended the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. No objection is made to his receiving that money during the years that he did go across the seas, but during the years that he did not go, he should not have received the money. I believe that the great majority of the people will support my view that, having received the money, it is his duty to return it to the treasury of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to support the resolution, because if men holding high positions in Canada who gat money that they did not earn or obtain money under false pretences are allowed to hold the money and go scot-free, how shall we prosecute the poor

man, woman, boy or girl who steals because he or she is cold or hungry? I hope the Government will not condone any such action simply because the man in question holds a high position. Much of the unrest in Canada to-day is caused by just such actions as this. The poor man and the poor woman have the idea that because a man holds a high position he can get away with any amount of money. I hope the Government will see that this money is returned, as it should be if it was not earned.

The member for Fron-tenae (Mr. Edwards) said that the wording of the resolution appropriating these sums of money was changed in 1915. Was that change made by the Government on its own initiative, or at the request of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
(Acting
Minister of Justice): The resolution which the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) has brought to the attention of the House is of a character not only unusual, but involving upon this House a very deep responsibility. The adoption of the resolution unquestionably would very seriously challenge the personal honour of a citizen of Canada, and I am sure that no hon. member will feel like supporting it unless he is convinced that the necessity for the passing of the resolution is based upon the demands of reason and of justice.
The citizen involved is a man distinguished in our public life, I do not argue that on that account his honour should be any more jealously guarded against unjust aspersion by the House than should the honour of the most humble citizen of our country. But he is a citizen of Canada, and only upon the gravest cause should we take any step which would impugn his honour as a public man and as a citizen.
In order that the House may decide whether or not there is behind the resolution that principle which compels its adoption, that is whether or not the resolution is fair, just and right, it is necessary that I should review very hurriedly and briefly the circumstances connected with this matter. As I do so, what I say will be an answer to the question just addressed to the House by the member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx).
For some years the Appropriation Act of this Parliament contained a provision under which this House appropriated out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund, $2,500. I ask the House to note the exact wording of the resolution making this appropriation:

Travelling expenses of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick attending sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $2-,500.
In 1913-14 and 1914-15 -the vote was put through in that form, and my information is that in those years the moneys were drawn by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick only when he actually attended the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and not otherwise.
In the Appropriation Act of 1915-16, the words employed were as follows:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, $2,500.
Precisely the same words were employed in the succeeding year, 1916-17, but for the following year, 1917-18, they were changed to read as follows.
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending the sittings of the judicial committee of the Privy Council.
The House will observe that all three wordings are different. In the first, the word "allowance" is not used at all. The words employed are:
Travelling expenses .... attending sittings of the judicial committee.
In the second:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with-
And in the third:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending-.
It is of the utmost importance that the House should have clearly in mind the three distinct wordings which the Parliament of Canada employed in voting the money in question. Under the first wording, while that rwas the language of Parliament, the money was drawn by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick only during the years that he attended the sittings of the judicial committee. Under the second wording, during those two years when it read simply: "to cover expenses in connection with-" Sir Charles Fitzpatrick drew the money although, as I am informed, he did not actually attend the -sittings of the Judicial Committee. I am not sure what actually occurred in the succeeding year, but in that year he would clearly not have been entitled to draw the money unless he attended the sittings, because the wording is:
When attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Parliament is now requested to pass a resolution calling upon Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to return the money which he drew for the years 1915-16 and 1916-17. I am using only the language of moderation when I say that the House could not justify such a resolution upon any ground of its own mistake, upon any ground of wrongdoing whatsoever, unless that wrongdoing is attributable to the party who is to suffer. I am neither admitting nor denying mistakes on the part of this House. Parliament may have been mistaken, but the country must pay for the mistakes of Parliament-not a single individual. It is to the country we are responsible.
Does the minister think the Chief Justice should profit by the mistakes of Parliament?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me to finish with the subject I am discussing, I will deal with that in a moment. Parliament has, in the history of this country, made many mistakes, as has every Parliament in the history of every country. Parliament has often voted money for which the country has not received the full equivalent in value. Sometimes Parliament has undoubtedly voted money for which the country has received no equivalent in value, and many instances could be cited of votes and actions on the part of this House where the country has not received full consideration for the money voted. We might, for example, go back to contracts made by this country in days gone by, contracts which to-day would, I think, by any dispassionate observer, be freely declared to have been improvident contracts on the part of this country, contracts by which this country suffered and in respect of which this country did not re-, ceive anything like the equivalent in value,, and there have been instances in which-no value whatever was received for the money voted. But in those cases I do not think Parliament would, for a moment, consider visiting the injury upon those, who were parties to the contract. Suppose,, for example, we were to go back to a contract made in 1908 and refuse to-day on behalf of the citizens of this country to-recognize the legal rights that arose by virtue of that contract, such a course would1 be indefensible. I think, therefore, I am on safe and impregnable ground in asserting that whether Parliament made an error or not is not the question now. The question now is whether or not Parliament is justified in asking a man who, as a result of this appropriation, received money from this country, to return that money to the

treasury of Canada. Parliament could pass such a resolution and could take that position only if the party receiving the money should not in honour have taken it, was not entitled to it, or used any dishonourable means to get it; if, in a word, circumstances of dishonour attached to the receiving itself. Is that the case here? What was the intent of Parliament in voting the money? What must Parliament now say frankly was its intent in voting the money in these words? It is to be noted that a change was made in the wording. The old language which made the resolution apply only if .Sir Charles attended, and only for travelling expenses, was abandoned, and Parliament, rightly or wrongly, employed other language instead, voting that money as a special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee. Parliament has, in other cases, employed similar language. Parliament employed similar language even in the case of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick himself, in connection with his duties as administrator in -the absence of the Governor General. The ianguage in that case is:	.
Special allowance to the Chief Justice of the [DOT]Supreme Court of Canada to cover travelling and other expenses in connection wjith his services while acting as deputy to His Excellency the Governor General.
My information with regard to the paying out and receiving of the latter money voted is that such was done in exactly the same way as in the case of the money paid out and' received in connection with the appropriation now under discussion. My information is further that that language was employed in connection with the appropriation in question prior to the use of it in the present case. The question arises: Must Parliament now take the position of saying that, in changing its language and in using the language there employed, it did not intend that money to be drawn in the same way as in the previous case when the same precise words were used, but only when actual attendance on the Judicial Committee took place?
Had Sir Charles Fitzpatrick any other duties than going overseas in connection w'ith the Privy Council?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not hear the question of my hon. friend1.

Had Sir Charles Fitzpatrick any duties that he could perform otherwise than by going overseas for the purpose?
{Mr. Meighen.]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am not aware that he had. I see the point my hon. friend is making. The information given to me by the Department of Justice is that this allowance in connection with acting as deputy to the Governor General, has always been paid without inquiry at all as to whether any expenses were in fact incurred. This appropriation was in the same language, and evidently
3	p.m. was intended by Parliament in the same way. As to whether in the present instance consideration for the appropriation was actually given or not, it is quite true the same consideration could not be said to have been given as if Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had attended. But similarly, under the other vote, it is quite clear there might be cases,-I do not know whether there were or not,-in which it was not actually necessary for the Chief Justice of Canada to act as administrator of this country. It must, however, be kept in mind that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had to hold himself in readiness to go overseas, and it can quite forcibly be argued that the intention of Parliament was that an allowance should be made to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick either for attending, or in years when he did not attend, for holding himself in readiness. Before Parliament could be justified in passing a resolution which challenges the honour of a respected citizen of this country, Parliament should be fully convinced that there was moral wrongdoing on the part of the receiver of that money in taking the money so voted by Parliament under that wording, and it must remember that the same wording had been employed in other cases; and that no such course has ever previously been pursued.

Was the wording under which this money was paid out changed previously to the first year that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick did not attend the sittings, or at the end of the first year that he did not attend?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My information is that the first year that he did not go, but accepted the money, was subsequent to the change in wording. I am concerned with the legal aspect alone. My duty merely is to state the circumstances, and to ask Parliament to consider the principle which should inspire us in determining this question, and to point out that we should not be swerved from that principle by any but vital considerations, because, if there is one thing more vital than another it is that the Parliament of this country shall not lightly

and for insufficient cause challenge the integrity of a citizen of this country.
(Mr. DENIS: The minister has pointed out the three different wordings in the Estimates. I should like to know whether the money was voted, no matter what the wording may have been, with the specific object and intent of paying the travelling expenses of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The intent of the vote must be gathered from the wording of the vote itself. The intent in other cases of similar wording has been as actually shown by the result-the paying of the money, although the attendance did not necessarily take place.

I think it is merely playing upon words to say that the Chief Justice should have drawn the money when he was not put to the expense of attendiing the sittings of the Privy Council. It seems evident from the three wordings that this money was voted for the specific purpose of defraying the expenses of the trip overseas and the stay in London of the Chief Justice, in order that he might attend the sittings of the Privy Council. I think it would have been preferable if the Chief Justice had been obliged to file a monthly account of his expenses, just as the judges have to do under the. Judges' Act. However, Parliament decided to vote a lump sum, but it was certainly the intention of Parliament that this sum was for defraying the expenses of the Chief Justice while attending the sittings of the Privy Council, and the Chief Justice should have known that that was the intention of Parliament. I should like to know whether the wording of the resolution was changed by the Government with or without a request from the Chief Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know of no request.
What explanation has the minister to make with regard to the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that this money would be returned by the Chief Justice?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps I should read his exact words. On Page 2479 of last year's Hansard, in answer to a question, the Minister of Trade and Commerce read a letter from Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, the last paragraph of which reads as follows:-
If, however, it is now considered that the intentions of Parliament have been misunderstood I can only say that I shall be prepared to return the amount of the allowance received during the two years in question. My first object is to avoid all personal embarrassment to you.
In effeot, that means that if Parliament -or the Government, I presume, to whom he was addressing the letter-considered that he had drawn that money against the intention of Parliament he was prepared to return it.
That is not the paragraph to which my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin) refers.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must remind hon. members that the House is in committee, and that the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) has the floor.

The resolution in the Estimates of 1915-16 uses the word "expenses." It says: "Special allowance to cover expenses in connection with the sittings of the Privy Council." The wording of the resolution of the following year is a little different, because the words "when attending" are added. But both resolutions contain the word "expenses."
I say that if the Chief Justice did not attend the sittings the money should not have been paid; I think the Department of Justice was negligent in not requiring a certificate showing the expenses incurred before paying the money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Department of Justice does not pay the money.
Under the Judges' Act, the cheques are paid by the Justice Department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

The certificates, at all
events, go to that department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Do they go to the Auditor General?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, the cheques.

Then the Auditor General should have required a certificate that the Chief Justice had attended the sittings of the Privy Council. We have been paying money for which we have received no consideration. According to law, there must be consideration in every contract. If you give a promissory note, and no consideration passes, and you are sued for non-payment, you cannot be made to pay because there was no consideration. In this particular case, there might be difficulty in getting back the money. The minister says that Parliament made a mistake. I do not

admit that Parliament made a mistake. I think the intention of Parliament was clearly expressed by the word " expenses," and I say that the Government was negligent in paying this money. I understand that last spring Sir Charles Fitzpatrick offered to return the money, and I certainly think it is the, duty of the Government to request a refund of the amounts paid for which there was no consideration given. The Government are the trustees of the people, and they should take care of the people's money which is entrusted to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quite agree with the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), that the House should give most earnest consideration to this matteT and have all the facts before it so far as possible, before supporting this resolution. I have given the question some attention by way of making careful inquiry in my own department and in the Department of the Privy Council with a view to ascertaining precisely what happened in connection with the changed wording in the Estimates of 1915-16. The Acting Minister of Justice has referred to the payment of the special allowance by the Finance Department upon the requisition of the Department of the Privy Council, of which the Prime Minister of Canada is the head.
As a result of my inquiry I have come to the conclusion that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick accepted this money in entire good faith, and I feel bound to say so to this House. I asked the Deputy Minister of Finance (Mr. T. C. Boville) for a statement of the matter which he has presented to me in a memorandum that reads as follows:
Department of Finance, Ottawa, Canada, March 26, 1919. Memorandum respecting Sir Charles Fitzpatrick.
In 1912-13 the sum of $2,000 iwas voted under the heading " Miscellaneous '' for
"Travelling expenses to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council '[DOT]
The sum of $2,500 was voted in each of the years 1913-14 and 1914-15 in the same wording for the service in those years.
The amount for* 1912-13 was paid in two sums.
In 1913-14 the vote was not expended.
The amount in 1914-15 was paid' in one sum on June 15, 1914.
In these three years it will be noticed that the allowance was to cover the travelling expenses of Sir Charles when attending the sittings of the committee.
When the estimates for 1916 were toeing prepared the wording of the item was changed so as to read,
"Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council."
This change in the wording of the vote was conveyed to the undersigned in January, 1915, toy the Secretary to the Prime Minister who asked

that the vote be amended to read in the same way as the vote for expenses in connection with the services of the Deputy of the Governor General, which, being in the nature of a special allowance, was paid monthly.
The effect of this change in the wording of the vote was to convert what had hitherto been a vote for travelling expenses for Sir Charles when attending the Committee into a grant which might he paid to him apart altogether from his attendance on the committee.
The expenditure of the vote naturally fell under the administration of the Privy Council Office, and was applied for month toy month hy that office in the ordinary process through the office of the Auditor General, who interpreted the vote as above, and authorized the payment month toy month. The allowance was so paid during the years 1915-16 and 1916-17. Thereafter it was changed to read,
" Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending the sittings of Judicial Committee of the Privy Council."
(Sgd.) T. C. Btoville.
Now, a question has been raised as to what was the intention of Parliament and of the Government in this matter. I do not recollect distinctly concerning the change that was made; it is not in my memory that the matter was specially called to my attention at that time. I cannot say what the intentions of Parliament were, but of course those intentions would be gathered from the language in which Parliament expressed _ itself; and that language was contained in the Estimate, which my deputy points out was handed to him by the private secretary of the Prime Minister. I think it must be admitted that the deliberate change in the wording must have been intended to have some significance, else why would it have been made? I would ask Die House to note that the item deliberately omitted the words "attending sittings," which had appeared in previous years as a limitation on the use of the amount, and also the qualifying word "travelling," which had formerly appeared in connection with the word "expenses."
I would like the minister to observe that in the year 1916 the word-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member may rise to ask a question with the permission of the hon. member who has the floor, but for no other purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The memorandum which I have for the year 1916 is this: "Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses-"
Is it for the next year?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question is raised whether, if the word "expenses"

occurred in the item, the money could be paid unless the expenses had been actually incurred and vouched for. On a certain assumption it undoubtedly could. It might have been the intention of those responsible for the change in the item that the vote should be an average vote of $2,500 per year for expenses. If the expenses exceeded the amount the Government would vote no more, and if they fell below the amount it would still be paid. Now, I would draw t)he attention of the House to what the late Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said respecting this matter during last session. He was dealing with the question of a vote which purported to cover expenses and yet which was paid to the party to whom the money was voted, irrespective of whether or not the actual expenditure had been incurred. At page 2599 of last year's Hansard (unrevised) the late leader of the Opposition is reported as follows:
This special allowance to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court to pay his travelling and other expenses while attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council goes back to the days when Sir Oliver Mowat was Minister of Justice. At that time the then Chief Justice, Sir Henry Strong, went to England, to sit as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council under an Act which had been passed by the Imperial Parliament inviting judges of colonial courts to sit with the members of the Judicial Committee. Their services were required especially for colonial cases. The Government of that day, at the instance of Sir Oliver Mowat, placed an item in the Estimates of $2,500 to cover the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice. I do not remember the exact wording of the item, but it was to pay the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice while attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, or some such wording as that. This item goes back to 1897. It was for travelling expenses. It appeared in the Estimates in that form until 1915 or 1916, when the item was changed from " travelling expenses "to " special allowance." Why this change was made from "Travelling expenses" to "Special allowance" I do not knoiw.
Then further on the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:-
It so happened that in one or two years the Chief Justice was not called upon to attend a sitting of the Judicial Committee, and in those years he had received the money. If the item had been left as it was before with the wording " travelling expenses " the money could only have been paid when there were travelling expenses, but it was changed to " special allowance," and there the matter stands to-day.
The position therefore is that the Government, which is responsible for the bringing down of the Estimates, changed the wording which had prevailed up to 1915-16, and which covered the travelling expenses of the Chief Justice when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council to special allowance to cover expenses. I am advised, and believe, that the payment which was made by the Finance Department was legally and regularly made. That was the view of the Auditor General, who authorized the payment, and it was the view of the Privy Council officials who obtained the money from the Finance Department. iMy own view is-although I do not recollect the matter distinctly, I have had a good deal on my mind since 1915- that it was the intention that that language should be changed so as to authorize the payment to Sir (Charles Fitzpatrick month by month. I do not pretend to say what was in the minds of other members of the Government, but reviewing the situation in the light of what I am informed by the responsible officials was done-the change in language which was made at the instance of the private secretary to the Prime Minister-I am of the opinion that the intention was to assimilate, or practically assimilate, this to the language of the vote to the Deputy Governor, and that the money was paid out by the Government and received by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick on that basis. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick received those payments monthly. He might have gone overseas in September, having received monthly payments from the end of March, or the first of April rather, the beginning of the fiscal year, up to that time, and continued to receive the monthly payments after that. His expenses might have been more than $2,500. If they had been, he would not have been entitled to receive any money in excess of the $2,500 which was specially voted. If, on the other hand, he did not go Overseas, then he was not to account for the money. Now, I do not say that that was the intention of the Government, or of any members of the Government, because my recollection of the circumstances is imperfect, but it is a possible explanation; and I cannot understand why the language of the item was changed from what it was in 1914-15 to what it was in 1915-16 unless there had been the intention to make a change. Why would the change have been made in the language if there was no intention of change? I am driven to the conclusion-
To get the appropriation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

C. Fitzpatrick.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Sir iSAM HUGHES:	To what officials

I presume he
would mean the officials who had to do with the paying out of the money, including the Auditor General. Now, permit me to make my position clear. I understood from the memorandum which the Acting Prime Minister read that the wording of this vote was changed in 1911?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
If Sir Charles Fitzpatrick drew money from the first of April, 1915, to the first of April, 1916, he did so for at least one year under the old wording?
iSir THOMAS WHITE: I think not, because the Estimates are voted in advance.
Mr. C A. GAUVREAU (Temiscouta): When the Chief Justice of Canada was empowered to sit on the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council the wording of the estimate to cover his expenses was "travelling expenses." It was discussed between the Minister of Justice and Sir Charles Fitzpatrick that perhaps some day he would not be obliged to go, but that he would lit' to draw rthe money all the same. Then it was understood that the Minister of Justice would change the phraseology of the item under which, instead of "travelling expenses" the word "allowance" was used. The Minister of Justice adopted that word because he was a little scared that some of his best friends, like the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) would kick against the vote. Thus under the term "allowance" even if the Chief Justice did not attend the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council he could draw the money voted. This is the explanation I have to give to the House.
Mr. W. F. NICKLt; (Kingston):	Mr. Speaker, I quite agree with what the Acting Minister of Justice says, that the matter under discussion this afternoon should be approached with all the seriousness that this House can muster, because if the House should decide-and certainly no matter whether the House decides or not-that this money should be repaid, there is a certain reflection on the former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court in the fact of this discussion taking place this afternoon. The Acting Minister of Justice says that we should be particularly careful because the reputation of a man who occupies, and has occupied, a particularly high place in Canadian national life is under review. But I would draw the attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that it was thought that Caesar's wife should

be beyond suspicion because she was Caesar's wife, and those who occupy high positions should be particularly careful to see that not even the shadow of a suspicion is cast over their lives, and certainly the fountain of justice should be careful to see that the waters of justice are in no way discoloured.
I do not agree with the Acting iMinister of Justice when he says that the passing of this resolution will necessarily mean that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick committed a moral wrong when he took the money. I am sure the Acting Minister of Justice feels, as does every member of this House, that it would be a ridiculous contention, a contention that no court would uphold, that no lawyer would endeavour to sustain, that the misreading of an Act of Parliament-not intentionally misread, but misread in an honest belief-would be considered as fraudulent intent as distinct from misapprehension I am quite prepared to admit that if the former Chief Justice of the Supreme Court knew that the estimate, which is in effect a statute, did not anid could not have carried the meaning that he put into it, then it was a fraudulent thing for him to have taken the money, and morally wrong. But if the Chief Justice believed that he had a right to take the money, then this House in asking him to return it is not saying that he did that which was in itself morally wrong, but is taking him at his own word when he told us in the letter to the Prime Minister, read by the Minister of Trade and Commerce last session, that if his view of the intention of Parliament was mistaken he was prepared to return the money to this House and to the country. And it is on that argument in part that I purpose this afternoon to direct my remarks.
What was the intention of Parliament? The Acting Minister of Justice says that that is the test which must be applied in discussing and deciding this matter. The Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) takes practically the same point of view. How, what was the intention of Parliament, and how are we to reach a conclusion as to what it was? I would like to direct the attention of the House to this matter in some detail, because, as I said, Sir, in rising, this is an important matter- it is a matter that probably will have a wider bearing than those of us who are taking part" in this discussion this afternoon have any idea. For I am satisfied that from one end of the country to the other the public have their eye on this discussion and on this vote. That is the conclusion I have reached from what I have
heard in my own constituency and the questions that have been asked me in reference to the matter.
The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier told the House that in 1897-if my memory of dates does not fail me-the original vote was passed for the purpose of allowing the late Chief Justice Strong of the Supreme Court to go to England and attend the Privy Council. Regardless of what the original intention of the vote was, the vote from 1907 until 1914 was couched in this language:
Travelling expenses of Sir H. E, Tasohereau-
Or Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, as the case might be.
*-attending sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
That contemplated a journey being taken by the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and it contemplated his expenses being paid in reference to that journey. In 1911 that was the form of the vote, in 1912 it was the same, the same again in 1913, and the same language Was used in 1914. In 1915 the vote was made to read as follows, and it will be found as item 320 of that year's Estimates:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
There was a change in the language, certain words were omitted from this vote, as the Acting Minister of Justice has said, and there was a change in the phraseology in that the words " attending sittings of the Judicial Committee " were left out.
How are you going to judge what was the intention of Parliament when that vote came before it? Now, Sir, the position I am taking this afternoon J am taking as having been a member of the House when that vote went through. If it went through and I misunderstood what the House meant, then I am prepared to take the responsibility that must be mine, because even if I were desirous of doing so I cannot evade it. But as the Acting Minister of Justice says, the question is: What wat the intention of Parliament?
You can tell the way the wind blown very often by the direction of the smoke from the chimney tops, and you can tell the direction of the current by the straws that float upon the surface of the water, and I would draw the attention of this House to the fact that in the Sessional Papers of 1915 at page 92 this language is found:	.
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

Then there follow two perpendicular parallel columns, the first column headed 1914-1915 and below that the sum of $2,500; and the next column headed 1915-1916 and below it another sum of $2,500. That means to you, Sir, and to me and to every member of this House that when these Estimates were brought in the apparent intention was not that there was to be a new vote for a totally different thing, but that the old vote was being revoted and the purpose of the vote for 1914-1915 was being carried forward in 1915-19161
But, Sir, I am not going to stop at that. The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) often asks questions. In 1915 on the 19th day of March when he asked a question in this House, I very much doubt, Sir, if he understood how much light it might throw on the discussion that is taking place this affernoon. In column 1250 of Hansard for 1915 the following appears:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee ot the Privy Council, $2,500.
How many trips to London does the Chief Justice make each year?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
He usually goes twice, so far as my memory serves me.
Notice the language, Sir. In answer to that question the right hon. the leader of the Government did not say that Sir Charles Fizpatrick went twice; the member for Prescott did not ask how many times Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had been in the habit of going to London, he asked the Prime Minister: "How many trips to London 'does' the Chief Justice make each year." "Does" is the present tense; it means something that is or is to be done. Sir Robert Borden answered:	"He usually
goes twice, so far as my memory serves me," That implied that the practice had been that the Chief Justice went twice to England, but the question of the member for Prescott and the answer of the Prime Minister, taken in conjunction with the fact to which I have just referred, certainly meant that this House had reason to suppose-and I as a member of this House did suppose-that that $2,500 was being voted for identically the same purpose as the votes which had been passed from 1911 until that year-and these are the years that I have been in this House.
Let us go further. I realized that it was a question that should be considered seriously, and after the member for Frontenac first introduced the subject into the House I was not satisfied with the answers given by the members of the Government who replied to the question or with the answers

given to the public by the Chief Justice through the press. I placed on Hansard a series of questions, which I propose to read to the House,, together with the answers given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). If you turn' to Hansard of 1918, pages 2478 and 2479, you will find the following:

1. Is it the intention of the Government, in the event of voluntary repayment not being made by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick of the $5,000 paid to him to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for the fiscal years 1915-1916 and 1916-1917, and not incurred nor disbursed, to take steps to recover this amount?
To which the answer was:
1. No. In view of criticism made in the House of Commons, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has offered to return the amount mentioned although he strongly urges that he is legally entitled thereto under the Act of Parliament which authorized the payment. In this opinion the Department of Finance and the Auditor General concur.
The second question was: "If not, w'hy not?" To which the answer was: "Answered by No. 1." The third question was:
3. Does the explanation given by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick in the memorandum read to the House by the Prime Minister on May 15, for the acceptance of the said sum, express the practice and policy of the Government?
To which the following answer was given:
3. The explanation referred to as given by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick does not purport to express any practice or policy on the part of the Government but merely the views of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick as to the effect of the legislation governing the payment of the allowance and his rights thereunder. In this connection the following additional letter has been received by the Prime Minister from Sir Charles Fitzpatrick :
"My Dear Prime Minister,-May I trouble you again with reference to the payments made to me as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council and as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General, to which objection has been taken by two or three members of the House of Commons as having been accepted by me contrary to the terms of the Parliamentary appropriation which authorized them.
"Dealing first with the 'special allowance to the Chief Justice to cover travelling and other expenses in connection with his services while acting as Deputy to His Excellency the Governor General' : as you are aware, during the early years of Confederation, the rule assigned to the Administrator one-half of the Governor General's salary. Subsequently this provision was considered neither jusit nor advantageous when applied to a Governor General when absent from his Government for a brief period either on leave or on the public service. As a result the emolument was reduced, about 1875, from one-half to one-fourth. In 1906 the question was again reconsidered and it was then decided that it did^not comport with the dignity of the high

office of Representative of the Sovereign in this country to make abatements of his salary and the regulations which authorized them were revised' so as to provide that in case the Governor General of Canada was absent for a period of thirty days consecutively there should be no reduction of his salary for reason of such absence. In 1907, another change was made which provides that in any case of absence although exceeding thirty days no deduction should be made for the period of twenty-nine days.
"Subsequently it was thought proper that the Administrator should receive ia fixed sum of $2,500 in lieu of those allowances. At a later date the Government thought proper to increase this allowance from $2,500 to $5,000. That this latter amount was voted with the sanation and approval of Parliament cannot be doubted. For two years, the amount was put in the estimates and voted in the regular way and paid without protest. In the estimates for 1917-18 as originally brought down that special allowance was reduced to $2,500, but on the 19th September, 1917, as will be seen on reference to Hansard, p. 6049, an item was introduced in the supplementary estimates 'to complete the special allowance for the Chief Justice so as to make it equal to that allowed the previous years, $5,000.' This did not pass unnoticed. Mr. Edwards, M.P., drew attention to this increase and asked for an explanation, which explanation was given by Mr. Reid, the minister in charge of the estimates, who said it had always been the custom to pay this amount to the Chief Justice, 'and the Government feel that as he has been receiving $5,0'00 for the position it is hardly fair to reduce it at the present time.' It was alsd intimated that the payment wais made partly for the purpose of implementing the salary of the Chief Justice. Although the allowance is made to me personally I have always paid over the proportion due to the senior puisne judge of this court who has acted as administrator during my absence.
"Dealing now with the two payments of $2,6 00 each, made to me as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, one during the fiscal year 1915-16 and the other during the fiscal year 1917-18.
"The amounts in question were voted by Parliament as 'special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to oover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council'- the provision in regard to 'travelling expenses' attending sittings of the Judicial Committee, which was a condition of payment in previous years, having been Intentionally omitted-and were paid in monthly instalments on application from the Privy Council office to the Auditor General who evidently certified in the usual course that the cheques asked for might be properly issued by the Finance Department.
"I perhaps never gave the matter as much consideration as I ought to have done but my view was that an allowance to cover expenses differed from the payment of actual expenses and was at any rate not dependent on their being incurred in any particular period."
Just a commient in passing. If the late Chief Justice of the Supreme Court admits that there was -a condition precedent that the expenses should he incurred in some particular period, then, to use a slang expression, it was up to the Chief Justice to
show that he incurred expenses at some particular time that exhausted the money for which this vote was made. The letter continues:
"The expenses of attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee must always vary with the length of the sittings and of course attendance is not necessarily confined to one sitting in the year. If there were more than one attendance in any one year the expenses would certainly exceed the allowance.
"The war has brought about an exceptional state of things. Though I have offered each year to go over to assist at the sittings of the committee I have been advised that it was not considered necessary to ask me to do so under the conditions actually obtaining.
"The fact that this exceptional position had continued for two years no doubt properly called for an alteration in the vote and this was made for the fiscal year 1917-1918.
"I do not think that any representation of mine can be responsible for the view which I suppose both the Auditor General and the Finance Department must have held that the payments could be properly made.
"If, however, it is now considered that the intentions of Parliament have been misunderstood

I commend this remark to the careful consideration of the Acting Minister of Justice and of the Acting Prime Minister. I shall r<ead it again from the beginning, so that it may not escape their attention:
"If however, it is now considered- '
" Now " must mean the present time. (Reading):
-"that the intentions of Parliament-
That is, the intention of this institution, which is made up of its components parts called " members."	s
-"have been misunderstood-
That is, if th.e intention of members of Parliament have been misunderstood.
-"I can only say that I shall he prepared to return the amount of the allowance received during the two years in question. My first object is to avoid all personal embarrassment to you.
"Yours very truly,
"C. Fitzpatrick."
The next question I asked was:
4. Are payments of the nature of those referred to in the statement of Sir Charles made without the concurrence or consent of the Auditor General?
To which the answer was:
No. The allowances in question were drawn with the concurrence of the Auditor General of the Department of Finance.
The last question was:
If so. why?
The answer was:
Answered by No. 4.

As I have said, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has, in that letter, offered to return the money if the intention of Parliament has been misunderstood, and, I think, I have shown on general principles that the intention of Parliament was misunderstood in this respect, that the answer of the Prime Minister to the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) indicated the members believed the vote was for expenses to be incurred. I think it is also abundantly clear, from the manner in which the vote was put in the Estimates, that the intention was not to direct the attention of Parliament that this was in any way a different appropriation. I want, however, to go just a little further than that. I want to endeavour to deal with this question as a matter of law. There is a fairly celebrated case from British Columbia called Bex versus Clement, where a judge, Mr. Justice Clement, got into considerable difficulty^ because he took a travelling allowance to which he was found not to be entitled, and as far as my inquiry has enabled me to find a precedent as to the meaning of the word " allowance," that case is the best guide I have been able to secure. I want to be quite frank with the House. As I said in rising, I approached this question from the point of view of a member of Parliament sincerely desirous of doing his duty. My first angle of approach was this-and I do not want to make myself out as being any better than any other man, because the chances are I am not,-I wanted to catch the spirit of the House, and I said to myself: What would I have done if that money had been offered to me? And I am not going to answer that question. Then I said: What would other members have done if that money had been offered to them? And I have asked, not one, but half a dozen members of this House, some professional men, some business men, some men on the farm, and they have all said: We do not think we should have taken it; the intention was that the Chief Justice should have attended the sittings, or else not have drawn the money. Satisfying myself, therefore, as to what I might call the common-place point of view of the ordinary man on the street, I turned to this question: What is the law on the matter? What are those special allowances? Are they increases in emoluments or are they indemnities? Are they intended to add something indirectly to a man's salary, or was it the intention to defray 4 p.m. expenses honestly incurred? I set out to find a precedent, be-
cause, as you know, Sir, when lawyers are in doubt on a point, they endeavour to find a case to elucidate their arguments. 1 found the case which I have mentioned, Rex versus Clements, heard in the Exchequer Court of Canada, as reported in the Canada Law Journal, volume 50, at page 67, and on appeal, taken to the Supreme Court by Mr. Justice Clement, the Supreme Court sustaining the findings of the court below, as to the meaning of allowance.
Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was a member of the Supreme Court.

While it is quite true that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was a member of the Supreme Court at the time That judgment was given, my recollection is-and I want to be quite fair to His Lordship-that he did not give a judgment. The case was apparently argued before the other members of the court. As regards the interpretation of the law; the provision in the Judges' Act is not on all fours with the provision,in the Estimates. The provision in the Judges' Act to which I have referred reads:
There shall be paid for travelling allowances-
Jn the Estimates of 1915 the wording is " special allowances "-
-to each judge, whether of a superior or county court, and to each local judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court, except as in this section otherwise provided, in addition to his moving or transportation expenses, the sum of six dollars for each day, including necessary days of travel going and returning, during which he is attending as such judge in court or chambers at any place other than that at which he is by law obliged to reside: Provided that:-
(a) No judge shall receive any travelling allowance for attending in court or chambers at the place where he resides.
The facte >are briefly these. Mr. Justice Clement h;ad been living at Grand Forks and he mowed to Vancouver. When the question arose as to where his residence was, he alleged that he had a technical residence at Grand Forks, but th'e court held that, in the terms of the statute, his residence was at Vancouver, and that he was, therefore, not entitled to the $6 a day mentioned in the statutes. But I want to emphasize this, that there was the " tail," if I may so express it to the section of the statute, stating definitely:
No judge shall receive any travelling allowance for attending in court or chambers at the place where he resides.
This made it abundantly clear that if a judge resided in the place where he at-

tended court, he could not draw the $6 a day. But I quote from the case-and I do not want to obscure my argument-for the purpose of giving -a judicial interpretation to the word " allowances." The caste came first before Mr. Justice Cassels of the Exchequer Court, and Me said:
Now it seems to me too clear for any reasonable doubt that this statute only contemplates an indemnity to the judge for expenses he is put to in travelling from and to his place of residence. It never could have been intended as a statute to augment the salary prescribed by statute. The sole legal question is where was the place of residence of the defendant as contemplated by the statute during the time the charges in question were made'?
Mr. Justice Cassels found that, the place of residence was Vancouver, and he, therefore, disallowed the charge of $6 a day. The case went to the 'Supreme Court (see Western Weekly Report, Vol. VI, page 414), and Mr Justice Duff, Mr. Justice Anglin and Mr. Justice Idington gave a decision. Mr. Justice Anglin -see Western Weekly Report, Vol. VI, page 428-said:
I agree with Mr. Justice Cassels that the purpose of this section was not to augment a judge's salary, but to indemnify him for outlay occasioned by travelling and absence from the place where he resides in the discharge of his duties.
The Supreme Court gave judgment confirming the point that the allowance was an indemnity for travelling expenses incurred, and that His Lordship, Mr. Justice Clement, was not entitled to draw his $6 a day during the time that he was in Vancouver. I, therefore, think that authority proves quite conclusively that the word "allowance" as used in a statute means compensation for something done or to be done on indemnity against expenses. I am forced to the ponclusion that the expression "special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council," as used in the Estimates of 1915, and taken in conjunction with the method of the vote, as well as the remarks of Sir Robert Borden as elicited by the questions of Mr. Proulx, means that the allowance was given in condition that the expenses were incurred, and that His Lordship attended the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Will my hon. friend tell me how proceedings in the Clement case were instituted?

Speaking from memory, a motion was passed in the Legislature of British Columbia, of which the Dominion Government apparently took notice, and an
action was launched to recover from Mr. Justice Clement the money which it was alleged had been improperly paid to him.
Does my hon. friend not think that precedents are good procedure, as well as law?

If the hon. member will give me the opportunity 1 hope to prove to him before I get through why the procedure he suggests is not wise. The hon. leader of the Opposition is an ex-judge, with a reputation of knowing the law. He ought to know, and does know, that we lawyers make a very sharp distinction between mistakes in law and mistakes in fact. I do not believe he will dispute my law this afternoon when I state that if a mistake at law is made, you cannot recover money from a man to whom it has been paid through that mistake. My hon. friend nods his head; I therefore assume that he assents to the proposition that I. have enunciated. But if a mistake in fact has been the cause of money being paid out in error, then the money may be recovered. Now the question is, was there a mistake in fact in this case? Was this money paid to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick under a mistake as to the facts underlying the payment? Were those who paid over the money under the impression that the Chief Justice had been to England? The Acting Prime Minister has told us this afternoon that those who paid over the money were under no mistake as to the facts; they knew Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had not been to England. There was no misrepresentation on the part of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick; he did not pretend he had been to England; it was known that he was in Canada. And the leader of the Opposition has the temerity to rise and ask me: Is not legal procedure just as good in this case as it was in the Clement case? He knows perfectly well that if an action were launched in the courts it would be ineffectual, because this Parliament, represented by the Department of Justice, would be compelled to admit that they knew that the Chief Justice had not been overseas; they could not show that any representation to the contrary had been made, and on the very principle of law which I have just enunciated and to which my hon. friend has assented, the money could not be collected as a matter of law. We are not discussing these votes in any narrow, legal way, but on the broad ground of national honesty and righteousness, if I may say so.
I wish to direct a few remarks to another phase of this question. I want to say that whoever drafted Sir Charles Fitzpat-

rick's letter is a marvellous draughtsman. It is as subtly drawn a document-I did not say corruptly-as the pen of a man could draw. I want to read my questions and the answers again, because the leader of the Opposition has directed my attention to a certain point:
1. Is it the intention of the Government, in the event of voluntary repayment not being
made	to take steps to recover this
amount?

1. No. In view of criticism made in the House of Commons, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has offered to return the amount mentioned although he strongly urges-
Strongly urges what? Not that he was entitled to receive the money, but:

that he is legally entitled thereto.
What does legally entitled thereto mean? It has a double-barrelled meaning. It may mean, entitled to receive or entitled to retain. I am quite prepared to admit that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is legally entitled to retain the money, because possession is nine-tenths of the law, and self-possession the other one-tenth. But the Chief Justice does not say that he is entitled to the money. He qualifies his answer by saying "he is 'legally' entitled thereto." What does " legally entitled " mean, to the man who knows his law? It means that if you enter the courts of law, with their rules and precedents, you could not recover the money as there had been no mistake of fact influencing payment. He qualifies the word " entitled " by the word " legally," and the hon. member knows that the Chief Justice is legally entitled to retain that money because he has got it, and we cannot show there was any mistake in fact.
Let us look a bit further. I was not as subtle in drawing those questions as I should have been, but I have learned since. One question I asked was this:
Are payments of the nature of those referred to in the statement of Sir Charles made without the concurrence or consent of the Auditor General?
I made a slip when I used the word "concurrence." I should have used the word "certificate," but I did not. In answer to my question Sir George Foster replied:
These moneys were paid in monthly instalments on application from the Privy Council office to the Auditor Genera], who evidently certified-
He does not say "who certified in the usual way," but he uses the word "evidently." Evidently from what? Evidently because the money was paid over. I understood the Acting Prime Minister to say this

afternoon that the items were never certified but went through the ordinary course, and the Acting Minister of Justice says: This House is estopped this afternoon because the payments went through in the ordinary course. I ask him, what do we private members know as to how items are paid?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
please quote me correctly. I never made any such statement.

I have no desire to misquote him. If my hon. friend did not say that, I must have taken down incorrectly what he said. If we were estopped, it would mean that we were absolutely prevented from going further at law. But I say this House is not estopped-and I am using the word not in its narrow, legal sense, hut in a different sense altogether- I say we are not reasonably prevented in common sense and decency from inquiring into this matter-

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I say the same too.

-and taking a vote on it, simply because payments were made in the ordinary course of which we knew nothing.
There is one other point to which I wish to draw attention. I am going to vote for this resolution for three reasons: First, because as a member of Parliament I certainly never intended, and I do not think Parliament intended-I do not know what the Government intended-to increase Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's salary by $2,500 in the years 1915, 1916 and 1917, when we were preaching economy and thrift from the housetops. If the House did intend that, the members who were present in 1915, 1916 and 1917 must testify their intention by their votes.
What is his salary?

I am not discussing his salary. I do not care whether his salary is $100,000 or $100. It is purely a question of principle, and I approach it from that standpoint.
The Acting Prime Minister read a telegram this afternoon which purported to be a repetition of the offer made by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to this House through the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) in 1918, and I shall show how vastly different are the two messages of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, and what a wide divergence there is between the principles enunciated in 1918 and those enunciated by telegraph this afternoon. If those hon. members who are not lawyers will listen

carefully and bear in mind what I said a few moments ago as to the difference between a matter of law and a matter of fact, they will perceive the subtlety that lurks in the message which we have heard this afternoon. In the year 1918 Sir Charles Fitzpatrick said this: "If, however it is now considered"-Let us give the benefit of the doubt, Mr. Speaker, he may mean, considered by the Government, or by the House, but he admits that the intention of Parliament should be accepted-"if it is now considered that the intentions of Parliament have been misunderstood, I can only say that I shall be prepared to return the amount of the allowance received during the two years in question." That, I take it, is tantamount to saying: "If Parliament says the money should be returned I bow to the judgment of those who voted the money and return it to the country, as Parliament thinks it should be returned; I took the money believing I had a legal right to it, but if Parliament thinks otherwise, I am prepared to accept its decision." The Acting Prime Minister read a telegram this afternoon in which Sir Charles Fitzpatrick says: "You are at liberty to state, when Mr. Edwards moves his resolution, that I adhere to the explanation given in my letter to Sir Robert Borden and which was read in the House last session in answer to Mr. Nickle's questions." What does he adhere to? He adheres to his explanation; but he makes a radical departure from his offer of 1918 to return the money if Parliament asked for its return. On March 26, 1919, there is no such offer.
