The offer now, I repeat, is in effect this: That if the Government, or any of the officials through whom the money was paid will say that there is any doubt as to the regularity or legality of such payment, he is prepared to return the money. In one case he gives the positive assurance that he will return the money if Parliament expressess a desire that it shall be returned owing to a misunderstanding of its intentions. In the other case he falls back on the narrow legalism, "I will return it if you can show by law that I should not have received it or retained it." The two positions, Sir, are as far apart as the poles.
Now, I have spoken longer than was my intention, and I should not have gone as fully into the matter as I have done had it not been for the objection of the leader of the Opposition. I think that this is a question on which we should have a vote this afternoon entirely on principle. The hon. member will either vote this after-55
noon that this money shall be returned because Parliament never intended that it should have been received by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick unless the expenses for which it was intended to be voted had been incurred, or he will endeavour to side-step the issue. I, Mr. Speaker, am going to vote for the resolution because I believe the intention of the members of Parliament was that the money should not have been paid unless the expenses were incurred. I am of opinion that that was the intention of this House in the broad way in which Parliamentary intentions should be construed. If I took the narrow legalistic view and argued from the standpoint of precedent I should conclude that the money ought to be returned; and I say frankly, as a lawyer and on my reputation as such, that I do not believe this money could be recovered in a court of law, for the reason that I have given, the money having been paid over without a mistake in fact. But I am going to vote for the motion for another reason,-and I am sorry that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick did not pay the money back in 1918.-1 am going to vote for it because I believe this will be an object lesson to those who occupy high positions, that they must stand out fearlessly before the people and show by conduct that they are above and beyond the temptations that they condemn in others.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 must say at once that I am not rising to speak on this question as the leader of the Opposition, nor a partisan Although 1 may have a poor reputation in many respects, I think that in this House at least I am reputed to he a good partisan. But it is not as a partisan that I shall speak. I shall address myself to the observations of the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). He did not understand my question or he would not have taken any exception whatever to what I said. The hon. member was quoting a precedent in law-the case of Rex vs Clement, That case was one in which Government money was obtained by a judge who, it was contended, should not have received it, and it was considered by the authorities that that money should have been refunded. From that case the hon. member quoted authoritatively the judicial definition of "allowance." I ask him the question: If he is quoting good law from that case as to what allowance is, is not the manner in which the Government went about getting that money back a question of precedence that we should follow in this



case as well? If that case is light and guidance as law, is it n-ot also light and guidance as to procedure? I do not think there is anything offensive about that question. My hon. friend said the leader of the Opposition had the temerity to state that fact in this free Parliament. If that is a matter that requires extraordinary temerity, or temerity of the most ordinary kind, I do not understand my position in this House; and I think my usually perfect and complete friend should rather apologize for the way in which he construed my remarks. I did not intend to interrupt the hon. member, but simply to suggest that this House, although the highest tribunal, and nominally the highest court in the land, is in the broadest sense of the word, not a court at all. Consequently, if a case which has run the gauntlet of the Exchequer Court of Canada and the Supreme Court of Canada, is quoted to this Parliament as an authority on any question, the whole case, I contend, must be applied to the subject under discussion. And if in the case of Judge Clement it was proper that he should be haled into the court before his peers-according to the procedure provided by our constitution and the British constitution, which recognizes the fact that no man can be affected in his person or property except by fair trial before his peers-will the hon. member for Kingston say that this Parliament, because of its high prerogatives, should adopt a different course and try a person in his absence?
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Does my hon. friend suggest that if a man elects to be tried in a certain forum, that forum has no right to take him at his word?

I certainly say that a
man's choice of tribunal does not confer jurisdiction upon that tribunal. I may be charged with murder and, knowing a friendly magistrate somewhere in Hull or in Ottawa or elsewhere, I might admit to the sheriff my guilt in the matter but request to be tried at the place I might designate.
May I ask another question? Does not the hon. member's parallel fail, in that trial of murderer is regulated by statute, whereas the recovery of any amount paid by Parliament is not so regulated?
We have a precedent-

Not precedent; what is
the law?
Mr. McKE'NZJE: We have a precedent.
Not a precedent.

Yes, we have a precedent, which is the law. That is the famous case of Rex versus Clement. If my hon. friend from Kingston will please listen to me, these moneys which are paid as allowances are voted every year by Parliament. Allowances are paid out by the authorities to the judges, and if they are paid in a place where they have no right to be paid they are in exactly in the same position as the moneys which were paid to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick from a vote of this House-it is a vote of the House in both cases, and in both cases, the money paid out by the officers of the Government.

Will the hon. gentleman give us
his views about the failure of a " consideration "?

I might well have expected that the rapid, running mind of my friend from Peterborough would get so far ahead ihat I could not hope to answer him. By this time next week I may catch up to the hon. gentleman.
I was saying, (Mr. Speaker, when my oldtime interrogator came to his feet, that these cases could not be more alike. I want it understood at once that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick does not require, or claim, any defence from me, nor am I here to act in any capacity of the kind, but I want to make this perfectly clear: That the moneys paid out to Judge Clement, and the moneys paid out to Sir 'Charles Fitzpatrick are identically in the same position-they are public moneys paid out to a judge in the one case, and public moneys paid out to a judge in the other. Now, the Clement case in an older one-that is to say, the initiation of the procedure to get the money back is of an older date. What was done in that case? I presume that a flat was obtained by somebody from the Crown, proceedings were commenced in the Exchequer Court in behalf of the Crown, and the case was tried out properly in court. Let me say to my hon. friend from Frontenac, or to anybody who is interested in this matter, that those proceedings having been established by the authorities, the course taken in the Clement case was the proper one to follow. Why depart from it and ignore the Exchequer Court, ignore the Supreme Court of Canada, ignore the Supreme Court of Ontario-this proceeding having happened in the province

of	Ontario,	and	come under thejurisdiction of the Ontario courts? I say	that it is	entirely irregular,
at all events it is entirely a departure from the precedent that was established in the case of the Crown against Judge Clement. In that case, Judge Clement, I am sure, had the opportunity of coming before the court and making the best explanation he could, and the issue was tried out; the pros and cons having been heard. But a forum is selected here at which Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is not present, and at which he is not given a chance to tell his own story or to put up his defence. That being the case we are not within the safeguards and bulwarks which are given to every British subject, and which provide for a man being heard by his peers before any judgment is given against him which affects either his person or his property. That is the position which I take as to the matter of procedure.
Now, my hon. friend from Kingston (Mr. Nickle) is not happy in his reference to the facts. The hon. gentleman says that this is a case in which the money was paid by a mistake of law, and that being so we cannot go into a court of law to recover it. That is perfectly good law as far as our courts are concerned. But if the money has been paid in consequence of a mistake of fact, of course we can get it back. But the hon. gentleman, however, says that there was no mistake of fact, that we knew all about it; consequently we cannot plead ignorance of the facts. Well, the Prime Minister of thfs country is supposed to speak for the Government, and when we get a statement of the facts relative to a Government transaction from the Prime Minister, I am not aware that there could be any higher authority, and I submit that we have a right to accept the facts as stated by him. The hon. member fox Kingston read an answer from Hansard, in which the Prime Minister gave it as his opinion that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick went twice a year to attend the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Now, that is the knowledge of the Government on this matter. Well, if it turns out that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick did not go, and that he got the money under a mistake of fact,-the Prime Minister having stated that the Chief Justice was going to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council twice a year, whereas he did not go at all, and the officers of the Government, under the belief that he was going, paid him the money,-then there is clearly a mistake of fact, and the 554
law which my hon. friend from Kingston quoted does not stand in the way of going to the Exchequer Court, having the facts determined, and the case properly tried. There is another thing that I wish to submit: This is the High Court of the Parliament of Canada. We are here sitting- those of us who are not burdened with the responsibility of judicial office-like the jurors in court, and those hon. gentlemen who are familiar with court practice know that the jurors must take their law from the judge. He may be absolutely wrong, but the jurors sitting there, having heard the facts of the case, must take their law from the judge; he tells them what the law is. I regard myself as a layman and a juror sitting in this House to-day.
I hear such facts as are presented, and I am bound to receive the law from the Minister of Justice. I must apply a logical, clear-cut analogy to my position here to-day as to my position if I were sitting in court, under a judge, as a juror. The Minister of Justice in this case gives us the law, and he tells us that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was entitled to receive this money, that he got it absolutely honestly under the prevailing rules.
Did not the Minister of Justice use the expression "legally entitled?"
He said Sir Charles Fitzpatrick got the money properly.
Did he not use the expression "legally entitled?"
I am not aware that he said any such thing. I do not know how a man gets a thing properly unless he gets it legally.
Don't you?

No, I do not. I must admit that I am not up to trisecting things like the hon. member for Kingston, but I thought that legally, honestly, and properly were concomitant and conjunctive terms and went together.
Not overlapping.

But now it appears we can get a thing legally and justly which is not properly got. If that were so we would not have the same high opinion of our laws that we have to-day. But whatever the interpretation the Minister of Justice puts upon the case, he tells us this money was legally obtained, and, as far as I am concerned, taking the law from him, and I have nothing to do but with the facts, I

think we have to stop there. Let us transfer ourselves for a moment to the House of Commons in England, and consider a question of this kind coming up there. In England, perhaps, the officers of the law fill a higher position in the estimation of Parliament than they do with us. Whether they do or not the functions of the law officers are the same. If a question of this kind comes before the British House of Commons, where questions of law and fact are involved, the Parliamentary officers of the law hand down a certain decision upon the point and that is the end of it: Their decision is accepted and there the matter stands. Now, we have the decision of the officers of the law of this Parliament to the effect that this payment is all right, and that we have nothing to do with it-that it is the payment of a mere indemnity to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, just the same as the indemnity that he received as Deputy Governor.
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the Acting Minister of Justice said this afternoon that this was not a legal question at all?
I was not aware of that, otherwise I would not have said what I did.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I never made such a statement. I said I thought a question of law was involved, and I also said that the honour of a citizen of this country was involved.

It is worth while to find that the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) is wrong for once. It is worth while to discuss the whole thing to obtain that knowledge.
I was just saying that this was according to the interpretation that was put upon it by the officers of the law, that it was by way of indemnity to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick just the same as the allowance that was made to him as Acting Governor General. If that is the interpretation, I do not think we have anything further to say about it.
One more word, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend from West Peterborough asked me whether there was any consideration for this money. I think that the duties thrown upon Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, or upon any other Chief Justice of this country attending the sittings of the Privy Council, are very onerous indeed, and that it would be absurd that merely his travelling expenses should 'be paid. Every professional man in this House who has special responsibilities will understand that he must have certain qualifications and make special prepara-

tions for those duties which he has to perform. If a judge of one of the Ontario courts is going on circuit he has to prepare himself for that duty, and for that duty only, and for that duty he is paid; but if he is asked to go and sit in the Privy Council, what has he got to do there? He has got to know something about the laws of Australia from which appeals come, something about the laws of New Zealand from which appeals come, something about the laws of South Africa, India, and every other colony,-he must acquaint himself with the laws of all these different countries, otherwise he is rather an impediment and a nuisance and a danger to that court than a help.
Might I ask the hon. member a question?
Certainly.
Does the Canadian representative on the Privy Council have anything to do with colonial cases other than those from Canada?

As far as I understand it, he sits upon that court and he hears every case that comes before it, and cases come before it from every country that I have mentioned. For that reason he must have a knowledge of the laws of those different countries, and certainly the duties which he has to perform are very onerous. Therefore I think there was good consideration for any further compensation that might have been given him.
Apart from that, let me say at once that if the words of this vote are to be interpreted, let them receive judicial interpretation as in the Clement case. There is no question of difficulty in getting this before the Exchequer Court, from the Exchequer Court to the Supreme Court, and from the Supreme Court to the Privy Council. That is the place where this matter should be dealt with, and not in this House. Then we shall have a full and proper interpretation of what is meant by the language of this vote. If there is anything wrong, it is not traceable to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, rather it is traceable to the Prime Minister of this country-at all events, it is traceable to his office. We have heard from the memorandum handed to the Acting Prime Minister by his deputy minister, that word came to him from the office of the Prime Minister that a change was to be made in the language of the Estimates for years past so as to convert this from a matter of actual expense to an indemnity. There the fault is traceable, if fault there be, and from the

time that the Prime Minister of this country, through his secretary, passed that word down to the Department of Finance, where those Estimates were prepared, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had a perfect right to take advantage of the change of mind of the Prime Minister and of all the officials of the Government by which he was receiving this money. There is not a scintilla of evidence that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick ever asked for that change. Is it fair, without giving him a chance to be heard in one of our courts, that we should pass a condemnatory resolution in this House? I suggest to my good friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), he having heard the case now, and having had all the satisfaction that he can possibly get out of it, and knowing, as he does from this Clement case, that there is another and a proper way of getting this money back, that he withdraw this resolution.
Mr. WILLIAM S. MIDDLEBRO (North Grey):	Mr. Speaker, in my opinion the
whole matter resolves itself down to a question of interpretation. It is a fundamental rule of law that the meaning of an Act of Parliament must be gathered entirely from the words in which it is expressed, and there are many cases where the intention of Parliament has not been carried out by the expressions used in the statute. I think a very good illustration of that is what occurred in this House a couple of years ago, when in passing the Act to take over the Quebec and Saguenay railway it was enacted that the Government should pay the cost of that railway as determined by the Exchequer Court, and an hon. member of this House asked a question of the Minister of Railways and Canals who then had the Bill in charge, if the word " costs " included interest paid for money borrowed during the time of construction. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals said: Yes, cost would cover interest paid by the contractors for money borrowed during the time of construction. When the case came before the Exchequer Court, that court decided that interest paid during the course of construction did not enter into the question of cost at all as a matter of law. So that I say the interpretation of what we meant when it goes to the courts is left to the courts, and I am willing to argue this case upon that ground.
I contend that the three clauses mean practically the same. The first clause says:
Travelling expenses of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick attending sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
The next clause says:
Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
If the words "to cover expenses" had not been in there would be no doubt whatever in my mind that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick would, as a matter of law, be perfectly entitled to receive the $2,500, which would simply be an addition to his salary as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. But it is not given to him in that way; it is given to him to cover expenses. We do not require a statement as to whether his expenses are more than that amount or less than that amount, but the money is given to him for that special purpose.
The last clause says:
Special allowance-
The same words again.
-to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses when attending the sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
Now, I am assuming that there are no expenses in connection with his services as a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council unless he does go to England, and if there are not, then 'he is not entitled to those expenses, because I find in this memorandum prepared by the Justice Department that the word "allowance," as defined in "Wharton's Law Lexicon" which, as members of the legal profession are aware, is the standard legal dictionary, as "something conceded as compensation." If a man has incurred no expense, he cannot claim any compensation for expenses. According to the terms of the resolution appropriating these amounts, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, as a matter of law, is not entitled to the $5,000 which he received during those two years. In saying that I am not saying anything disrespectful of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. To a certain extent he was justified in taking these amounts because of the change which was made in the wording of the resolution. I do not know whether the change was made inadvertently or purposely, but whether inadvertently or purposely, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick would naturally believe that it had been made for the purpose of enabling him to get that compensation. Personally, I never intended, and I doubt whether any other member on this side of the House intended, that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick should receive $2,500 to cover his expenses in going to England when he did not go to England and did not incur any expense. For these reasons I must vote for the resolution of the member for Frontenac.

I have listened with a good deal of interest to the discussion this afternoon. The legal aspect of this matter has been put before the House in all its phases by the member for Kings-ton( Mr. Niekle), the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) and others; I desire to approach the matter entirely from the point of view of the remark of the Acting Minister of Justice (Hon. Mr. Meighen) that the honour of a citizen is involved. I do not know that my thoughts will lead to the same conclusion as his, but I uo feel that the honour of a citizen is deeply concerned -more deeply because the citizen in question sat at the fountain-head of justice as the Chief Justice of the highest judicial tribunal of Canada, the summit of all law That court, above all courts in the land, and the Chief Justice of that court, of all officials, should keep clean.
Any one listening to the discussion to-day could not help but feel that there has been a lot of specious argument around the question of legality. Whether the action of the Chief Justice was legal or not, was it honourable in him to take the money ? I think that is the whole question. He himself did not think that it was-at least, he had doubts, because in the letter read by the member for Kingston the Chief Justice said that if Parliament considered that he should not keep the money, he would return it. The matter is, therefore, "out of court;" he has sent it back here for the opinion of this House.
Let us see what the member for Fron-tenac asks us to do. His resolution reads:-
That, in the opinion of this House, the amount of $5,000 received by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick for the fiscal years 1915-16 and 1916-17 to cover expenses in connection with the udi-oial Committee of the Privy Council, should be returned by the said Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to the Treasury of Canada forthwith.
Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has said two things about returning this money. First, he said that if the House was of tthe opinion that he should return it he would do so. After thinking the matter over for a year, he sends in a telegram which reads:-
You are at liberty to state when Mr. Edwards moves his resolution that I adhere to the explanation given in my letter to Sir Robert Borden and which was read in the House last session in answer to Mr. Nickle's questions. I then offered to return the money-
He then offered to return the money if Parliament was of the opinion that he should. Note what he says now in this telegram, from which I quote further:-
I then offered to return the money and I now repeat that if the Government or any of the

officials through whom the money was paid will say that there is any doubt as to the regularity or legality of such payments I am prepared to return the money.
I thank the Acting Minister of Justice for the phrase " the honour of a citizen is at stake." This citizen has apparently forgotten his own honour and has descended to depending on regularity and legality. There is no doubt in the mind of any one in this House that that $2,500 a year was voted to enable the Chief Justice to go overseas and perform certain duties, and if we look at the matter in a fair way we will realize that no honourable man would take that money unless he did go overseas to perform those duties. That is the whole issue; there is no legal quibble about it. The member for Frontenac wants to get the opinion of this House on the question whether it is honest and decent and right that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick should keep that money, and the opinion of the House should be given in no uncertain way. It is then up to him to say: " The House of Commons, having been asked by me to give their opinion, has declared, by a majority vote, that I, sitting as the Chief Justice of 'Canada, while well cared for by the Government, being in receipt of $17,500 a year in all, should return the money voted to me during two years for expenses that were not incurred, for the performance of services that were not rendered." The Acting Minister of Justice said to-day, in answer to my question, that there was no duty to be performed in this connection except that of going overseas to attend the meetings of the Judicial Committee. So that the late 'Chief Justice has taken $5,000 out of the treasury without having turned a hand for it. Probably he did it legally; probably he did it regularly. I am inclined to agree with the member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gauvreau) that there may have been some conversation between the Chief Justice and some one else-I would not say with the Minister of Justice. But Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is astute enough to frame up anything for his own benefit to work through somebody-in a way that people understand. The point I make is that we are not seeking to sue him for this amount. If this resolution carries, the opinion of this House will be conveyed in the public press or through Hansard to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. His question will be answered, and the honour of the citizen will be up to the man whose honour is at stake. If Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, after that opinion has been expressed, feels that it is worth his while to keep the money of Canada, I, as a citizen of Canada, will say:

You are very welcome to it, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick; you will answer to yourself and your conscience in attempting to hold on to that which you did not properly obtain.
Mr. ROBERT J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):	Sometimes there come
up for decision by members of Parliament, questions in which the easier course would be for a member to refrain from voting.
I must confess I am in some doubt on this question, and I would find it a good deal easier to leave the chamber, as I felt tempted to do, so as to miss the vote if a vote takes place, but I generally do not like to run away from risks, if I may so term it. I have listened to the arguments put forward this afternoon by members on both sides of the House as intelligently as an ordinary layman can listen to the arguments of lawyers. I do not pretend to be able to follow the subtleties-that was the word used, I think, by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle)-of lawyers' minds. I have listened to the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) and the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) explaining the position, not of the Government, but of their legal advisers in this matter, and my interpretation of their remarks is to the effect that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had, at least, a legal, if not a moral, right to this money. If we take it into account that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had a legal right to this money-and even my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy), who thinks this money should be returned, admits that he has a legal right to it-and if we are demanding it back from Sir Charles Fitzpatrick simply on the moral ground, then it should be the duty of this Government, if Parliament insists, on moral grounds, on getting this money back, to investigate thoroughly the administration of the Government at the present time and to make other people who have taken money to which they have no moral right pay it back; and to go back over the record of the late Governments and make the crooked contractors pay back moneys which they had no moral right to take.
If I felt convinced that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had no right to retain this money, I would have absolutely no hesitation in voting in favour of this motion; but because I had a doubt in my mind in regard to the matter, I made it my business to chat with a few of the ministers who knew the situation and they are all of the same opinion as the Acting Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Justice, namely,
that this $5,000 should be left as it stands at the present time. One of the reasons put forward which impressed me very much was that, if this Parliament voted in favour of demanding the return of this money, that would practically be saying that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was a thief and stole that money. I am not prepared to go as far as that. I am not, however, convinced that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had a moral right to this money, and I will tell the House, in a moment,
5 p.m. what I would do if I were Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. I think the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) stated that if Sir Charles Fitzpatrick wanted to play the right game, he would have paid the money back last Fall. I do not know Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, I have not had the pleasure of meeting him, but in my opinion the reason why he could not pay the money back while under this cloud, was that if he did so, he would be admitting to the people of Canada that he stole it.
That he took it improperly.

Possibly he took it improperly, but I do not suppose Sir Charles Fitzpatrick would care to admit that he took it improperly even if, in his inner conscience, he thought he did. I do not blame him for that. I think his proper stand would be to stand by his guns; otherwise, he would be admitting that he took it improperly, a thing which no man would care to admit. To take a thing improperly is a drawing-room phrase for stealing it. One of the ministers with whom I spoke expressed the opinion that if Parliament passed this resolution it would wipe out any reputation for honour that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has. There is a great deal of truth in that, and I am not prepared to vote away the reputation of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick for $5,000. Not only is his honour at stake, but the honour of this Government is also at stake. That is the conclusion I have reached, and I have endeavoured to give in a few words my reasons for supporting the view held by the Acting Prime Minister and the Acting Minister of Justice. If the vote taken by the House on this matter does not support Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, I suppose he will have to pay the money back; but supposing the vote supports him in keeping it, in that case, if I were Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, I would pay back the money after I was exonerated, as a doubt has been cast upon him.
Oh, oh.

I hear laughter from different parts of the House. I do not think that view differs from my first conclusions in this matter. I repeat what I said at the outset, namely, that every hon. member who has spoken has admitted that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has a legal right to this money. Therefore, he has not stolen it, and I do not see why he should admit he has stolen it. But as a doubt has been cast upon him, the proper course for Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to pursue, if this vote exonerates him, is to hand back this $5,000 to the people of Canada.
If we vote for this resolution, will that defeat the Government?

I understand this has nothing to do' with either a defeat or a support of the Government, and I am not, as is implied by the hon. member, tied by any chain to supporting this Government, if 1 feel like voting against it.

I wish, in just two or three sentences to make my position clear on this question. I may say at the outset that I intend to vote for the resolution for reasons which are perfectly clear to my mind. I remember very well, when the items referred to were before the House, it was clear to me that we were voting from year to year this sum of money for a particular purpose, namely, to pay the expenses of the Chief justice of Canada, whoever he might be, to attend the sittings of the Privy Council. Last year-and I use the argument I am now going to use, for the particular benefit of my hon. friend (Mr. Manion)-when the Estimates were being considered, this question was raised by several members, and a large number of members who intended to speak did not speak for the reason that they were given an assurance by the Government, on the strength of a letter from Sir Charles Fitzpatrick read by a responsible minister of the Crown, that this money would be returned. On that assurance being given to the House, opposition was at once removed and the item was allowed to pass.
Another feature of the case to which I wish to draw the attention of the House is this. The question of law has been discussed very carefully and earnestly by hon. members. One principle is accepted in all courts, namely, that where in law a phrase or a clause of a contract is in doubt, the lawyers and the judge usually look for some precedent or some action which went

before which might interpret the meaning of the clause.
We have a dozen precedents for this. From the year 1897 to 1915-16 this item was in the Estimates year after year, and it was there for a particular purpose, and the money was used for that purpose. In the year 1915-16 the wording was slightly changed, but the item as it had appeared the previous year was placed alongside; in other words, the vote was interpreted in the terms of the vote of -the previous year. I submit to the Government this point: If we, as private members, were to be forced to analyze in detail every item that comes before this House we should never get through the Estimates in a hundred years. Every item in the Estimates is condensed in as few words as possible, and we trust to the officers of the Crown to carry out the intention which Parliament undoubtedly has in passing these items in this abbreviated form. It was clear to Parliament what this particular vote was intended for; it was clear to Parliament last year that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick intended this House to understand that he would return the money. But a year afterwards we find that the money has not been returned. I shall certainly take the opportunity of expressing my opinion in a vote on this matter.

If
I agreed with my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) in what he said, I should vote as he is going to vote, but the only thing he said with which I agree was that we are dealing with a very disagreeable question. I am no apologist for Government by Order in Council, but if this matter could have been settled by an Order in Council it would have saved Parliament a very ugly situaJtion. I think, for once, I would be in agreement with my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr.' McKenzie) who seems to want it settled somewhere else than here anyhow, and we are at one in not fearing to derogate from -the rights and privileges of Parliament on the present occasion. I must say I rather resent the duty of having to discuss and decide on this question; it should not have been thrown on the shoulders of Parliament. It appears to me, as my hon. friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) suggested, that there has been some intercourse between the Government and Sir Charles on this question, and the Government should have saved Parliament from having to discuss and vote on this matter. I do not attach much

importance to the legal cobwebs that we have had spun here this afternoon. OE course, it is a long time since we ascribed first place in that particular art to my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen), but I thought this afternoon he would have to look to his laurels because the Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White) really made a splendid exhibition along the same lines. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) was willing to enter into the competition, hut I am bound to pronounce him a bad third. When I listened to these gentlemen I wondered if I could lay claim to being an intelligent layman, and ever since I have been trying to persuade myself that I am a reasonably intelligent layman.
I am sorry for Sir Charles Fitzpatrick in this connection. I do not share the habit of my hon. friend from Fort William of wishing to use strong language where I can possibly avoid it, and I differ very profoundly from the attitude that he has just taken up in asserting that those who vote in a certain way in this matter will proclaim that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is a thief. I should like to warn my hon. and young friend against the use of such language; even if he thinks it, he should modify his language. It is sometimes well, it may be generally well, to call a spade a spade, but there is excuse in some circumstances for calling it a horticultural implement. In this case I neither think Sir Charles Fitzpatrick a thief, nor will I have my vote represented as indicating '*at I think so. I do not blame, primarily, Sir Charles Fitzpatrick for the situation. I think it should have been settled when there was a chance to settle it, without ihe House having to vote on this question. I have a slight acquaintance with Sit Charles Fitzpatrick, and I think he is a man who by his intellectual gifts and by his high character has been an adornment to many public positions in this country. That is all one needs to say upon such an interpretation cf the vote here as was given by my hon. friend from Fort William.
While I am sorry for Sir diaries Fitzpatrick, I am sorry for myself, as a member of Parliament, in having to deal with this matter. From the view expressed hy the Minister of Justice that this House is the guardian of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's honour I sharply dissent. Every man is the guardian of his own honour; it must be so; and I refuse to assume the guardianship of the honour of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. Neither am I the guardian of the business capacity of the Government. This question has been
allowed to drift into the House of Commons for settlement, and what I have to remember is what I am guardian of. I am the guardian, in the humble capacity of a single member of this House, of the public purse; that is a duty which I cannot avoid; it is put upon me by those who elected me here, and by the constitution of our country. We all know, in spite of legal contentions to the contrary, that this five thousand dollars was paid to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. I do not think any one contradicts mat. That is a fact known to everybody, including the hon. leader of the Opposition. He may not know' it in his legal capacity, but as I do not know what that is, I am content if he knows it in his capacity as a member of Parliament. I believe, and I want to state my belief, that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick in taking that money tooiv it under error. I will not permit myself to say of any other man whui he should have done when he had committed that error-and I am using the language of straightforward sincerity. I do not know that I would even answer on my own account a question which I suppose the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) addressed to me with the other members of this House. He seemed to turn in my direction wrhen he asked, would I have taken this money? I thought at the time, my mother was Scotch, and it is a large sum, and I am not bound to answer the question. I should be in the same difficulty if he had gone on to ask, would I have given it back, and for the reason that if I had got the sum I should not have retained it till this time, as I have not been able to exercise the Scotch quality of taking care of money too well So I have not to answer this question as to -what Sir Charles Fitzpatrick should have done or what I would have done myself under those circumstances.
The money was paid by the Government to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to enable him to travel. He did not travel. It w'as said during the war by somebody-the Minister of Public Works, I think-that we must " work or fight," and I think that in this case the question was, " travel or return the money." That, at any rate, is the view I shall take of the matter. The money was paid for travelling expenses; travelling was not done, therefore it is due back to the country, and I say that without any reflection upon Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, but merely as indicating the way in which I shall vote. For once I was pleased to take my law-if it was law; the commonsense of it anyway-from my old friend the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx), who

was, to my mind, by far the clearest-brained lawyer who spoke on this subject in the House to-day. I have tried to put this question from the point of view of the layman, and to put before the House the reasons which shall guide me if the question comes to a vote.

When I voted, as I did, for the resolution at the time the vote was taken, I believed that the money was to be paid to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick as a sort of salary, somewhat in the form of a retainer which is Sometimes paid a lawyer by a corporation for the purpose of securing his services at any time if required. I might have been wrong in my view of the question at that time, and I am not saying that I was not. I have listened to most of the discussion this afternoon, and have heard a great deal of legal opinion. The Acting Prime Minister has told us that the changing of the wording was made at the request of the Prime Minister's secretary. Now, the money was paid by the Finance Department at the instance of the Department of Justice and the Privy Council, without any question, and with the sanction of the late Auditor General, who, we all know, was very capable. In these circumstances it is my opinion that the money was legally paid, and, as far as I can gather, it was honestly accepted by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. I therefore have no other recourse than to endorse the payment that was legally made by those who were in authority to make payments such as this, and to oppose this resolution.

There is no doubt in my mind that previous to 1915 and 1916 Sir Charles Fitzpatrick would not, according to the way the money was voted then, have been entitled to it; but under the vote of 1915 and 1916 I think the money was legally paid to him and that it was accepted in good faith. There must have been some reason for the change that was made in the wording of the Estimate, and I feel I must vote against the resolution and at the same time express regret at some of the remarks that have been made concerning Sir Charles Fitzpatrick.

It is extremely difficult to understand the attitude of any hon. member in this House who defends Sir Charles Fitzpatrick in his retention of this money. Sir Charles himself, in his letter last year, offered to return the money if this Parliament thought he should do so, and that was an absolute

admission on his part that there was certainly a doubt in his mind as to the propriety of his retaining the money. One hears many legal arguments on a question of this kind, but it seems to me that the bald facts are so self-explanatory that a wayfarer, though a fool, could not fail to decide what is Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's duty in this matter. When the late Dalton McCarthy some years ago was addressing a meeting in the town of Selkirk, Manitoba, in the course of a criticism of the Government of the day in which he made some deductions that were perfectly logical, an obtrusive person in the back who was opposed to him politically asked him: "How do you know, Mr. McCarthy, that what you say is right?" Mr. McCarthy, with that dignity and strength of character that distinguished him, paused for a moment and replied, "Because I am not a damned fool." Now the people of this country are not fools-I omit the adjective -and they know that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick received $5,000 for services that he did not render. The matter has been referred to this House for decision. The people are exceedingly critical, and the average Canadian citizen regards $5,000 as a large amount of money-which indeed it is, Mr. Speaker. The people are waiting to see what attitude their representatives in Parliament will take in this matter. The money was improperly accepted. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick did not spend one farthing of it, and yet his salary is $17,500.
If you give him this additional money as an honorarium, he will have $20,000, nearly three times, perhaps more than three times, the salary of the average minister of the Crown. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick was the Chief Justice of Canada, the fountain of justice in this country. In addition to that he was the administrator representing the Governor General of Canada, and the people have a right to look to him as the fountain of honour, as he was the official fountain of honour. And yet he takes this $5,000. He practically admits he did not earn it, he did not spend it, and he had it improperly; and to ask this House to say that he should be allowed to retain the money is, in my judgment to insult the intelligence of members of the House, the intelligence of the people of this country. I did not hear the remarks of the Acting Prime Minister, or of the Acting Minister of Justice, but taking the interpretation of their remarks as I heard it secondhand from members of this House, I must confess that I am surprised that either, or both, of those gentlemen-while they may not have de-

fended the payment-should have left the impression that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is legally entitled to this money. A man may be legally entitled to $100,000, and yet not have one scintilla of moral claim. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has no moral claim on this money; and let him understand, as the reperesentative of the Crown in this country, that the Parliament and the people of Canada do not propose to allow him to go Scot free in this matter. Sir 'Charles Fitzpatrick, by reason of his position, should he placed in the pillory, and it should be given out to the people of Canada that this Parliament does not intend to allow a man of his position, and of his supposed honour, to escape responsibility. Let the declaration of Parliament this afternoon be quite clear, so that the country will have no doubt as to the mind of the people's representatives that we propose to insist upon having this money returned. If under the circumstances, 'Sir Charles Fitzpatrick should wish to retain it, 'then on his head be the responsibility. I agree with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) that Parliament cannot be the keeper of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick's honour, or of any man's honour-every man must be the keeper of his own honour-and if we make an emphatic pronouncement on questions of this kind, we will have struck a strong and hearty blow for honesty and for honest public service in this country.

I do not take the same view of the question as is taken by my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) and quite a number of other hon. gentlemen who have preceded me. If blame attaches to any one as a result of this unfortunate matter, I think the blame should be put upon the House of Commons itself, or upon the Government administering affairs in 1915-16, rather than upon the shoulders of Sir Charles Fitzpatrick. In my judgment no stigma whatever, no degree of moral turpitude whatever attaches to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, in respect of the two payments of $2 500 each which form the subject of this resolution. Parliament must be presumed to know what it is doing when it passes its Estimates. Deliberately it changed *he language which had prevailed in this House with respect to this item for years. When this vote was made in 1915, an item which stated in express terms that the money was given for travelling expenses was changed. We assume that it was done deliberately, because that action was taken with the knowledge of hon. members who were then in this House. We are supposed to know
what it meant, and we approved of it- we must have known what it meant when we took that course. The blame for anything that has gone wrong since must be attributed to us; if a mistake was made, we made it. Why did we make the change referred to? To my mind the matter is clear, and I agree writh the view taken by my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. E. W. Nesbitt) with respect to it. The language of the vote was changed expressly to permit Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to accept an allowance practically as an addition to his salary. What was the wording of the vote of 1915? " Special allowance to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to cover expenses in connection with the Judicial Committee of the Privy . Council." My hon. friend from Springfield and my hon. friend from Red Deer said that money was paid to enable Sir Charles Fitzpatrick to travel. There is nothing in the vote which limits the payment to travelling expenses. We are assuming that there was no expense in connection with the office but expenses of travel. We do not know whether or not Sir Charles Fitzpatrick employed clerical assistance or stenographers, or disbursed money for telegrams, postage, or the like. So long as any expense was incurred at all the payment of the money cannot be withheld. Let me give a little instance by way of illustration. Every hon. member of this House who were here fifteen or twenty years ago accepted mileage every year and travelled on a railway pass. Members of the Dntario Legislature do that yet. In the Militia Department the higher officers receive an allowance per diem; they do not give details of their expenditure for travelling expenses, they do not vouch their accounts. The allowance, I believe, is some $12 or $15; at any rate whatever the amount may be, I am told they do not give an itemized account of their expenditures; they accept the allowance no matter how small their expenditure has been. Our judges do the same thing. We give them a per diem allowance of $6 or $8 for expenses, and if the expenses happen to be $2 or $3 below the amount, the allowance is drawn just the same. The money is not given for actual expenses, it is an allowance, and it was so in connection with the money that was voted to Sir Charles Fitzpatrick.
Will the Solicitor General definitely state that this money was voted for work done by Sir Charles Fitzpatrick?
I do not quite catch the question.

This money was voted in connection with attendance at sittings of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The Solicitor General says that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick may have used it for certain other expenses, but he does not say that it was expended for work in connection with the Judicial Committee.

I have just as good a right to say that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick might have used it for other purposes as hon. members have to insinuate that he did not use this money for expenses. I have just as high and firm ground for doing that as hon. members have who are criticising this payment. The fact still remains, however, that when we voted this money we voted it in plain, distinct, language as an allowance, and having done so we should assume the responsibility. I quite agree that no good end is going to be served by a discussion of this unfortunate question in this forum. In my opinion this discussion is purely academic, and I do not think anything will come of it, whether we adopt or reject this motion. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick may say: " I do not propose to return this money," even if we adopt this motion. How are you going to compel him, if he takes that attitude?
What about his telegram ?

He may not act on it, he may even change his mind with respect to it. How are you going to exercise compulsion? Where is this going to end? When is any finality going to be achieved? There is a forum where this question could be disposed of, and I think the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition is the correct one in view of the statute which says that a claim of the Crown may be adjudicated by the Exchequer Court of Canada. I believe that is the proper form to which this whole question should be referred and there be dealt with. Sir Charles Fitzpatrick can be heard there. We have not had the other side of the matter, except in the somewhat discursive communication which has been read from Sir Charles Fitzpatrick himself, but if we have a claim, or believe we have a claim, the Exchequer Court is the forum where this question should be decided. In that court we should get finality, a definite finding. Here the discussion may have the result of casting a slur upon Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, which, in my humble judgment, is entirely undeserved on account

of anything that has occurred in this transaction.

Mr. Speaker, the member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) does not place Sir Charles Fitzpatrick in a very favourable light when he tells us that even if we vote that this money ought to be returned to Parliament Sir Charles Fitzpatrick will not return it, although he has offered to do so. I shall not attempt to follow the legal side of the argument. I think it was well that that side should be stated, and it was stated very completely by the member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle). I do not look at this matter from the legal standpoint, neither do I think the people of Canada so regard it. I think the member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) gave the right view of it. The people of Canada see an item in the Estimates of $2,500 for expenses, and as far as they can learn no expenses have been incurred. Nowq I submit, Sir, that if any expenses had been incurred sufficient to warrant the taking of that money some member of this House would be able to say so today. No person has ventured such a statement, no person has even insinuated that any expenses had been incurred. We are told that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick might have spent something on postage, clerical help, or something of that sort, but no effort is made to show how much that is or how little, and if it was anything like sufficient to justify this payment I am sure that fact would have been stated here to-day.
If a postman, Mr. Speaker, takes fifty cents improperly wre send him to the penitentiary for five years. I do not mean to' say that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has stolen the money, but I go this far, that the one man in Canada who should be careful of his position in matters of this kind is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. Every man should be careful of what he does in financial transactions if he is an honest man, but the one man above all others in this Dominion who should be careful that nobody can say he has taken five cents improperly is the man who presides over the Supreme Court of this country, and it is most regrettable that he should have allowed this matter to go so far when he knows the feeling of Parliament from former discussions.
Is it any wonder, Mr. Speaker, that working men, farmers and others who have to work for five years to earn $5,000 should get restless when they see that amount taken by a man already drawing $15,000, and taken improperly. How are we going to

prevent unrest, how are we going to satisfy the people that we are doing the square thing by them when men who have the highest paid positions in this country resort to these means to add to their incomes? Whether Sir Charles Fitzpatrick is able legally to retain this or not, he has no moral right to it, and that is the view I take and I propose to give effect to it by my vote.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman purposes to speak he can only do so in closing the debate, and if he exercises his right to reply now, other hon. members will be precluded from speaking.
I only wish to say, Mr. Speaker-
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Wright (Mr. Devlin) has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words upon thiB question, but if my hon. friend the member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) wishes to make a statement that he withdraws his resolution, then I will give way to him.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of withdrawing my resolution. I am aware of the fact, as I presume my hon. friend is, that it is a quarter to six. I believe the sentiment of this House is that we take a vote on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, I have done my best to follow the reasoning of the hon. gentlemen who have already spoken. I am
indifferent in this matter as to whether the charge is made against a man who calls himself Fitzpatiick, or whether it be made against a man who might call himself by any other name. I desire not to give a silent vote, but, I hope, an intelligent one, and in order that I may give that vote, as I mean to give it, I want to say a few words in explanation. We have been dealing this afternoon with a case that I might call the case of Edwards vs. Fitzpatrick. The complainant in this case asks us to constitute ourselves into a transferring court to transfer the charge in the case of Edwards vs. Fitzpatrick to one of the King vs. Fitzpatrick. I understand that the Government take the position that they will not recommend, nor will the officers of the Crown recommend, that the case be styled one of the King vs. Fitzpatrick, but that it must continue to be the case of Edwards vs. Fitzpatrick.
I was brought up, Mr. Speaker, under the British system of justice, and you all know it is a rule of British justice that every man in this country must have a fair and a free trial, that the evidence for and against him shall be heard, and that both parties shall have access to the court to give their version of the case.
I put it to hon. members of the House: Is this a fair trial to give to the defendant in the case of Edwards vs Fitzpatrick? The hon. gentleman asks us to sit here not as judges but as jurors and to render a verdict upon the facts as he has stated them, without giving the accused, or the defendant, an opportunity of stating his version of the case. Is that fair? Is that British justice?
I want to emphasize the further point that there are jurors in this case who do not stand indifferent as between Edwards and Fitzpatrick. It is a rule of Britffh justice that when a juror is not indifferent as between the King and the accused, he shall stand aside and not be allowed to decide upon the facts of the case. The member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) told us that he was not concerned with the law in this case; that he did not want any instruction to the members of this House- the jurors in this case-on questions of law. Is that British justice? What would he say, for instance, if in some famous trial, after the judge had charged the jury upon the points of law, one of the jurors called upon to decide on the questions of fact stood up and said: "Your Lordship, arway with your questions of law. We do not want to know any law in this case;

we want to decide it according to the facts as we wish to see them, not according to the facts as they have been placed before the court."
Hear, hear.
Will the hon. gentleman who said: "hear, hear" he good enough to stand up?
What does the hon. member wish to know?
I was not referring to the member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham).
Is the hon. gentleman asserting that it is not the right of the jury to decide the facts in any case heard before them? I say to him that it is absolutely the right of the jury to decide the facts.

My hon. friend is a lawyer and he must know well that I am not propounding any such doctrine. It is perfectly within the province of the jury to decide upon questions of fact. But let me ask the hon. gentleman: is it not within the province of the judge to instruct the jury upon questions of law? Will he be fair and answer that question?
Yes.

The judges in this case are the law officers of the Crown, who tell us that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick had a legal right to keep the money. Are we to take that into consideration, or are we not? Will the hon. gentleman again be fair and tell me what his view is on that point?

speechtext:
I think the hon. member should confine his remarks to his discussion of the subject before the House, and not address another hon. gentleman.
<^(r. DEVLIN: Then I ask you, Mr. Speaker, at the present moment the judge of this court, whether you would simply take the facts of a case brought before you and set aside all the law, where the case had to do with facts and law? I take your silence, Mr. Speaker, as indicating that you thoroughly agree with me.
With the statements that we have before us-the statement of the mover of the resolution and some of his friends and the .statement of the Government advised by the law officers of the Crown-what can we poor mortals, layman jurors, decide in this case? Have we not the right to ask that the defendant at least be heard in some way before we decide this case against him? Unless that right is granted, Sir- 
that right which is a principle of British justice-I propose to vote against the resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the legal luminaries on both sides of the House and have come to the conclusion that every hon. member must have come to: That this is really not a legal, but a moral question. With regard to the moral question-the fact that Sir Charles Fitzpatrick has agreed to leave it to the judgment of this House, notwithstanding the fact that he knows the packed jury and the mentality of them-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that remark.

Well, I withdraw that remark. -notwithstanding the nature of the jury, I am perfectly satisfied that in his own mind Sir Charles Fitzpatrick stands acquitted, as stainless -$s a star. Now, to give you my own attitude I shall paraphrase a few words from that grand old moral philosopher, Robbie Burns:
Who made the heart, 'tis He alone Decidedly can try us;
He knows each chord, its various tone,
Each spring its various bias.
Then at the balance let's he mute.
We never can adjust it;
What's done we partly can compute But know not what's resisted.
Then, gently scan your brother man,
Still gentler Charles Fitzpatrick:
Tho' he has gang a kennin'wrang His company's full of bad tricks.

Mr. Speaker, I beg to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion negatived.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member has exhausted his right to speak.

A
question of principle has been raised today in the discussion of this whole question. The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) stated that in his opinion the money had been unduly taken. Whether it was legally or illegally taken, so long as it was unduly taken, it should have been returned to the treasury. I will not lay very much stress on the question whether the money has been taken legally or illegally, but I will call to my assistance another principle which has been applied ever since Confederation. I refer to the separation of the three distinct powers which are at the foundation of our constitution-the executive power, the judicial

power and the legislative power. It has been the constant practice of all statesmen not to allow any one power to trespass on the province of another. The executive power, the province of which is well defined by our constitution, should not trespass on the legislative power. That is one of the reasons why we so much object to the method of procedure by Order in Council. We consider that by the method of procedure by Order in Council, the executive power is trespassing upon the province of the legislative power. The hon. member for Frontcnac (Mr. Edwards) has, in this resolution, asked us to substitute the legislative power for the judicial power. It is the duty of this House to enact laws, but it is not the duty of this House or of this Parliament to pass judgment on the laws that this Parliament has enacted.

The House adjourned at 6 p.m.

speechtext:
There occurred in the Capital yesterday an event which I feel the members of this House would not desire should pass without fitting and appropriate reference. I allude to the sudden death of the Hon. George Taylor. As is known to the members of this House, the hon. gentleman was a member of the Senate, having been appointed to that body in 1911, but it was through his long association with this chamber that he was best known to parliamentarians and to the public throughout Canada. In the general election of 1882 he was returned with a majority of less than 300, and at each ensuing general election he was re-elected by a gradually increasing majority, which in the year 1911 had reached nearly 1,000. He was a member of the House of Commons for almost thirty years, serving under the premierships of Macdonald, Abbott, Thompson, Tupper, Bowell, Laurier.
The late Senator Taylor belonged to a generation of public men that is fast passing away. In his earlier days party spirit ran high and men were strong partisans. Senator Taylor was a staunch party men, and there was never any doubt as to where he stood upon a public question. He had the most implicit and abiding faith in the tenets of the Conservative party, and his devotion and loyalty to its leaders were unbounded. As has been the case with almost all men of his type, his strong partisanship in no wise prevented his being held in high esteem and respect by his political opponents. I am sure that the House will support me in saying that he was a man who was always well liked by both sides in this chamber.
For a period of twenty-five years he was Chief Whip of the Conservative party, and he enjoyed in very marked degree the personal friendship and confidence of the Right Hon. Sir John A. Macdonald. I know that he also enjoyed the esteem and respect of the late leader of the Opposition, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and there was no man in the councils of the Con-servati\e party whose advice was held in h gher regard by Sir Robert Borden, the present Prime Minister, than was that of the late Senator Taylor. In addition to the confidence which was reposed in him by his leaders, and which he continuously enjoyed,
he was popular with the rank and file of the Conservative party, and indeed, as I have stated, of all members of the House. In his own constituency, which I have the honour to represent in Parliament to-day, he was regarded as the foremost citizen of the town of Gananoque, in which he had lived since early manhood. The late Senator was a man of fine public spirit and good works; a man of high benevolence, whose benefactions were many and most generous.
I think the outstanding feature of his personality was his exceeding kindness of heart, which endeared him to all who knew him. He was never so happy as when doing a kindness to a neighbour or extending a helping hand to any of his constituents, or to any with whom he might be acquainted, or even chance to meet casually. In his constituency and here at Ottawa, where he was best known, he was regarded, and rightly so, as a man of most sterling integrity and probity of character. He will be greatly missed by his associates in both Houses of Parliament. I am sure that this House will join with me in an expression of deep regret at his passing away, and of sympathy with his widow and other members of his family circle in the bereavement they have sustained.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we are all pleased to join in the handsome tribute paid to the memory of the late Senator Taylor by the leader of the Government. By his death we are, Mr. Speaker, once more reminded of the uncertainties of life, that we are merely pilgrims in this land, and that our sojourn here is but a transient one. The departed senator was for many years a conspicuous figure in the public life of this country, he having occupied a great many municipal, provincial and federal positions, to all of which he brought a full sense of responsibility and of public service, and, as has been well said by the leader of the Government, he also brought to them an extraordinary amount of energy and devotion. We all remember him with respect and kindly feelings, for he was a sincere and faithful friend and a man upon whom at all times the country and his friends could depend, for he held decided views, and there was no misunderstanding his attitude where the interests of this country were concerned. I wish to connect myself, as, I am sure, my hon. friends on this side of the House do, with what has been so appropriately said in regard to the memory of our departed friend, Senator Taylor.
