If the amendment means anything, it is what is known as the " six months' hoist," which is merely a motion to adjourn and is not debatable. On the other hand, the meaning might be that it is not expedient to re-enact the Daylight Saving Act now, but that it should be enacted six months from now, which would bring it in force next autumn. I fancy that the amendment has not been very carefully worded, and if one voted for it he would render himself rather ridiculous. The main motion can be met with " Yes " or " No." If the amendment is merely a six months' hoist, it should not be debated; if it is merely a negative, it should be ruled out of order.
I submit that we should have a ruling on this point before the debate proceeds further.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: While this amendment purports upon its face to be a motion for the six months' hoist, in actual fact it has not that effect. The sense of the amendment is that daylight saving be enacted six months hence, not that the subject should be considered six months hence, which would be the six months' hoist. The second point raised by the Solicitor General is whether a motion .to effect a six months' hoist is debatable. If that motion is made in the form of an amendment to a substantive motion which is before the House, it can be debated, because there remains sufficient of the original motion, which is debatable to permit debate. On the other hand, a motion made not by way of amendment, but "that the subject be considered this day six months," would be a straight motion for the six months' hoist, and, under Rule 17A, would not be debatable. As the motion of the member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) is in the form of an amendment, it is debatable. Although it is not very happily worded and does not, in my judgment, convey the meaning which the mover had in his mind, it is technically in order.

The amendment was
worded as it is for the purpose of permitting a discussion of the matter. Had I worded it differently, it would not have been debatable, as I think you, Mr. Speaker, will rule. I was going to ask the consent of the House, at the conclusion of the debate, to change the wording to make the amendment read: "considered this day six months."

I have received letter after letter from my constituents expressing their opposition to daylight saving. I was the first man to start a canning factory in Canada, and I have been in the business ever since; that brings me in close touch with the farmers, and enables me to speak with some authority on this subject. Last year we contracted for 30,000 acres of corn, peas and tomatoes, all produced by the farmer. If there was ever a time when we should try to make things pleasant for the farmer, it is now. The daylight saving measure interfered very much with our getting contracts from the farmers this year. They say "we have to stop our work at five o'clock instead of six, and that interferes with the harvesting of our crops."

I am quite in sympathy with what has been said by the member for Kent (Mr. McCoig). When the ground is damp you cannot work many of the crops produced for canning; consequently daylight saving would he very detrimental to the farmers, and in expressing my opposition to it I am expressing the views of the people whom I represent.

Last session I supported the Daylight Saving Bill and when I went back to my constituency I found that apparently I had done the right thing, because so far as I know all my constituents are in favour of daylight saving. I think I am safe in saying that the people generally of British Columbia are in favour of daylight saving. About two-thirds of my constituents are farmers.
I represent about 50,000 people, two-thirds of whom live outside the city. I have recently received from many organizations in the city requests that I should support daylight saving, and at the same time, I have received no objections whatever from the farmers. I presume, if my farmers objected to daylight saving, they would advise me of their objections just as farmers in other places have advised their representatives of their objections. I, therefore, take it for granted that my farmers are in favour of daylight saving. Possibly, the farmers of British Columbia are a little in advance of the farmers of the East in their ideas in regard to daylight saving. It is, perhaps, not . surprising to see the farmers of the East opposing an innovation of this kind, because farmers have opposed many innovations. It may be remembered that when the first locomotive appeared in this country, the farmers were opposed to it; they said that locomotives were a nuisance; that they frightened their cattle and so forth. When automobiles were invented, the farmers opposed them, saying that they should not be allowed, and, if I remember correctly, it is only within the last year or so that in Prince Edward Island automobiles have been allowed to use the roads and now they can use them for only two or three days a week. My opinion is that in a few years the farmers will appreciate the fact that in this respect it is the right thing for Canada to fall in line with the rest of the civilized world. I trust the Government will see fit to re-enact the daylight saving measure this year.

When the Daylight Saving
[Mr. Marshall.!
Bill was brought down last year, from what I could understand of it, I was opposed to it. After the session was over when I went home I made inquiries amongst the farmers and the labouring classes of my constituents. I found the farmers were absolutely opposed to daylight saving and the labouring classes said: We do not like it at all; it means more expense to us, especially in the fall of the year; it is an hour lost to us. Therefore, I am going to vote against the re-enactment of this measure just as I did last year. Some hon. members contend that daylight saving is a great thing for the cities and towns. While it is true I come from a small town, I find that when the merchants open their stores at seven o'clock in the morning, or six o'clock under the old time, there is practically no one around, so that they lose an hour in the morning, and in the evening they lose another hour.
So far as the farmer is concerned, Parliament, instead of giving him an hour in the morning, should give him an hour in the evening so that he can harvest his grain. As has been stated, farmers cannot start harvesting until ten o'clock in the morning, and the afternoon from two o'clock to six or seven o'clock is the best time for the farmer to harvest his grain. The morning I left to attend this session of Parliament, I met one of the most important farmers in my constituency and he told me to do all I could to prevent this measure being reenacted, because it is against the interest of the farmers. I have been asked to tell the Government to keep its hands off the farmers, to give the farmers all the latitude possible, because they are the backbone of the country, and should, therefore, be given every advantage, and the same may be said of the working classes. For these reasons, therefore, I intend to oppose the re-enactment of daylight saving.

I was very much amused at the hon. member from British Columbia, who wants to make us believe he represents a farming constituency. They are truck farmers, and in the East we do not take much stock in truck farmers. I do not think any hardship will be caused by the people of the cities working an hour or two hours in the morning, as they choose. We do not want to dictate to them, but we do not want them to die-tate to us. I come from a constituency comprising mostly farmers and dairymen and my opinion is that if 'this measure be re-enacted, a great hardship will be suffered by them. I believe also the people in the cities who are supporting daylight

saving are standing in their own light, because if this measure be re-enacted, it is bound to enhance the cost of the production. We cannot go out into the fields to cut grain until eight o'clock in the morning, and the greatest part of our day will be lost. If the farmers do not know their own business when to begin and when to quit work, without being dictated to by the people of the cities, they are not endowed with as much common sense as I thought they were. I think the great majority of the people of the cities do not want daylight saving, only a few who do not get up until nine o'clock in the morning and who want to play baseball, cricket and so on in the evening are in favour of it, and if they are the ones who are going to rule the farmers of this country the farmers want to know it. Do not aggravate the farmers too much. So far as I can make out, there is in existence a little organization, just about as big as a man's hand, called the Organized Farmers. If you aggravate the farmers too much you will get that organization down here, and while I am a strong supporter of the Government, I ask the Government to be very careful, or those people will drive it out and my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best) will, perhaps, become Minister of Agriculture. I trust that the result of this discussion will be that the farmer will start work whenever it suits him and the city people the same.

I want to say a few words on this question on behalf of the farmers of Toronto. There are, in my constituency, a great many farmers, and although, of course, they are truck farmers, as the hon. member (Mr. Boyce) has stated, yet they produced a great deal last year and they did so after they had performed their day's work, so that I think in that respect they are entitled to some consideration, as in doing that they show that they are willing to work overtime in order to bring about that production which the country needs. The statement has been made by the Fuel administration at Washington that 1,250,000 tons of coal were saved by daylight saving in the United States during the past year. I have not figured out what proportion of that would be Canada's saving, but the proportion must be very large.
Will the hon. member explain how one pound of coal can be saved? I have never heard 'that explained yet.

It is saved by not starting lighting plants so early in the day as
under the old system; that accounts for a very substantial saving in coal. Large quantities of coal oil are also saved by people not having to light their lamps so early. The saving in light and fuel has been enormous in the United States, and proportionately large in Canada.
Does the hon. member think, now the war is over, that it is desirable to save coal? Would it not be better to keep people digging it and keep all our industries going?

We have a Commission of Conservation in this country, the purpose of which is to conserve our natural resources, and I submit that if we can save two or three hundred thousand tons of coal, that is a saving worth while. I appreciate that I am in a decided minority in this House, judging by the speeches that have already been made, but I want to say that there never was a more popular measure than daylight saving so far as the big cities are concerned. The workers in my own plant and in my constituency-and I represent 90,000 industrial workers-are unanimously in favour of daylight saving; they think it is the greatest boon ever given to this country. On the other hand, if we do not enact this measure, there will be a state of great confusion in this country Tne hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) has said that daylight saving will mean that the farmer will have to get up an hour earlier to catch the milk train. But he will have to do that anyway, because the railways of this country are going to conform with the American time.

What
authority is there for that statement? I am very interested in this matter and would like to know from the Government whether it is a fact.

I saw the report in the newspapers, and I think we may take it for granted that our Canadian railways are going to conform with the American railway time. In the county of Haldimand the people did not adopt daylight saving last year, but held all their meetings in churches, schools and other places on the old time. I want to warn the House that if daylight saving is not adopted) by Parliament this year there will be a state of great confusion in our industries all over the country, because transportation is our principal industry, upon which all the others depend. I realize that the sentiment of the House as expressed is abso-

lutely against me, but I am here to represent my constituents and my personal opinion also is that daylight saving is one of the best measures that this Parliament has ever enacted.
At six o'clock the House took Tecess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I think that the Government should he fully informed as to the sentiments of the people on the daylight saving question. It is immaterial to me whether the proposed legislation is put into effect or not, and I may say that the people in the greater portion of the constituency from which I come are not interested in the matter either. They feel that there is ade-. quate daylight for all their purposes, and in fact more than enough. I am, therefore, able to look at the question from an absolutely unbiased standpoint. Some of the constituencies, however, think differently. I have travelled <a good deal and am satisfied that the farmers in Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan are almost unanimously opposed to any change. I do not propose for a moment to go into arguments from the farmers' viewpoint; they have already been advanced by others more qualified perhaps to speak on the subject than I who have had no actual experience on the farm. It has been suggested that there might be some difficulty or confusion in the railway service between the United States and Canada if there were a change of 'time, but I see no reason why there should be any more confusion in the service between the two countries than at different points along the lines in Canada, such as Port Arthur, Broadview and Field, where the time changes in any event. The prevailing sentiment in Manitoba has been fairly well expressed in the letter which has been read from Hon. Dr. Thornton, and I believe that the farmers generally throughout Canada are strenuously opposed to this proposed legislation. This is not a vital question to the future welfare of Canada, it is one that might well be left to the majority to decide; and if the minority should happen to be those who are in favour of daylight saving, then they have the privilege of legislating to suit themselves in their own cities and towns.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to put myself on record as being opposed to

the Daylight Saving Bill, although I supported it last year as a war measure. The arguments that have been advanced by the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) are practically identical with my own, and express the views of the people of the riding I have the honour to represent. My district is a dairy section. Some of the milk is shipped to Toronto but 95 per cent of it is sent to the Cheese factories. I believe that under the by-laws of the cheese factories that the milk drawer must be at the end of the route at five o'clock. If the change in time were effected that would mean four o'clock, and the farmer would have to rise too early. _
The Government has spent considerable money in an endeavour to educate the farmers in the proper methods of dairying, and one of the things which they have advocated is the regular milking of cows. It has become the practice to milk at five o'clock in the morning and at five in the afternoon. Five o'clock in the afternoon their hired help leave and the farmers are obliged to do the milking without assistance. Besides, the sun is still high at that time and it is more difficult and expensive to save the milk. The cheese companies have passed resolutions opposing daylight saving, and several have requested me personally to oppose it. The school sections are also strongly opposed to it; it is not necessary that I should give their reasons. The hon. member for East Peterborough has taken up this point and I agree with all he has said. The farmers' co-operative associations have passed resolutions against it. The county council of Hastings composed of thirty-one members-twenty-six farmers, and five members representing four villages and one town-have also unanimously expressed their disapproval of the proposal. Another disadvantage that attends the daylight saving is that the hired man is idle in the morning, while he loses an hour in the afternoon. Looking at the question from these standpoints therefore I do not think the Government should put this legislation into force.
I must commend them, however, for having given the members an opportunity of expressing their views on this question. As far as I can see there is no need for the amendment, and I am prepared to vote against the resolution.

I have listened with a great deal of attention and interest to the discussion, and the views of the farmers as expressed by various hon. members have my entire sym-

pathy. There is no doubt a grave feeling of unrest among the farmers, and I agree with the statement which has been made that the farmer's occupation is a very precarious one. Now if there is an unrest among the farmers, such as we have evidence of on all sides, it is the duty of the Government to address itself to this state of affairs and remedy such grievances as may exist for the day will come when the farmers will be industrially organized and will obtain their rights. I also agree with the statement made by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. T. H. Thompson) that the farmers should be at liberty to express themselves in this House.
But there is more than that goes with it: If the farmer is entitled to express his opinion in the House and it prevails, then the farmer has a right to rule this country as well as express his opinion here. The way in which this question has come up to-day brings to my mind, and will bring to the minds of the people of the country the responsibility that rests upon the Government of the day in dealing with this question, which cannot be made an open question and cannot be relegated to private members to settle. My contention is, although I may be wrong in my doctrine, that the Government must take the responsibility of dealing with this question. I have heard conversations of late in regard to the responsibility of the Government, and I thoroughly agree with what I have heard in those conversations, viz:-That while members may speak and express their opinion, the responsibility rests on the Government of the day of dealing with questions at issue, and especially of dealing with a question of this kind. The statement appears in to-night's evening papers that the Canadian Railway War Board, has assumed to deal with this question, and says that the daylight saving arrangement of the United States is to obtain in regard to the railroads of Canada. I would like to know at this point, if I can, whether the Government intend to assume responsibility for the policy of this Board. If it does, then we shall have daylight saving in spite of the expressions of opinion here, and especially in spite of the expression of opinion by the farmers. It would be a disappointment to the farmers, however, if they are merely to have the opportunity of expressing their views, and that in some way an irresponsible body, like the Railway War Board, shall assume to give us daylight saving in this country.
Then there is another view of the matter. This country forms part of the continent
of America, and we have, more or less perhaps, to continentalize our policy, daylight saving to-day is the rule and is the law in the United States. Heretofore the administration of our railways in this country has largely been based on the system that prevails in the United {states, and has worked in harmonious arrangement with the administration of the railways of that country; the two systems have always run together. I want to know whether, if this House votes, as I expect it will vote tonight, against daylight saving, the order that has gone forth of the Railway Board is to obtain, or whether the grievances that have been expressed here this afternoon as far as the farmers are concerned are to end in nothing? Will the Government tell us to-night that it intends to assume the responsibility on this question, and to be responsible for the acts of the Railway Board, or if it intends to recall, after the vote takes place to-night, the order that has gone out from the Railway Board? If the Government assumes that responsibility and recalls the order referred to, it will be a party to something that will result in great dislocation of the business interests of the country. An hon. gentleman sitting near me suggests that I should ask the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) now. If the minister cares to offer an opinion well and good, but I do not think I can fairly press him to do so. However, I want to point out first, the dislocation, as far as the business organization of America is concerned, which is involved in the present situation, and second that the Railway War Board, an irresponsible organization, proposed to retain daylight saving in Canada. I want the farmers to understand fairly what they are going to get. Are they to get daylight saving or not? Are they to be satisfied with a mere opportunity of expressing their dissent? There is a great deal of reason in that dissent. I say that although I voted for daylight saving and intend to vote for it again to-night, for I know what is the condition of the farmer in Canada. I am not going to say that I have tried to do a little farming myself, because it seems to be an offence for some of us who were born in the country, and who would like to have, and do have, a home in the country, to make such a confession. I have been unbraided in this House on account of that, and yet it is my right, and I intend to exercise it, to express my opinion. On behalf of the farmers I say that if the House to-night votes to defeat daylight saving then the farmers are entitled to get

the advantage of it. If not, the Government must assume responsibility for the action of the Railway War Board, and compel the farmers to submit to daylight saving, and I do not know what is going to be the outcome in that ease.
But I revert to the question that I have raised, that we must harmonize ourselves with the rest of the continent to which we belong. We have heard a good deal on that subject in this House. I disagreed to a certain extent with some hon. gentlemen in this House when the question was up before. But the more I study the question of the recent great war, and the more I see of it, the more I am convincel that it is the duty of this country to associate itself with the continent of America in the matters arising out of it, and to keep clear of, and keep away from, as much as possible, the present issues that are embroiling Europe. We have over there to-day, representing Canada, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice, the Overseas War Minister, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Customs. We have those ministers who, from my point of view, are butting somewhat into the affairs of Europe, and are open to the charge,-and I am not saying it in any spirit of disrespect,-that they are actually porch-climbing to get into the conferences of Europe.
Question.

I am talking to the question, I am talking to the question of responsibility. The Speaker may call me to order, but I wish to point out that in view of the responsibility that goes with this question, and what has taken place in Europe," our duty is to keep our country in harmony with the rest of the Continent, and not to dislocate our railway arrangements. I do not know whether other hon. gentlemen appreciate the situation; I have tried to appreciate it, I have studied the railway question. It may be that the dislocation that I fear will not occur, that the problem will be satisfactorily worked out. Nevertheless, I fail to understand how the great city of Toronto will maintain its business connection with the United States, or with the ports of Europe, unless we have harmonious arrangements, or how the city of Montreal, or the other great manufacturing centres of Canada will maintain their present situation.
Let them change their time table.

Changing their time table will not do it. Perhaps the Minister of Railways has a plan to meet the situation, and if he has I shall be only too glad to learn of it, and to understand it. As I size the situation up, however, our business is going to be dislocated, and it will be a very serious matter if we dislocate our transport service by such a change in the law as is proposed here tonight. Let me repeat that we have always arranged our railway policy so as to harmonize with that of the United States. There was a time when we had railways of broad gauge. That was the case with the old Great Western. But the gauge was brought to standard and into harmony with the American railroads.
There was a great business built up between the two countries and a great amount of traffic came to Canada because we had standardized our gauge, which enabled us to fake the traffic of the American roads and carry it over our lines to our own Atlantic ports or to the American ports. Today we are allowing the great New York Central line to handle from the Niagara frontier all its traffic which originates in Chicago and to carry it over its lines in Ontario to Buffalo and New York. Now, is all that to be dislocated? So, my contention is that the responsibility must be assumed by the Government, and the farmers who are voting for this change are entitled to get what they expect, and their expectation is that there is to be this dislocation of the railway transportation of Canada-that daylight saving is to be at an end in this country. I feel that it would be better to leave things alone and to try out daylight saving a little longer. Of course, the cities have the opportunity of passing by-laws that will give them daylight saving, and I know all our cities and manufacturing towns will have it.
I know that the farmers who have been expressing themselves here this afternoon have a grievance. They have to gei up too early in the morning in order, to ship -their milk to the cities. But if the Railway War Board at Montreal orders the railways to run on the daylight saving schedule, what is to become of the farmer?
May I ask the hon. member a question? What has the running of the railways to do with the farmers? What difference will it make to them even if you make the change to-morrow?

This is what the farmers say:	Ilf the trains run an hour
later in the morning they will get the bene-

fit of rising that much later. If the Railway War Board orders the railway companies to operate their train service on the daylight saving schedule the farmers are going to draw a blank. They think they are considering something else here this afternoon, and that an expression of their appreciation for the opportunity of stating their views on this question is all they want. I venture to say that they want something more:	They want results. And
again I say, after all this war experience we should be careful before abandoning daylight saving. During the war we had to change many things, we had to abandon, more or less, responsible Government and take refuge in commissions, and we are to-day dealing with the transportation question by means of ,a war measure; we have appointed a receiver for the Grand Trunk Pacific as a war measure; we are governing the country still by means of war measures, and probably we are going to have daylight saving as a war measure by this Government. But if that is the case is it not time that we had responsible Government in this country?
Let us have peace.

Let us have responsible Government first now the war is over. Let the farmers come here and express themselves, and if they express themselves in a certain direction, then if that expression of opinion by them is respected, they are entitled to carry on the Government of this country. That is the way it impresses me. I may be mistaken, but after studying this question very closely- and I am again speaking now from the business standpoint-I want to see the farmer have his grievance remedied in some way if possible, and a compromise may be effected, continuing to the cities and towns daylight saving in regard to . railways and other things, and allowing the farmer to make his own time to suit himself. I know that is rather hard and I confess it may not be feasible.
I want the House to be seized of what the issue really is. We have been talking all the afternoon and I have waited for some one to tell us how our railways were to be run, ami just at six o'clock I was made acquainted with a statement in the evening papers-I suppose it is correct- that the Railway War Board had settled that we were to have daylight saving. I will take the liberty of asking the Minister of Railways and Canals whether we are to have daylight saving in regard to our railways according to that statement?

I have not any word from the Canadian Railway War Board. Of course, the Canadian Railway War Board may make arrangements to run their railways on whatever time they like, but in so far as the operation of the railways is concerned they must be operated in the public interest. If they are not being operated in the public interest Parliament can correct that condition; and as we shall practically own half of the railway systems of Canada in a short time, I think Parliament can make the railways do whatever they like.

But I do not know yet from the statement of the hon. the Minister of Railways whether we are to have daylight saving. I hope he will give me credit for not speaking from a political point of view. I am trying to speak for many of the farmers of this country, I am also trying to speak for the business and the manufacturing and the railroad interests. I do not know what is going to happen to the railways who have this large transportation problem ahead of them retaining the very large international traffic which comes to them from their American connections. The funny thing is we are discussing this great question without a responsible proposition before the House. I do not remember a similar situation. Somebody must take the responsibility, and if the Government are convinced of the truth of the position of the farmers let them say: "All right; the farmers have made out their case and we assume responsibility of giving them the relief they ask." But we are told now by the Minister of Railways that the business interests of Canada are to be guarded. I am not going to abdicate my function as a member of this House by handing over this question to any irresponsible Railway War Board to deal with, and I do not think the Government ought to abdicate their functions or contract themselves out of their liability, as to the legal phrase is, but they must deal with this question, and I submit that before this discussion is over we ought to have a statement of the Government's policy.
Just one word more in regard to the advantages of daylight saving. These are many and have been demonstrated in the countries of Europe, and we are the first country to go back on what was called progressive legislation. The European countries may have been wrong, but I have seen no one yet who has brought forward a scientific explanation for the difference be-

tween our country and the countries of Europe on this question. A large portion of my reading has been in the direction of the increased benefit that has come to the working classes of this country by reason of daylight saving in connection with giving their children a little better chance, and my idea of the object of government is to improve human welfare. Now, if the farmer has a grievance it should be remedied. I do not feel justified in saying that the statements made by hon. gentlemen this afternoon with regard to the position of the farmer in this matter are not correct. If, then, they voice the views of the farmers, we must do more with regard to these grievances than merely allow them to be expressed in this House.
-Sir SA-M HUGHES:	Wouldn't the
simplest way be to let the farmers alone and let them mind their own business?

I am not interfering
with the farmers. The Canadian Eailway War Board has interfered with the daylight saving proposition; it has said that on Monday the clock is to be set back in every railway station.
Set forward. That is what the whole trouble is about.

The hon. gentleman intimates that there is trouble because somebody wants to set the clock forward. Will he, then, assume the responsibility of setting it forward. Somebody must assume responsibility in this matter. If the farmers are to get, what they are after, a declaration should be made by the Government that daylight saving is at an end and that the farmer will not have to get up earlier in the morning. But as a result of the order issued by this Railway Board, on Monday morning the farmer, willy nilly, will have to get up early to milk his cows and get his milk to the train in time for shipment. If he is to get what he wants, he ought to know it to-night. The business community and the railways should know to-night what the policy of tne Government is to be; otherwise each city will do as it likes in the matter, and instead of a well-ordered community we shall have something more or less in the nature of chaos. The members of tnis House should not go away to-night without knowing what is to be the law; without knowing whether the clock is to be put forward an hour next Monday, or whether it is to be left as it is.
Mr. P. R. DuTREMBLAY (Laurier-Outre-mont): Mr. Speaker, the cities and towns

of Canada, representing a majority of the people, are in favour of the daylight saving system, and more than half the rural population is in favour of it. This Parliament, therefore, should re-enact the daylight saving measure. I do not see what great inconvenience would thereby result to the afrmers. The daylight saving measure was given a good trial last year and it gave satisfaction; I did not meet a single person who believed that the measure was not a good one. I agree with the hon. gentleman who preceded me (Mr. W. F. Maclean) that the Government should take some stand in this matter. Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with all his eloquence, brought the Daylight Saving Bill before Parliament; he was very insistent upon having it passed, and for my part I was pleased to support it. Now that daylight saving has had such a good trial and the people have become accustomed to it, why does not the Government bring down a Bill to re-enact daylight saving for this year? Are they afraid to take the responsibility? It is not proper that the Government, which is supposed to lead the people, should not take responsibility in this matter. In the views which I express I voice the opinion of practically all the people of the great city of Montreal. On Sunday the hour will be changed in the United States, and failure to adopt the same system here will result in great inconvenience to our large centres, our railroads and our economic system generally. The suggestions of hon. gentlemen as to the complaints of the farmers are not based on facts. I hope, therefore, that a daylight saving Bill will be introduced and adopted by the House.	'

In order to have a clear expression of the views of the House on this matter, I wish to move, in amendment to the amendment:
That the words " until this day six months " be struck out of the amendment and the following substituted therefor:	" during the year
1919." .

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Mackie moves in amendment, seconded by Mr. Douglas (Strathcona) that the words "until this day six months" be struck out of the amendment, and that the following be substituted therefor:	"during the year
1919," so that the resolution will now read as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to re-enact during the year 1919, chapter 2, Statutes of 1918, "The Daylight-Saving Act, 1918."
That is not the amendment that I suggest. I ask that instead of giving the six months' hoist to the daylight saving proposal, the Bill be not introduced during the year 1919.
Will the hon. gentleman tell us what the effect of this amendment is? I want to vote intelligently.
The hon. gentleman ought to be able to see what the effect of it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
To make this matter quite clear to the House, I shall again read the sub-amendment. The resolution is as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to re-enact at once Chapter 2, Statutes of 1918, "The Daylight-Saving Act, 1918."
It was moved by Mr. McCoig, seconded by Mr. Ross:
That the said resolution be amended by replacing the words: " it is expedient to re-enact at once " by the words " it is not expedient to re-enact until this day six months."
It was moved as a sub-amendment by Mr. Mackie (East Edmonton), seconded by Mr. Douglas (Strathcona):
That the words " until this day six months " be struck out of the amendment and the following substituted therefor " during the year 1919."
The resolution as amended will read:
That in the opinion of this House, it is not expedient to re-enact during the year 1919 Chapter 2, 'Statutes of 1918, "The Daylight Saving Act. 1918."

Addressing a few remarks to the motion, the amendment and the amendment to the amendment, I think the House is quite clear on the main issue and both the amendment and the amendment to the amendment are of very little importance in this discussion.
As I listened to the various addresses, this is what I gathered, namely, that the principal objection to the so-called Daylight Saving measure is made on behalf of the farmers. Several reasons are given: First that the dairy interests are seriously affected in connection with the shipment of milk and other dairy products to the cities in the morning; second, that the farmers who have large areas of hoe-crops thereby lose an extra hour in the morning on account of the dew and so forth; third, that it interferes seriously with harvesting operations for the same reason; and fourth, that farm labour near the towns is also seriously interfered with. These
arguments deserve careful consideration on the part of every hon. member.
On the other hand, I desire to present to the House a few arguments in favour of daylight saving, and the House should consider both sides of the question and decide accordingly. I am speaking to-day on behalf of that great army of workers in Canada, particularly of those in the city which I represent, who spend long hours of confinement within the walls of the factory, shop and office, and also on behalf of the wives and families of those workers in the hot and ill-ventilated flats in the congested areas of tne cities. To all these the extra hour of daylight in the evening is unquestionably a great boon. It is of value to them from the standpoint of health as well as from the standpoint of adding, in a certain degree at least, to the small amount of pleasure they get in life.
It has been stated as a strong argument in favour of daylight saving that the United States of America has passed a similar measure, and that, therefore, we should follow suit. I have no sympathy with that argument, my opinion being that we should decide the matter as Canadians in our own country's interest.
I wish to refer to the argument advanced by some opponents of daylight saving that the only persons who are asking for it 'are the idle rich in the cities, a few gentlemen who wish to play golf and- so forth. That is not the case. I can assure my hon. friends who represent country districts that we do not represent that class of people, who can look after themselves pretty well. Where there is one individual of that class, there are a thousand or more of the other class to which I haye referred-the workers confined in the shops, factories or offices. It is on their behalf that I support the re-enactment 'of the daylight saving measure.

I feel to-night I am in agreement with the majority in this House, and that is a comfortable feeling to have. I am always inclined to say a good word for a departed friend, and I feel to-night, as we are attending what I consider to be the wake of the Daylight Saving Act, I should like, before it passes out of existence, to say a good word for it. A year ago I felt that it was a matter of very little concern whether the Daylight Saving Act came into force or not. I did not see much advantage in it, and I did not, at that time, see that there was going to be very much disadvantage.

After a year's experience, however, I have learned that daylight saving has advantages, and I should like to enumerate one or two which I have observed. We have today heard a good deal about the school children in the country, and I want to say a word or two on behalf of them. It is a great benefit to the school children in the country to be relieved, under daylight saving, from their school duties at three o'clock in the afternoon instead of being kept in school until four. That is a decided advantage which is perhaps not appreciated as it should be. It is far better for the welfare of the child to be in the schoolhouse from eight to nine o'clock in the morning and to be relieved at three o'clock rather than to go into the schoolhouse at nine and to remain there until four. The same argument may be used in behalf of the factory employee. The day is at hand when Parliament, employers of labour, educationists and others will have to give very much more attention to the physical welfare of the people, and anything which adds to the comfort and good environment of the factory employee is of advantage not only to the employee, but to the employer and to the country at large. If we can, under any measure, have the employees of a factory engaged from six to seven o'clock in the morning by sun-time, and relieved from their duties at five o'clock in the afternoon rather than have them entering on their duties at seven in the morning and being relieved at six in the afternoon, we are doing them a great favour, inasmuch as from five to six in the afternoon-and I am speaking of the factories in the small towns-is the worst hour of the day for the factory employee to spend in the factory employed at his work, because in the summer time it is the hottest hour of the day in the factory.
I would like to say a word for the people in the offices of our towns. I do not at all agree with some of the remarks made this afternoon which would lead us to believe that the farmer is the only person who works. While I know that no person works harder than the farmer, there are, in 'our offices, stores and factories, many people who are working just as hard as they possibly can.
They are not idle by any means, and because their work differs in kind from that of the farmer it does not mean that they are not being worked to the limit. I have found, during the past year, that daylight saving was an advantage to these people, allowing them to get away from their offices 
an hour earlier in the day and have that much more time for outdoor recreation. I believe that if we could total up the results of daylight saving during the past year we would find that the health of the people of this country has been considerably improved.

What about the flu?
Mr. STEEiLE: Having said that much, I think I have stated the chief advantages of daylight saving. But notwithstanding all these advantages, I think the disadvantages have been very much greater, and I therefore propose to vote against the re-enactment of daylight saving. I speak especially for the dairy farmers, inasmuch as I believe they are the ones who have been inconvenienced the most by the passage of the daylight saving measure. I want to say this to the people of our large cities: we hear a great deal of criticism these days of the producer of milk and the enormous profits he is getting, but it is my opinion that in the near future people will have to pay a good deal more for their milk than they are paying now. They can afford to pay a good deal more, and still be getting the cheapest food supplied to the people of this country. At fourteen cents a quart there is no cheaper food than milk, and when the people of the cities expect farmers to get up at three in the morning, milk their cows, haul the milk three, four, five, or six miles, and ship it to the city people so that they can get it early in the day, they are expecting something unreasonable from the agriculturists. I think the time is not far distant when the city dairies will have to have refrigerator cars left at points in many of our large cities, where the farmer can leave his milk at a convenient hour during the day. I must vote against the amendment to the motion. I cannot imagine how two representatives of agricultural constituencies could move and second such an amendment as was moved by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McOoig) and seconded by the hon. member for West Middlesex (Mr. Ross). Their amendment read: "That it is not expedient to re-enact this measure until this day six months." How any person can argue against daylight saving in the summer time and favour its coming into effect on the 26th day of September I cannot understand. Surely the farmers of Kent county will not sympathize at all with the attempt of their representative to bring daylight saving into force on the 26th of September, and I am equally confident that the farmers of West Middlesex will

not approve such a move. I shall vote against the motion also, for the reasons which I have given. I believe it is in the best interests of this country that it should not carry, and I am quite satisfied that the majority of my electors are opposed to it.

I have not any pronounced views upon this question, except that uniformity throughout the whole country is very desir-
9 p.m. able. Still, in view of the large number of petitions and resolutions I have received, I feel that I must say a word. One resolution I received was from the county council of Norfolk, which county I have the honour to represent, declaring unanimously against daylight saving. I have also received petitions from farmers' clubs and many other organizations and associations, all opposed to the measure, also several letters from residents of towns stating that we should favour the views of the farmers. Then, Sir, in keeping with the new order of things which has come into this world and which will remain so long as the world lasts-this beautiful world clothed everywhere with garments of Deity but now desecrated by the violence of man-in keeping, I say, with this new order in which women are not merely followers but great leaders in every movement which is for the welfare of the people; I have received an angelic petition from a group of mothers asking me to oppose this measure. Under the circumstances I feel perfectly justified in voting for. the amendment to the amendment and against the resolution.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks made by the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) this evening, as I always do, particularly when he is speaking on matters pertaining to agriculture. iMy interest was aroused by the hon. member some years ago, when he suggested that the problem of farm labour be	solved by	the farmers
hiring two shifts of men, working eight hours each.	His close and * intimate
knowledge of farming conditions made a deep impression upon me at that time, and I have since listened with very great interest indeed to the words of wisdom which always fall from his lips. But I thought he came very near to violating the second paragraph of rule 18 this evening; if he was not violating that rule in the matter of irrelevance, he was dangerously close to violating it in the matter of tedious
repetition. 1 am also in the habit of listening with interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), who is also the distinguished member from the rural constituency of Gaspe. I represent only one constituency in this House, but it is perhaps the most strictly rural constituency in the Dominion of Canada, because there is not within its bounds a city or town or even an in-coroporated village. It is very convenient indeed to be in the position of the non. member for Maisonneuve, representing as he does, two constituencies, one a city constituency and the other a rural constituency; and it is particularly convenient when a matter of this kind comes up on which there is a certain amount of conflict between the people who reside in the cities and those who reside in the country; because if the hon. member wants to keep in line with the rural population he represents Gaspe, and if he wishes to line up with the city dwellers, he is the distinguished member for Maisonneuve, which is an urban constituency.
I rise on this occasion for two reasons: First, because, representing a rural constituency, I think I should express my opposition to the re-enactment of the daylight saving measure; second, because I want to propose a solution of this vexed question So far, it has been considered from only one standpoint. Daylight saving proposes that every person should get up one hour earlier than in normal times and quit work one hour earlier in the afternoon, thus having an hour for play at the end of the day's work. Why not turn the clock the other way, and instead of getting up one hour earlier in the morning and quitting one hour earlier in the afternoon, get up one hour later in the morning and quit work one hour later in the afternoon? Then those who are interested in daylight saving-'the dry goods clerks and the golf enthusiasts-could get up in the morning and play golf.
Then they will appreciate what it means to play golf when the dew is on the ground, and at the same time will realize the position of the farmer who has to go to work in the morning when the dew is heavy. Of course, if they played golf in the morning on moist ground they might probably soil their canvas shoes, and their fingers when they handled the ball, but they would find the atmosphere just as exhiliarating in the early morning as at any other time; and I venture to say that if they took their recreation at that time they would find



that the farmer had been at work an hour before them at that. I am told also that those who indulge in the game of golf and similar semi-manly recreations are people who have rather a tendency to stoutness; and, as I am credibly informed that the early morning dew is almost a specific for gout, there is an added reason why it would be advisable to change the time around and take this hour for recreation and pleasure in the forenoon and not rob the farmer of his best hour in the day.
Seriously, Mr. Speaker, I object to reenactment of the daylight saving law because I believe that the vast majority of the people in the country are opposed to it. I am sure that the hon. gentleman who moved the resolution was perfectly sincere when he gave his opinion as to the percentage of those in favour of daylight saving. I do not question his sincerity, but 1 certainly question the correctness of his figures. I believe that if a census of opinion were taken on this question it would be found that fully sixty per cent of the people very determinedly and positively oppose it, and of the other forty per cent, half would be as strongly in favour of daylight saving while the other half would be indifferent. That is a fair representation of the sentiment of the country, I think, whether it represents the sentiment of the House or not. I am opposed to the re-enactment of the measure because it not only puts the farmers to unnecessary inconvenience but subjects them to considerable financial loss as well. Some will probably disagree with me in the statement, but I am convinced that I am right when I say that last year considerable financial loss to the farmers attended daylight saving. Not only does it inconvenience the farmer, but it imposes extra work on the housewives in the rural part of the country and the wives of the labouring classes in our large centres of population. Who is benefited by it, and from what source comes the request for daylight saving? The newspapers? Why, certainly. It is all very well for the newspaperman who gets down to his office at eight o'clock in the morning and whose staff may want to go off in the afternoon; and there are no doubt a number of clerks who would like the change. But the farmers and the great bulk of the people who are working in factories and industrial plants, people who have to be at their work at seven o'clock in the morning, do not. I think, really want this law. Should we follow the example of the United States? I think not. Let us legislate for ourselves.

Conditions in Canada are not the same as those in the United States. One hon. member referred to the fact that England, France and Germany had adopted daylight saving. Well, what of that? Has that anything to do with Canada? The conditions in those countries are absolutely different. The hon. gentleman forgot that we have only a few people to the square mile in Canada while in the countries to which he referred there are one hundred, two hundred or three hundred people to the square mile. The population in each of those countries is very largely urban, dwelling almost entirely in the cities and towns, while the rural population is only a small percentage. Canada on the contrary is a rural country.
A few years ago the Government thought it wise to adopt on government works an eight-hour day. I expressed myself against the measure on former occasions, because I considered the adoption by the Government of an eight-hour day made it just that much harder for the farmers and the people in farming communities to obtain the help that was necessary to work their farms. That was one concession that the Government made to the labouring class when they agreed to the eight-hour day on government works, and I ask them now to make a concession to the farming .class in regard to this matter of daylight saving. I do not think there can be the shadow of a doubt in the mind of any member of the House, after having heard the speeches delivered this afternoon, that the farmers are opposed to the Daylight Saving Bill. And if hon. gentlemen in this House believe that to be a fact, I ask them to respect the wishes of the farmers in this matter and vote accordingly.
Hon. MARTIN BURREiLiL (Secretary of State): My hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) was very much surprised that a resolution of this kind was put on the Order Paper or permitted to be taken up at this time, and he seemed to think that not only was there no need for it, but that the people did not want it in any shape or form. I must differ from him in that view, because I think that however we may vote-and I may frankly say that I will support the resolution-it is not at all a bad thing to have had this free and open discussion in Parliament on a question in which there is considerable interest, and which, after all, is not .a political question in the ordinary sense of that word. I do not think my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best), quite did justice to the mover

of the resolution when he placed him in the position of having interjected a question, and said that he was engendering very bitter strife between large sections of the community. I did not so understand the mover of the resolution. I understood him to say that there would be a n.atural conflict of opinion between the rural and urban sections. I think my hon. friend from Dufferin need not have been so warm in some of his remarks, because after all, Sir, we can afford to hold different views and express them temperately.
II cannot agree with the statement made by some opposing the resolution that as low as three per cent of the population is in favour of such a resolution. iMy hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), I observe, put it very much higher. Of course we can only guess on a subject of this kind, but I think it is interesting to have the various opinions held in the different constituencies reflected by hon. members in the House.
I do not think *that the method of approaching this subject is particularly to be deprecated, as my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) seemed to think. Some hon. members who have spoken have accused the Government of shirking responsibility on a question for which they ought to shoulder responsibility. Again and again in this House, I have heard hon. gentlemen complain that in democratic governments the tendency is for the Government to run the whole country and make their followers fall into line by the threat that otherwise the Administration would be smashed. I am rather inclined to agree with my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) that it is not a bad thing on a question like this to have a free discussion in the House, and to feel that even if members of the Government hold divergent views in regard to it they would still be justified in continuing to hold office. I am glad of that because on this question I may find myself differing from my distinguished friend from Leeds (Sir Thomas White).
However, there were one or two remarks made during the debate that I want to answer. Some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken very strongly against daylight saving have stated that they believed it to be a good thing as a war measure, and they supported it last year on that account. I may be dense, or I may not perhaps have given the argument sufficient attention, but if daylight saving is good as a war measure because it instilled more energy into our people and caused more produc-
58J
tion in this country, it surely must be an equally good measure for Canada in days of peace.
I thought that my hon. friend from South Perth (Mr. Steele), who finds himself in the position of having to vote against the resolution, supplied one of the strongest arguments that I had yet heard in favour of the measure, when he gave it as his deliberate conviction, as a medical man, that on the whole the health of the people of Canada had been greatly improved through the operation of this legislation. If that is so I think it is a priceless blessing to achieve. The hon. gentleman also spoke of the very beneficial effects upon people who were working in factories, school children, and so on, that had resulted from the change in time. I am not disposed to dispute for one moment that in many respects daylight saving may have been somewhat detrimental to certain classes, and especially to the farming interests. I remember when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) first mooted the idea of this legislation I was then Minister of Agriculture. Sir George Foster seemed to think that the whole country was in favour of it, but I told him at that time that I was inclined to believe that a large section of the farming community would be against it. He said he had given a great deal of attention to the subject, and I think he had ascertained the feelings of a very large portion of the community. It is true that the view held in the country with respect to this matter may have changed somewhat. I am prepared to admit that a great many of the farming section, possibly most of them, are against it, and it therefore became a matter of balancing conditions.
One of the things that I do think has a material effect upon this question as it presents itself to-day is the operation of the railways, and the fact that in the United States daylight saving is in operation. My hon. friend from South York tried to throw some responsibility on the Government. He demanded that it should control the railways and compel them not to observe daylight saving, if this House, by its vote, decided that it should not be adopted. Well, my hon. friend must know that this is a question of railway operation and of railway time tables. Surely he would not lay down the principle that because the railways are adopting daylight saving and alter their time tables they should not continue to have the power they have always had of running their trains at certain particular times? I must say that I am not convinced yet that if the

railways are altering their time tables by an hour, and that consequently the large business interests of the country, the financial institutions, and so on, with their ramifications, are also going to observe the difference of an hour, in the main it will not lead to a very great deal of confusion and loss if the whole country does not carry out the same policy.
Looking at this matter from the British Columbia point of view, I may say that I represent a constituency very largely rural. Perhaps I do not. know the exact feeling which prevails throughout the province, but Ido not know that in my visits to British Columbia last fall I never heard a single word against the operation of the daylight saving law. I believe it was the opinion and the expectation of those people out there that it would naturally follow that daylight saving would continue this year, and the only communications I have had on the subject at all have been communications expressing gratification that daylight saving had been accomplished.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards)-not very seriously I am bound to admit-suggested that some of this campaign was instigated by gentlemen who do a lot of golfing. I am almost afraid to admit that although I was a farmer for twenty-five years I am still a golfer, and I am not, as he pictured, an exceedingly stout person or suffering from any physical disability of that kind. Nor do golfers always wear canvas shoes, which are exposed to the dampening influence of the dew. Daylight saving is .popular with the people in cities and towns, and I recognize the truth of the statement of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Cooper) that the workers in the stores and factories strongly support it. Personally, I am going to vote for the resolution and against the amendment. Whatever effect this particular resolution may have-according to my hon. friend from South Perth, it is almost dead now and we have come to assist at the burial-I am convinced that it is an excellent thing to have a question of this kind form the subject of a general discussion, and to afford to every hon. member an opportunity of voting on it without the question of party allegiance being raised. I think that it will be the means of fixing the attention of the whole country in a way that it has never been fixed before, and will ultimately lead to its being settled in a manner that will be for the good of Canada as a whole.

Lt.-General Sir SAM HUGHES (Victoria) :	I remember many years ago hearing an American stating that his doctrine in religious matters was to go to Hades his own way, and let everybody else go theirs. That is largely my doctrine on this question. I have not the slightest objection in the world to the people of the cities and towns advancing the clock an hour in the morning. If they think they can make a little better time in getting to or leaving their offices, they are welcome to it, but I am certainly opposed to upsetting the whole industrial conditions of the Dominion of Canada by enacting a statute of this kind. There is not a municipality in Canada to-day but can bring about the desired result by passing a by-law. As a matter of fact, in many towns to-day throughout Canada the whistles are started blowing at five o'clock, half-past five, six o'clock, six-thirty or seven o'clock, as the case may be. That procedure goes on and there is no great worry or turmoil over it; people adapt themselves to their environment. Those in the towns and cities who want their time advanced can easily find the machinery to do. it. But I protest, on behalf of the farming community, and those who do not want to have legislation of this kind forced upon them, against this kind of thing. This talk of it being a war measure is the merest piffle which has been resorted to in the case of any one with a fad to advocate until it has become nauseating.
The farming community want to be let alone. They say the old standard time is good enough for them. I am not very old yet, but I can remember, Sir, when Toronto had one time, then at Donlands we had to set our watches ahead a few minutes, we had to do the same thing when we got to Dumbarton, and I remember in the town of Bowmanville where I grew up we were four minutes ahead of Toronto in our time. Our watches had to be adjusted when we moved up and down the country one or two miles, and yet the people survived, they raised their grain and sold it, and got along very well without any standard time. Then standard time came in, and I remember on one occasion being in St. John where I found they had three different times; the old meridian time, the standard time, and some eastern or Atlantic seaboard time, so that you never knew what time any one was going to travel by. Yet St. John thrived and things went on quite satisfactorily. Therefore I take the liberty of suggesting to the Government that there should be no further interference

with our standard time. The farmers are content with the old standard or meridian time, but they have no objection to the cities and towns passing by-laws to put the clock ahead or back an hour to suit their own convenience. Daylight saving is all very well for those people who are fond of the pleasant pastime at which my hon. friend the Secretary of State is such an expert-golfing is a very pleasant exercise foi delicate women-and I have no objection in the world to cities and towns regulating their own time, but in the name of Heaven let us alone. Down in the city of Windsor they have one time, across the river another time. At Port Arthur our time is the same as it is at Sarnia; at Fort William, which is the dividing line, it is an hour ahead. So we have all that strip of Canadian territory from the Detroit line to Port Arthur with an hour's difference in time. I think there is a great deal of meddling in connection with this whole business, and I, Sir, shall vote to let the matter remain as it is without any interference with the standard time, leaving each municipality to regulate its affairs as it wishes.

Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to discuss the merits of daylight saving legislation. I am going to express my opinion upon it when I cast my vote, and I think after the discussion we have already had it is the best way to express it; but I want to vote on a motion wfiich is according to the Rules of the House, and 'I rise therefore for the purpose of raising a point of order against the amendment to the amendment as moved by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Mackie). The main resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to re-enact at once Chapter 2, Statutes of 1918, "The Daylight-Saving Act, 1918."
That statute, chapter 2 of the statutes of 1918, reads as follows:
2.	During the prescribed period in each year in which this Act is in force, the time, for general purposes in Canada, in each province, shall he one hour in advance of the time which under the law of the province is the time prescribed for such province, and, if there is no time so prescribed, of the accepted standard time.
3.	This Act shall be in force during the present year for such time as may be prescribed by the Governor in Council.
If the main resolution is adopted it will mean that this 'Act shall.be in force during the present year, that is the year 1919. So the amendment to the amendment,
which merely says that it is not expedient during the year to enact this legislation, is merely a negation of the main motion-and is not in order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In respect to the point of order raised by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) I must point out that he refers to a statute, while the resolution before the House is merely an academic one, or one calling for an expression of opinion on the part of the House, and it would have no effect upon the legislation of the country whatsoever. Therefore it resolves itself into a question purely of phraseology, as to whether the amendment to the amendment is actually an amendment to the amendment. In my judgment it is, because the motion calls for the enactment of a statute at once; the amendment says that it shall be enacted in six months; the amendment to the amendment says it shall not be enacted for at least one year. iSo it is an amendment in question of time, and in my judgment therefore it ig in order.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite concur in the views of the hon. gentlemen who have expressed their satisfaction at the manner in which we have been permitted to discuss this question. I know there are times when it is necessary that the Government shall accept the responsibility of a measure, but I think it would make for every good end if we had more frequent opportunities to discuss matters in the free and open way in which this House has had this matter before it to-day. I have only received one communication on this subject from my constituents; it is against the Diaylight Saving Act. Strange to say it does not come from a rural community, it comes from one of the incorporated towns within my constituency. In the town of Shelburne* the shire town of one of my counties, the Board of Trade has passed a -strong resolution against daylight saving, and the secretary in transmitting it to me informs ihe that the views of 'that community are in harmony with the action- of the board. Any hon. member will realise at once that the decision of an important body like a Board of Trade in one of our towns calls for profound consideration and respect from the representative of the county, and I certainly receive it in that way. That is one side of the question. The other side is this: Last year I briefly spoke and voted for the Daylight Saving Bill. After that I had an opportunity of visiting my constituents and

spending some time amongst them, and I am bound to say that no one offered any objection to the course I pursued so far as I heard; Wherever the question interested them at all they were perfectly satisfied and content. So I have on the one hand the apparent satisfaction of the [DOT] whole community, and on the other hand 1 have this resolution of the Board of Trade of one of my towns, to which I should like to pay great respect. Taking it all in all, I am inclined to think I have not found sufficient reason to change the ground which 1 took last year.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to the question now before the House, I should like to endorse the sentiments of the hon. gentleman from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding). I am thoroughly in accord with the course that the Government has adopted to-day, and I am not in accord with the course that the member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has taken. It would appear to me to be much better for this House and for this country that the members of this House should express their itrue opinions, rather than that they should express them wholly and solely under patty patronage, so to speak. The Acting Prime Minister '(Sir Thomas White) has very frankly risen an his place and said that the Government desired an expression of Opinion from this House.
He desired that the members of the House should voice their own opinions or the opinions of their constituents without regard to party. The member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) seemed to ask that somebody should take the responsibility, but suggested that he -should not; in other words, he wanted to be allowed to get in under the wing of the Government and say later to his constituents that he followed the Government, or did not, whichever suited his purpose. The course, therefore, followed by the Government in this matter is a fit and proper one.
We know from the experience of last session that a very decided cleavage of opinion prevails in this matter as between the urban and the rural population, between the country districts and the cities, towns and villages. The petitions and expressions of opinion that have been received by the great majority of members of the House from rural districts indicate that daylight saving is decidedly unpopular in the country and that the farmers do mot desire it. It appears to me, representing, as I do, a constituency made up of

both urban and rural districts, that, taking all things into consideration, the requests of the rural population in this case ought to be acceded to. It is true that there are two extremely arguable sides to the question, but the urban districts have unquestionably not expressed their view in as concrete and forcible a way as have the rural districts. Having regard to what the farmers have done for this country, considering the extent to which the prosperity of Canada depends on the rural interests and the definite manner in which those interests have expressed their opinion that the re-enactment of daylight saving would be absolutely detrimental to them, it is the duty of this House to listen to those representations and to carry out the suggestion contained in them.
Mr. GEORGE B. NICHOLSON (Algoma East): Like some other members, I represent a constituency the population of which is about equally divided between those whose business is agriculture and those who work in factories, saw-mills and mines. So far as I have been able to judge, just as much difference of opinion exists on one side as on the other. I took the opportunity of going all over the agricultural part of my constituency during the harvest season and finding out what the farmers thought of daylight saving. Many of them were decidedly opposed to it; many of them expressed absolute indifference. I found the same attitude among the men working in factories, in mines and in railway services. So that, so .far as my constituents are concerned I am possibly not compelled to take any particular standf in this matter.
In this whole discussion there has been too great a tendency to regard this daylight saving proposal as something in the nature of a class measure. Many references have been made to the millionaires and the golf-players, and not enough consideration has been given to the large number of people in the urban centres who are neither millionaires nor golf-players and who work in shops and factories ten hours a day. These men say to me: It is a decided advantage for us to have our leisure moments all at one end of the day, and that in the evening. But it has been pointed out to us that the daylight saving system works a great disadvantage to a large number of people who work on and are interested in farms, and we are willing to forego the advantage accruing to us by the enactment of daylight saving in order to do away with the disadvantage resulting to our agricultural population. Ii

the subject was discussed from that point of view, without any effort to create prejudice in the minds of any class of the people, we would arrive at a more satisfactory conclusion. My judgement is that in the interests of harmony those of us who benefit by daylight saving should be willing to forego the advantage accruing to us from it in order that the agricultural interests may have their way, so to speak. Unquestionably 95 per cent of the people interested in agriculture throughout Canada are opposed to daylight saving, notwithstanding what I said regarding my own constituency. I am going to vote against the resolution, without regard to the amendments, because I believe that the re-enactment of the daylight saving measure would not be in the interests of harmony among all the classes of people in this country. I suggest that hon. members should discuss subjects of this kind on their merits. Many of the class differences prevailing in Canada are largely due to the activities of loose-lipped agitators who do not hesitate to take advantage of every opportunity to encourage these differences, having very little regard to the merits of the subjects they discuss.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
I wish to say just a word or two on this resolution because of the fact that the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) laid particular stress on the railway situation. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, it is expedient to re-enaot at once Chapter 2, Statutes of 1918, "The Daylight Saving Act, 1918."
I cannot see any necessity at all for an amendment to the original resolution on which I should like to have seen a straight vote. Be that as it may, however, two amendments have been moved which, if carried, really mean that the resolution should not be adopted. When the Government introduced the Daylight Saving Bill last year, one thing that had a great deal of influence on the passing of that legislation was the fact that from one end of the Dominion to the other the people were undoubtedly led to believe and, I think, hon. estly-that we were short of fuel and that everything possible should be done, in the interest of the public and in the interest of the war, to conserve fuel. Therefore, when the Bill was introduced, the farmers of Canada, being willing, as they were during the whole war, to make any sacrifices necessary to bring the war to a successful issue, decided to give up what they believed was of
great value to them and perhaps make a sacrifice in order to conserve fuel and thereby furnish more ammunition and give better service to the men at the front.

May I ask the minister a question? I have asked it of several members and I have not yet received an answer. I should like to know how one pound of coal has been saved through the Daylight Saving Act.

Whether any fuel was saved
or not, there was at all events a feeling throughout the country that a shortage of fuel existed and that fuel might be saved as a result of daylight saving. For centuries, we have had a standard time in this country; we have got along very well under it; there has never been any trouble, and I want to say frankly that since since my birth I have, been satisfied with the standard time, and have not wanted it changed and would like to see it continued as in the past. There is, however, a difference of opinion on this question throughout Canada. As the hon. member for South York has stated, the most serious matter at present is the way in which it will affect the railways of Canada. He asked me for an answer as to what the railways would do. The railways are being operated under their own managements, and unless some trouble should arise and complaint is made to the Government, the Government will, of course, not interfere. When trouble arises and complaint is made the Government, of course, are supreme in this country in so far as rectifying anything that may not be in the public interest is concerned. I do not know what the railways will do, but frankly I cannot see that the situation that may arise will be as serious as has been represented.
