Travelling from here to Vancouver, one retires to bed at night and when one gets up the next morning the time is changed one hour. One moves one's watch ahead, and the change does not seem to make much difference; one gets along just the same. My view, therefore, is this, that when a train arrives at the Canadian side of the boundary line the time will be changed the one hour's difference, just the same as occurs on the time-tables of trains going from here to Vancouver. There is only this difference- and what effect it will have I cannot say- that on transcontinental trains the time is changed at divisional points. The question has been asked: What effect will this have where trains are crossing the boundary not at a divisional point? No one can answer that question until the thing has been tried.

There is no doubt, however, the railways of Canada will, in their own interest, make their time-tables to suit the interest of the people they are serving. But after all, we have, as hon. members know, the Board of Railway Commissioners, which has full power and jurisdiction over all the railways in Canada in rates and time-tables, and the interests of the people are guarded by that board, from which there is an appeal to the Governor in Council and from that to the Parliament, which is supreme. Personally, I should like to have the old standard time retained in Canada. I believe the cities can change the time to suit themselves, as has been done in other places.

Does my hon. friend, as Minister of Railways, not think that, on the first of April next, when the time tables of the American railway systems are changed, the Canadian railways will have to adapt their time tables to those of the American railways?

I am not doing any
thinking until the thing is done and I see what the arrangement is. I will then do some thinking as to whether it is in the interest of this country or not. When one is crossing at Detroit and other places, the time table shows one hour's difference. The standard tim'e is changed at American points, for instance at Rouse's Point. At present you leave New York at a certain hour and arrive at a certain hour at Montreal. I cannot see why the trains cannot simply change the time at Rouse's Point and run on Canadian time into Montreal. Perhaps, I am not an expert railwayman and so cannot see the effect of the situation on the railways of Canada, but this is a case where we should vote as our constituents want us to. I am quite satisfied from the petitions I have from my constituents that they are absolutely opposed to the daylight saving scheme, and until I feel that it is in the public interest to make a change, I consider it my duty to vote as my constituents would have me vote.
Mr. S. .T. CROWE (Burrard): I was not very imuch in favour of the daylight saving Act last year, but after watching its operation last summer I am certainly in favour of its re-enactment this year. I believe that I am voicing the sentiments of my constituents when I say that ninety per cent of them are in favour of daylight saving. I have heard very little criticism of the measure. I have received quite a number of telegrams and communications 
from the city of Vancouver, of which I am one of the representatives, and all these communications strongly endorse daylight saving. This afternoon my colleague from South Vancouver (Mr. Cooper) received a telegram from the Reeve of the Municipality of Point Grey, which, as it arrived after he had finished speaking, he has asked me to read to the House. It is as follows:
Point Grey Council, on behalf of the citizens, favours daylight saving and requests your urgent efforts towards that end.
George Fletcher,
Point Grey.
I received telegrams yesterday from the different athletic associations in the city of Vancouver, also a wire from the Retailers' Association of Vancouver, as well as a letter from the Kiwanis Club of that city, all in favour of daylight saving. I think myself that daylight saving is in the best interests of the great majority of the people of this country, and that is why I am going to support the resolution.

It seems to me there is a very important preliminary question to be determined before we vote to-night. The Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Reid) has not in ,my judgment cleared up the situation. Now, as I understand it, those hon. members who desire to vote against daylight saving will find themselves in this position, if the resolution is agreed to: The railways of Canada will follow the time tables of their American connections, and the result will be that instead of the farmers of Canada avoiding the disadvantage which some hon, members see in daylight saving, the trains will run an hour earlier just as they did last year. I therefore think that before we vote on this question we should have some assurance from the Government that if this House refuses to accept this resolution, the railways of Canada will not change their time tables but will run on standard time.
What have we to do with the railway time tables?

Everything. I am satisfied that the Canadian railways will change their time on Sunday next, and that means they will run their trains an hour earlier than at present. Then those who voted against daylight saving will have daylight saving in effect so far as train connections are concerned.

What effect will the
change of time have on any railways except those that cross the border?
It will affect every railway in Canada.
But why should it, except those that cross the border?

My hon. friend must realize
that a train leaving Ottawa this afternoon for New York must cross the border and-
I am speaking of the trains that do no't cross the border.

It seems to me the question has been discussed thoroughly, and I shall say only a few words. There appears to be a difference of opinion between the rural and urban population of Canada. As a farmer, and as a representative of an agricultural constituency, I am decidedly opposed to daylight saving. There is no question that it does a financial injury to the farmer by reason
of the fact that he loses an hour each day at the season of the year when time is most precious. Under daylight saving he rises by the clock as usual, does his chores, and is ready to proceed to the fields to cut his hay or grain probably at eight o'clock, but if the dew is heavy he will be unable to do anything until half-past nine or ten. That hour and a half is practically lost. Then, in the afternoon he has to stop at lour or five o'clock-five o'clock at any rate but usually at four-if he has chores to do; so that it is a direct financial loss to him. On the other hand, I can quite appreciate the fact that the urban population is strongly in favour of daylight saving. I am willing to grant that the opinion is fairly evenly divided pro and con on this question. But that is not the point. The urban population have only this to claim for daylight saving, namely, that it gives them an hour more in the evening in which to enjoy themselves, or to rest, although it does not benefit them financially, whereas, against that, the farmer argues that he does suffer a direct financial loss, and it does not seem to me under these circumstances that there can be any question as to what the decision of this House ought to be.
As to what has been said to-night with reference to the railways, I can conceive, if the report which we see in the press tonight is correct, that the Railway War Board has ordered all railways in Canada to adopt the American time on the 31st of March, all farmers who ship milk, cream and other produce in the morning will be compelled to adopt daylight saving. I do not doubt that this is attributable to the action of the United States, and am not disposed to blame the Railway Board, because I do not see how we can help adopting the time of the United States roads. We have either to do that or hold our trains up on the border for an hour.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
I occupy the somewhat unique position, Mr. Speaker, of having voted on both sides of this question during the last two years. When this matter came up in 1917 I criticised it very severely. In fact I gave what some newspaper called a very learned dissertation on the whole theory of standard time and other allied subjects, and as a result of the severe criticism which was levelled at the Bill it was withdrawn by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). Last year, in order to bring ourselves in harmony with practically all the rest of the

world, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was very anxious to put the Bill through, did me the honour of naming me as his seconder. Therefore, like many other hon. members I voted for the Bill. Now it comes up again, and as a member of the Government I take some credit for putting this matter up to the representatives of the people as we have done. I do not believe in the party whip system, as it has operated, I think, to the disadvantage of'Canada in public life in the past. There has been too much, on the part of both Government and Opposition, of a practice of a dozen men or fewer getting together and outlining a policy and expecting the others to accept it. I realize that under the system of responsible government the great majority of matters that are really questions of policy must be decided by a government, and the government must stand or fall by the vote oi the majority of the representatives. But this is not, in my judgment, a question of government policy. It is a question merely of what is best for the country. I was very much in favour of submitting this question to the House, and I am glad to see that the House accepted it in the spirit in which the Government put it forward, notwithstanding the objection of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean). I shall not enter into the merits of the question from the standpoint of either the farmer or the resident of the city. I am a farmer myself to some extent-my hon. friend smiles.
To what extent?

Well to the extent that I make some money, I am happy to say.
I am a farmer, and I can agree with every word 'said by the farmers. In the part of Canada from which I come we lose not only an hour, but an hour and a half, because we are on the extreme western edge of the Atlantic standard, and our standard time is half an hour faster than sun time. When you add another hour to that, instead of leaving work at six o'clock during hay and harvest we leave at half past four. The same condition of affairs exists in Western Manitoba and near the Rocky Mountains, and wherever you get beyond the meridian when the standard time is in advance of sun time, until you reach a point where you are an hour and a half ahead of sun time, which makes it almost impossible for the farmers to get along. This, however, has been so thoroughly discussed by hon. members that I do 
not intend to pursue this phase of the subject. I shall now deal with the question in its relation to the railways. I am aware that there is a very strong prejudice by the railway companies in favour of the adoption of daylight saving, not so much, perhaps, because of any intrinsic advantage in the scheme, as that the United States, having adopted it, great inconvenience and difficulty will arise in the operation of the Canadian trains if we do not follow suit. It has been pointed out that there are many places in Canada where railways will be compelled to run an hour earlier than they do at present simply because the United States has adopted daylight saving. There must be twenty-five or more places in Canada where trains run across the border. There is no doubt that a train that starts from New York bound for Montreal or Toronto will leave an hour earlier than ordinarily and arrive at its destination an hour earlier, and the man who desires to travel by that train has to rise an hour earlier than usual. But there are a great many other places where it will mean an advantage rather than a disadvantage. At four different points between the Atlantic and the Pacific the time now changes one hour, and on every train that goes from the Atlantic to the Pacific the clocks must be changed so many times. There are two places in my own constituency where Canadian trains running into the United States are now compelled to change time by one hour. To-day they are compelled to change the time an hour in crossing from Windsor to Detroit or from Sarnia to Port Huron, whereas under this arrangement there would be no change. It is therefore apparent that while there are disadvantages there are also corresponding advantages. I have consulted some of the railway men, and will state their argument in favour of the adoption of daylight saving.
I was not able to attend during all the debate, and possibly what I am about to say may be a repetition of what has been said before. If it is, the House will pardon me. The railway men admit that there is no difficulty in operating the trains where the time changes at divisional points because that is done all over the country. But there are certain places where trains cross the international boundary line which places are not divisional points and where there are no telegraph offices. An engineer running a freight train in the night may be handed an order that he is to stop at a certain hour. Either the train despatcher may make a mistake in not properly calculating the time, or the engineer may make a mis-

take, and there is liable to be an accident.
I am not sufficient of a railway man to answer yes or no to that, or to say whether there is a great deal to it, but I will state this: I have found that most of the things that are held up as reasons for opposing a measure can be overcome if men want to overcome them. I have a great deal more faith in the ability of the Canadian railway companies and their very intelligent employees than to believe that it is impossible that they can work out a little matter like this. If they can work out a change of time at all these different points, moving from east to west across the continent, it seems to me they will not have much difficulty in arranging for changes of time when moving from north to south.
I also realize that it is a great convenience to people living in cities and towns to have the time advanced an hour.
I think any person will admit that. But I do not agree that I am compelled, because of something that is a convenience to the dwellers in the cities and towns, to vote for a measure which, to my own personal knowledge, will result in great loss to the farming community. It is not a question of convenience or inconvenience to the farmers, it is one of absolute money loss; there is not a farmer in this House -I think there is scarcely one in the country-who would not tell you that the change of standard time was a real money loss to him. It is true that the inconvenience is worse in some places than in others; it is very much worse on the western edges of the standards than on the eastern edges. In the town of Riviere du Loup, for example, the adoption of this legislation would only mean the gain of half an hour, and therefore the disadvantage involved would not be very great.
The only great objection, from a business standpoint lies with the railways, and I do not think that is sufficient to justify me in voting to put the farmers of the country to a loss which I am sure they would incur if this legislation goes through. Therefore I will have to vote for the amendment to the amendment and against the resolution.

I rise for the purpose of asking a question, not with any desire to speak again. I understand that the resolution declares it to be expedient to re-enact at once chapter 2 of the statutes of 1918. I. presume that is the Act passed last year?
Yes.

That Act expires
shortly?
Yes.
When does it expire?
At the end of the current fiscal year.	[DOT]

In that case what
is the object of the amendments? If we vote down the resolution does not that settle the whole question? I think hon. gentlemen should have it established to their satisfaction exactly what they are going to vote on. If the motion is to reenact the Daylight Saving Act, and we vote it down, then the whole thing falls and there is no necessity either for the amendment, or the amendment to the amendment, because the law will expire in three days. Let both amendments be withdrawn, and then members can vote intelligently on the question.

After having listened for a considerable time to the various opinions expressed, I have come to the conclusion, somewhat reluctantly, I admit, that the inconvenience occasioned to the farmer by the passage of this law will not be greater than the disadvantages which will result to the city worker and dweller should the law not be re-enacted. In common with a great many members of this House I have the greatest possible sympathy with the farming community, so much so that the day before yesterday I voted to remove what I thought was a very substantial grievance under which they were suffering. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, a large number of the members of the House who belong to the farming class did not seem to want that grievance removed. Now, Sir, taking those circumstances for granted, I must look to my own constituency, and I find, from letters, telegrams, and communications of all sorts which I have received in the past few days, that the financial, the business, and the working classes of the city of Quebec are almost unanimous in favour of a measure of daylight saving. That being my own conviction as *well as the conviction of my constituency, I will take great pleasure in supporting the resolution introduced by the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Cooper).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object which the Government
had in view in facilitating the debate upon the motion of the hon. member for South Vancouver has been amply accomplished.

In view of the acute divergence of opinion in the country, and among members of the House, it was felt advisable and eminently proper that an opportunity should be given for a frank, free, expression of opinion, precisely such as we have had to-day. If ever there was a question with which a Government, or a Parliament, had to deal, which might properly be submitted for the opinion of the members of the House of Commons this is one. It is not a party question, nor, as I stated this afternoon, does it involve any political principle. No one will pretend to say that those in the country who are opposed to daylight saving represent substantially any one political party. No one will pretend to say that those in cities and towns who are in favour of daylight saving represent completely or in large measure any political party. It seems to me, therefore, that it was an entirely proper proceeding, and I am very glad to have had the views which have been expressed, particularly those of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) who has had a wide experience as a parliamentarian, and who was for so long a member of the Government of Canada, in support of the view which we have taken. Now it seems to me that Parliament was discharging a function to-day, which it might more frequently be called upon to discharge, and that is to inform the public geneially of Canada as to the opinions which are held in the various sections of the country which are represented in this House upon public questions. I am the first to say that in any matter that involves the policy of the Government, the Government cannot transfer its responsibility to the House.
The executive has its x responsibilities, and the House has its duties, but they are separate and aistinct. The Government cannot escape its responsibility in the matter of policy, and of course its measures must be such as commend themselves at all times to a majority of this House. I do not at all agree therefore with the views put forward by the hon. member for South York that the course which the Government has adopted in this matter is in any way a violation of the principle of governmental responsibility.	"

May I interject a remark?
It was made a Government measure last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am aware of that. It would have been perfectly open for the Government last year to have taken 
the opinion of Parliament on the matter had it so desired.
I do not intend to-night to discuss this question on the merits, because it has been discussed from every angle, and I am exceedingly grateful to all the members of this House who have taken part in this debate and given the Government and the country the benefit of their views. I was aware, generally speaking, of the views which prevailed in the country and in the House, but although I have had information showered upon me from various parts of the country, this debate to-day has been most informing and illuminating and has as I stated before, abundantly justified the policy which has been adopted.
But as to the merits, I have just this to say. It seems to me to be a matter of inconvenience on the one hand and of hardship on the other. I do not mean to say that that will apply to every section of Canada, dividing such section into urban and rural districts; but, generally speaking, it appears to me that whereas in the case of towns and cities there may be inconvenience by reason of the House not adopting daylight saving legislation, at the same time this discussion has abundantly shown that in the farming communities there is more than inconvenience-there is hardship. Let me state further, that I make that assertion having regard to the conditions which prevail to-day. What those conditions will be a year or two years hence I do not pretend to say. But it has been shown in this House that under prevailing conditions with regard to shortage of labour and otherwise, there will possibly be hardship in many of the rural districts if daylight saving legislation is enacted, and that view has been strongly supported in the arguments which we have heard to-day from the representatives of the rural districts.
Now, this is not a Government measure which is under consideration to-night. It is a resolution of a private member which, if it had been reached yesterday, could have been discussed by this House precisely as the House has discussed it to-day; therefore it is open to every hon. member on this side of the House, and of course to every hon. member on the other side of the House, and to every hon. member of this Government, to vote upon this question precisely as he pleases without reference to party lines or to the fact that members of the Government vote one way or vote the other. As for myself, I intend to vote for the amendment to the amendment. The hon. member for Springfield (Mr. MARCH 27, 1919
Richardson) has pointed out truly that it would be very much better if we could have a straight vote upon the original resolution, but that is not the position before the House. The position is that one hon. member has moved an amendment which does not, I believe, represent what he intended to move. There is before the House also an amendment to that amendment, and by voting for the amendment to the amendment, as I propose to do, I shall vote against the resolution of the hon. member for South Vancouver (Mr. Cooper).

Mr. Speaker, as I propose to vote on this question differently from what I did last year, I wish to express my opinion on the matter. When this same resolution was presented last year it appeared to me to be not a very sound proposition; I thought it was meddling with something that was outside the jurisdiction of the House, and consequently I voted against it. But after having tried it out for a year I am rather pleased with it, and I think it has been, in our section, a benefit rather than otherwise. I think it is one of the wise measures of the Government,-I am sorry I cannot congratulate them on all the measures that they have brought up and passed.
I can see no special harm in this resolution. I have a telegram to-day from my constituents, and I had a copy of a resolution, which I think has been forwarded to the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce, asking him to favour this measure; my constituents are very much in favour of it. Personally, whether daylight saving legislation is enacted or not does not affect me very much, because I have always had the habit of getting up before the law requires me to. But, as I say, in my constituency I think this daylight saving measure has had the effect of getting our people up earlier, and when you accomplish that you are moving in the right direction. It does not need any law to keep them out of bed at night, because most of them stay up too late; but if you can induce the population either in the cities or the country to get up earlier, I think it is a step in the right direction. I argued last year the farmer's standpoint, that he required his help in the afternoon, and that a man in the afternoon in haying or harvesting time or other busy seasons was of very much more value to him than a man in the morning That was especially true last year, and the year before probably, when the labourers practically dominated the whole situation. I do not think that the labour condition?
are the same just now as they were last year, and it is not likely they ever will be. Then df your foreman or the man in charge was not feeling very good it was better for him to keep away, because if he appeared before his men looking cross they did not want to stay with him. But this coming season, and probably the seasons to follow, when the farmer goes to town to get help in his haying or harvesting season, while he may have to pay pretty reasonable wages, which is not objectionable, I think he will be able to say to his help anyway, " I will dictate to you to some extent the hours of labour. If I do not ask you to work earlier in the morning, I will expect you to work later in the evening."
The United States have adopted a law putting daylight saving into force from the first day of next month, and that has a peculiar effect upon our railway services crossing the border. For instance, on one particular section of the Canadian Pacific railway whicr passes through the state of Maine, the Maine Central and the Canadian Pacific operate over quite a distance on the same tracks. It would certainly be very inconvenient to have two systems of railways operating on the same tracks but under different schedules. Possibly the same condition prevails in other localities throughout the Dominion. It is quite probable that whether this House adopts the daylight saving system for this year or not, the railways will have to adopt it in order to carry on their work satisfactorily.
I do not think the farmer will suffer by the adoption of this legislation. If he does not want his hired man to start work at seven o'clock, he can tell him to come on at eight o'clock, as under the old system, and work an hour or two later in the evening. It has been said that the labouring class is not in favour of daylight saving. I am informed by the general manager of our business that they expect to put the daylight saving system in force from the first of April whether the Government adopts it or not. I appreciate the position of the farmer, but I believe that the labour conditions are such that he will not have the trouble that he has had in the past. I voted against daylight saving last year because it looked to me like a silly and uncalled-for move, but having tried it out, I am pleased with it. To my mind, anything that has the effect of encouraging people to get up early in the morning is a step in the right direction.

This debate has proceeded for five hours during this afternoon and evening, and all the arguments that can be advanced pro and con have been pretty well exhausted. I should like to observe, however, that we have the experience of last year to go upon, and there is no doubt whatever that upon a very considerable part of the population the daylight saving measure did work a hardship last year. The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) referred to the fact that the legislation was to be continued in force in the United States for the present year. I think I am correct in stating that had Congress not talked it out, as one hon. gentleman observed this afternoon, the Chances are that the measure would have been repealed. The agitation against it was very strong indeed, and the consideration of its repeal was before Congress at that time.
I am not particularly impressed by the arguments that have been adduced as to the need of re-enacting this legislation in Canada in order to facilitate our railway train service. It is quite true that we may be obliged to alter our railway time tables in Canada so far as international train services, and possibly also so far as trains connecting with international lines, are concerned. But a large number of trains running daily in Canada are not connected with international train services, and there is no reason why they should be affected by the change of time in the United States.
The agricultural population of Canada are a unit in opposing this measure. It affects them peculiarly; it works a hardship upon them. If city dwellers desire to get up earlier in the morning, it is surely not necessary for Parliament to legislate in order to enable them to do so. The member for Sherbrooke on a little reflection will surely realize that that is a fact. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I propose to vote against the resolution.
Mr. THOMAS M. M. TWEEDIE (Calgary West): Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a position similar to that occupied by a great many members of the House with regard to this matter. I supported the Daylight Saving Bill last year, but after a year's experience I find that in the city of Calgary about as many are against the principle of daylight saving as are in favour of it, while in the outlying rural parts almost every one is opposed to it. It seems to me that the consideration of this matter resolves itself into a question

of deciding between convenience and necessity. The necessity is all on the side of the agricultural interests in that district. No necessity is involved, so far as I have been able to ascertain, in the matter of daylight salving a? affecting the people residing in the city; with them it is simply a matter of convenience. I propose to support the policy which has regard to necessity rather than to convenience.
The Bailway War Board was absolutely justified in issuing an order making effective on Canadian railways the same time as they have in the United States. Many Canadian trains go to Boston,, Bangor Portland, Chicago, Detroit and other important centres in the United States, and if the systems running these trains did not adopt the time effective in the United States, the railway systems of the United States would have to alter their time tables to suit the train schedules in Canada in order to prevent traffic from being held up twelve or fourteen hours <at points where connections are made. As the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Crerar) has suggested, local trains not connected with international lines can give the agricultural interests the same service as they are receiving at the present time.
speakername: Hon.  T. A. CEEEAE@Minister of Agriculture

speechtext:
I cannot see that there is any law which prevents the dwellers in the cities from getting up an hour earlier, if they see fit, and I am sure this House cannot pass any legislation which will compel them to get out of bed an hour earlier. I am opposed to the daylight saving scheme, because it is detrimental to the agricultural interests, and for that reason it is not good for Canada as a whole. I will just read a telegram which I have received from Mr. Morrison, of Toronto, secretary of the Organized Farmers of Ontario:-
Consensus of members' opinions on so-called Daylight Saving almost completely unanimous opposition to it. We do not believe rank and file of towns and cities are in favour of It, if so they can make local arrangements without changing the clocks.
That is all I wish to say in regard to the matter, and it will be my duty to oppose the daylight saving scheme.

I did not intend to speak to-night, but so much has been heard from the farmers this afternoon that I want to speak on behalf of the people in the cities. It has been stated that the farmers work fifteen hours a day and have no recreation at all, and that they should have some consideration. I repre-

sent a city of some 550,000 people; Montreal has a population of 750,000 people; Quebec,
150.000	people; Hamilton, 100,000 people; London, 75,000 people; Winnipeg, 150,000 to
200.000	people; Vancouver, 150,000 people, and there are other smaller cities. Surely the people of those cities should have some consideration.

What about Ottawa?
Mr. FOSTER; If I have* omitted any cities with large populations, hon. members are perhaps more familiar with them than I am. The point is that the daylight saving scheme was tried out last year and not one city has complained; the cities are all perfectly satisfied. Resolutions have been passed by the large cities endorsing daylight saving and I have enumerated hundreds of thousands of people who desire daylight saving. As has been said a dozen times, if the farmer wants to continue to work under the same conditions such as have existed for the last hundred years, let him do so, but let the city people work under such conditions as they find is most agreeable and beneficial to them. Surely the hundreds of thousands of people in the banks, factories, and all the other industrial institutions of the cities deserve some consideration. They must have recreation, physical exercise, and if they want to get that by putting the clock an hour forward so as to give them an extra hour in the evening, they should have some say and some Tights in this Dominion. They do not want to have all the say, but surely these hundreds of thousands of people should have somebody to voice their sentiments. I have found such a change in the last twelve months that hon. members are falling over themselves in order to get from under, to get to the other side, to please the farmer. They imagine from the development of the last twelve months* that the farmers are becoming a serious consideration in the political situation of this Dominion, and they want to stand on the right side of that influence. I am not going to be influenced by the farmers of the Dominion so far as to forego the rights of the people in the great cities. Where would Canada be, where would the farmers be if it were not for the consumers in th^great cities? Could the farmer earn a livelihood, notwithstanding his great production, if he did not have the people in the great cities to consume his products? If it were not for the people in the great cities of this Dominion, neither daylight saving nor anything else would be of advantage to the
farmer. The people of the cities are the backbone of this Dominion, financially, mentally and numerically, and it is not right for this House to be lop-sided on this question as it is to-day.
Mr. JAMES BOWMAN (North Huron); It seems to me absurd to add anything to what has already been said in opposition to the re-enactment of daylight saving, as numerous strong arguments have been brought forward in opposition to it, while the few arguments in favour of it have been very feeble. In the first place, I commend the Government for giving hon. members who represent the people of this Dominion an opportunity to say where they stand on this question. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Foster) claimed, I understand, that the urban population of Canada was in favour of daylight saving. The riding which I represent is composed oi
26,000	people, about one-half of the population being urban and the other half rural. I have not received a petition in support of the re-enactment of the Daylight Saving Act, and I have received from councils and co-operative societies in the riding, as well as from many private individuals, petitions against the reenactment of that measure. But we should go further than simply to depend on such evidence as that as evidence that the people are opposed to daylight saving. At the present time we are trying to place agriculture in this country on a good sound basis. We are also, through the 'Soldiers' Settlement Board, undertaking a very important work in placing our returned soldiers on the land. It is, therefore, very necessary that we should do what we can to make agriculture as profitable as possible, so that when those boys are placed on the land they will be encouraged to remain there. I am very much afraid that if something is not done along that line to aid agriculture, we shall find that the work undertaken by the Soldiers' Settlement Board will be wasted energy.
A number of hon. members, speaking in support of this resolution, have advocated that we should copy the legislation passed by the United States, putting daylight saving into force and effect for the ensuing year. I am not one of those who are prone to copy the legislation of the United States.
The people of Canada are the ones who should be consulted, and whatever legislation we place on the statute book should be in accord with the sentiments of the people of Canada. It has been said that daylight saving

was in .force and has been re-enacted in many of the countries of Europe and in the United States, but that is no argument that it will be in the best interests of Canada. Conditions differ. Canada has largely a rural population, and its people are largely dependent on agriculture, whereas those countries that have enacted daylight saving and are still in favour of it are composed mostly of the urban class. We in Canady should do as we think right, and vote in the interest of the great majority of our people. I have nothing further to say except this: I should feel I was remiss in my duty did I not oppose the resolution which has been brought forward to-day for the purpose of re-enacting the daylight saving measure.

speechtext: The hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) yesterday asked if Halifax had been substituted for Rimousbi as the port for the landing of the Transatlantic mails, and I promised to make inquiry and reply to the question to-day. Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, respecting bankruptcy.
He said: In moving the second reading of this Bill, perhaps it would be well if I were to give to the House a brief explana-
59i	'	!
tion of some of the main provisions of the proposed measure. The subject of bankruptcy and insolvency has not been dealt with by the Parliament of Canada since 1880. As the House is aware, under section 91 of the British North America Act, the question of bankruptcy and insolvency is one of the questions which was left to the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada. In 1875, this Parliament passed a Bankruptcy Act, and after two amendments in subsequent years, that Act was finally repealed in 1880, so that for the last thirty-nine years we have had no bankruptcy law in the Dominion of Canada. It seems rather surprising that we should not have had one, because, with the exception of China and Canada, almost every country in the world has bankruptcy laws. Great Britain has a bankruptcy law, and every British Dominion save Canada has one-The operation of the Bankruptcy Act in this country between the years 1875 and 1880 was not regarded as a marked success, and it was urged that the machinery provided was much too cumbersome; that delays in the administration of the Act were very great and tedious; that the whole administration of the Act was expensive, and that too great liberty was permitted to fraudulent debtors to obtain special privileges. The result was that the Act gradually fell into- disfavour and was finally repealed in 1880.
It has been thought proper that another effort should be made to pass an Act having general application throughout the Dominion of Canada. During the interval between the year 1880 and the present time, many of our provincial legislatures attempted .something in the nature of bankruptcy or insolvency legislation. It was at one time doubted whether they had power to pass any legislation in regard to bankruptcy .and insolvency, but that question was set at rest by a judgment of the judicial committee of the Privy Council in 1894. The province of Ontario,, it may be remembered, undertook to pass an Act in respect of assignments and preferences by insolvent persons; the jurisdiction of that province to pass such an Act was questioned by the Federal authorities and a case followed which went to the judicial committee of the Privy Council. That judicial body held that Ontario was within its jurisdiction in passing that enactment. The ground of that decision was briefly this:
That the provisions of section 9 of Ontario " Act respecting assignments and preferences by

insolvent persons " which relate to assignments purely voluntary, and postpone thereto judgments and executions not completely executed by payment, are merely ancillary to bankruptcy law, and as such are within the competence of the provincial legislature so long as they do not conflict with any existing bankruptcy legislation of the Dominion Parliament,
That decision simply meant that so long as there was no Dominion bankruptcy or insolvency Act in force the provincial legislatures might, by reason of the ancillary jurisdiction which they possessed, pass laws which, while strictly speaking, not bankruptcy or insolvency Acts, related generally to that subject. For instance, while provincial legislatures might provide for the abolition of preferences among creditors, they could not compel a debtor to go into bankruptcy or provide for a discharge to the honest debtor. The provincial powers were exceedingly limited. Only this Parliament can pass a bankruptcy law which will have uniform force and effect throughout the Dominion. One difficulty in the way is the fact that there are so many legislative jurisdictions in this country. In Great Britain, the Bankruptcy Act is a comparatively simple thing, there being but one central legislative authority for the United Kingdom. But in 'Canada there is the Dominion Parliament, as well as nine provincial legislatures, and during the last forty years all the provincial legislatures have made some attempt to pass laws approximating very nearly to bankruptcy and insolvency laws. The effect of the passage of this measure by this Parliament will be to abrogate and annul the existing provincial laws upon bankruptcy and insolvency.
There is another difficulty in our way. In eight of the provinces of the Dominion the basic principle which has been adopted is the English common law, while in the province of Quebec the basic principle is the civil law, and a considerable distinction exists between the two. In the drafting of the present Bill an effort has been made to unify, as far as possible, the laws of the various provinces. The object of the Bill is to give uniformity in all commercial matters pertaining to bankruptcy, to the extent of abolishing all preferences or priorities as between creditors, and allowing all creditors to share equally in the estate of an insolvent debtor.
In the next place, the object is to provide an expeditious means of administering an insolvent estate, and at the same time to render that administration as inexpensive as possible. In the third place, and this is one of the main objects of the Bill, provision is made for the honest insolvent 
receiving, under certain conditions, an absolute discharge from further obligations; that is, the man who has fairly and fully disclosed his business dealings and handed over his assets to the trustee.
This Bill was before the House last session, but not exactly in its present form. Last year, it was referred to a special committee, which held twenty-five prolonged meetings and examined very carefully the provisions of the Bill. The Bill was reported to the House, but the session was then so far advanced that it was impossible to give it any further attention before prorogation. During the interval certain changes and amendments have been proposed to the Bill as it was reported from the committee last year. While there aro a great many changes in the present Bill, with the exception of one or two the amend-rnents are not in any sense radical. The object has been to follow as closely as possible the phraseology of the English Act, although that has not been possible in many of the sections. Most of the changes that have been made are changes in phraseology.
One radical change, however, has been made. The Bill presented last year applied to all persons, firms and corporations doing business in Canada, with the exception of farmers and wage-earners earning not more than $1,500 a year; but the compulsory clauses of the Bill did not apply to corporations. The present Bill has been changed in that respect, making all corporations subject to its provisions. The various clauses of the Winding-up Acts in our Canadian statutes have been incorporated in the present measure, so that this Bill, if it become law, will apply to all persons, firms and corporations except banks, railway companies, trust companies, and in-suirance companies, which are governed by special Acts, and to all persons except farmers and wage-earners earning less than $1,500 a year. Farmers may take advantage of the Act, but they cannot be forced into bankruptcy against their own wishes. If they desire the benefits of the Act they can receive them by making an assignment. The Bill, of course, is somewhat complicated, and contains a vast number of provisions which are more or less technical.
The machinery for administering the Act is to be the Superior Courts of the provinces. The Bill does not seek to establish any new court for the administration of the bankruptcy laws. It has been suggested that a bankruptcy court might give greater uniformity, but this would involve

a very large increase in the judiciary of Canada.
Have the county courts jurisdiction in bankruptcy?

Not under this Bill. I assume that the principle of the Bill will receive the approval of the House, and I think that when the Bill itself comes under discussion in detail, many useful suggestions will be made. The Government do not for a moment consider that the measure is a perfect one, but it is as nearly perfect as they have been able, after a great deal of effort, to make it, and they will gladly accept any useful suggestions that may be made by way of amendment, as we carefully consider the Bill section by section. If the Bill is permitted to have its second reading, when it reaches the Committee stage every facility will be given the House for the fullest possible discussion in order to remedy any imperfections that may exist in the various complicated sections. The Bill also applies to the Yukon Territory, and the District Court of the Yukon is the tribunal specified there.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton):
speechtext: At this stage I have very little to say regarding the Bill, as it is only within the last two or three minutes that it has been distributed and hon. members have not had an opportunity of studying its provisions. I have carefully followed the explanation made by the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), and I agree with him that a bankruptcy law for Canada should be very useful. It is no doubt a necessary piece of legislation. Not having had opportunity to examine the Bill, I have nothing further to say at present; but I might suggest to the hon. Solicitor General that perhaps it might be well not to press it in Committee to-day, as hon. members, not being familiar with its terms, are not in a position to offer proper criticism.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. MACLEAN (Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries), the House went into Committee on the following proposed resolution.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
That it is expedient to amend the Fisheries Act, 1914, by providing that the annual fee for a license to operate a salmon cannery or salmon curing establishment in British Columbia for commercial purposes shall be five hundred dollars, and in addition, four cents for each
case of forty-eight one-pound cans, or the equivalent thereto, of soekeye salmon, and three cents for each case of forty-eight one-pound cans, or the equivalent thereto, of any other species of salmon, including Steel Head (salmo rivularis) packed in such cannery during the continuance in force of the license; and the said five hundred dollars shall be paid before the license is issued1, and the remainder of the license fee shall be paid as the minister may from time to time by regulation prescribe.
He said: The resolution is self-explanatory, namely that it is the intention to increase the annual license fee for canneries to $500.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: Increased from what amount?

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext:
Some two or three
years ago this matter, together with many others incident to the salmon fisheries of British Columbia, was the subject of an inquiry by a commission, one of the recommendations of which was that the salmon cannery license fee should be $1,000. The present license fee is $100. It was not deemed advisable to make the license fee $1,000, but rather to increase it to $500. The proposal seems to be approved by all interested parties in British Columbia, so far as I have been able to ascertain. There was some opposition to it, of course, but inasmuch as the salmon fisheries of British Columbia are regarded as a monopoly it is generally considered but fair that the amount of the license should be $500. When I say that the salmon fisheries of British Columbia are in the nature of a monopoly, I mean that those who are interested in the business carry it on by virtue of a license. A license is issued for the various contrivances that are used to catch fish, and the canneries must also have a license. It is conceded that it would not be in the interests of the industry to allow every one to catch or can fish, and inasmuch as those who are permitted to engage in the industry do so by virtue of a license, their business is to that extent a monopoly. It is therefore deemed proper by the department- that those who enjoy the privilege should pay more for it than they do at present.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: Can any one pay a license?

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext:
Oh no, they are limited in number according to locality. It is always desirable to license but a limited number of fishermen or canneries in any district. Some districts will stand more fishermen and canneries than others, according to the quantity of fish that periodically visit those waters. It is a matter of much dispute in British Colum-

bia as to the number of canneries and fishermen that should be licensed, but the consensus of opinion is that there should be some limitation. Every one who desires a license, or applies for one, cannot get it and in that respect the officers of the department responsible for the administration of the law must do the best they can and give licenses to those whom they believe, to deserve them most. It is also believed that this increase in the license to $500 will meet the expenditure made by the Department of Marine and Fisheries in connection with the administration of the salmon fisheries of British Columbia. To-day it costs more than $200,000 to administer the fisheries in that province. It is thought that this increased license will yield a revenue considerably above that amount and it is hoped that the department will be able to do more to encourage the fisheries of British Columbia and also to expend more money in the administration of the law. It is my intention at the proper stage to send this Bill to the Fisheries Committee.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext:
I do not profess to know very much about the fisheries of British Columbia but it would appear to me that it will only be strengthening the monopoly to make the license fee as large as $500. The same question arose in Eastern Canada in regard to the lobster fisheries. It was contended by the packers that it would be a good thing to have a limited number of canneries because there were not	enough fish	to supply
a large number	of canneries. It
is the same argument that is used in British Columbia.	That was always
resisted by	the people	in	Eastern
Canada who wished the industry to be thrown open to any man who could erect a factory and equip it. It was felt that he should be allowed to do so; otherwise the business is bound to fall into
4	p.m. the hands of a few people who will put up the prices on the consumer. If we charge $500 for a license to catch salmon I assume that the man who packs salmon will get that money out of the consumer. We are also charging four cents a case on the fish packed and that will represent a very large sum of money payable by the packers of British Columbia. These packers will turn this account over to the people who consume the fish and we are assisting them in making the price of the salmon higher than it otherwise would be. What do we get for it? It strikes me that we do not get

anything while we are making it possible for the few people who are engaged in packing salmon to create a monopoly. What do the public get out of this? The minister has not told us any benefit that is coming to the public from this change. I can easily see that it will be an advantage to the packer. I am not interested in the packer. 1 am interested in the people who consume the salmon. I would like the minister to explain, if there is any explanation, how this change that we are now asked to make in the law will in any sense benefit the consumer.
Mr. MiACLEAN (Halifax): It might perhaps be difficult to answer directly the question which my hon. friend from Guysborough has put to me. As I stated before, it is impossible to administer the salmon fisheries of British Columbia without the granting to a limited number of people only the right to fish and to can salmon. That is conceded; nobody, as far as I am advised, will question that statement. It is not questioned by the citizens of British Columbia or by the fishermen of that province. It is conceded universally, I think, that the fisheries must be administered by a system of licenses. It is disputable, of course, whether in any given water any given number of licenses should be issued. Every day there are applications from fishing sections in British Columbia for licenses to fish and can salmon, but they can not be granted. That is conceded, even by those who apply for them, and who are very frequently refused licenses.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: What is the reason that they cannot be granted?

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext:
Because of the nature of the salmon fisheries. They would be very rapidly destroyed if the fish were caught in too great quantities in any one season. I do not intend to go into the history of this particular species of fish this afternoon. I think that had better be reserved for the special committee or in Committee of the Whole House, but there are several reasons why this particular fishery must be protected. The salmon of British Columbia breed in the headwaters of the lakes and streams of the province. They then proceed when young to the sea. They return after two or three years to the place from whence they came and in proceeding back they are caught or proceed to their spawning grounds where they die. As a matter of fact but few return to the sea .because they die on the return to the breeding ground if they

are not caught by the fisherman. It is necessary that not all the fish proceeding to the place whence they originally came be caught; otherwise they would be extinguished. My hon. friend opposite seems to think that an increase in the license fee will be a disadvantage to the consumer. I do not think that is correct, inasmuch as if the persons licensed to catch or can salmon have a monopoly it is only proper that they return a part of the profit to the Government. That is the principle of the resolution.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: Will they not be allowed to increase the price to the cohsumer to the extent of the extra charge for the license?

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: I do not know. My hon. friend might as well put that question to me concerning any other commodity that is offered for sale.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: We are not making a monopoly in any other commodity.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext:
The salmon catch of British Columbia is marketed the world over. The greater proportion of the catch is marketed not in Canada but in Great Britain. I do not think that the additional fee proposed under this resolution will increase the price at all. But it is felt, and very properly so, in British Columbia, that they who have this privilege conferred upon them by a license from a department of the Government should pay a tax to the country, and that is one of the reasons for this proposed increase in the fee.
Some hon. gentlemen may object to the -fee of $500 as being too small and they might do so with very good reason. However, the judgment of the officers of the department is that, for the time being at least, $500 is sufficient. It is to be understood that that is not the only tax the canners must pay. Hon. gentlemen will see by the terms of the resolution that they will also be obliged to pay four cents for each case of forty-eight one-pound cans, or the equivalent thereto, of Sockeye salmon, and three cents for each case of forty-eight one-pound cans, or the equivalent thereto, of any other species of salmon, including Steel Heads, packed in such cannery during the continuance in force of the license. That provision has always been in the statutes.

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.
speechtext: Is the weight mentioned there the lobster pound or the salmon pound?

subtopic: FISHERIES ACT, 1914, AMENDMENT- BRITISH COLUMBIA LICENSES.

I would like the minister
to give us a little information as to how these licenses are granted. It seems to me that the argument which he advanced 'as to the likelihood of the extermination of salmon if more licenses are granted is altogether different from what can be urged with respect to other species of fish. I do not presume to know very much about salmon fishing in British Columbia, but I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman when he says that the salmon which go up the river one year to spawn will all be exterminated. The minister does not seem to realize that the salmon spawn before or .after, going up the river, and while perhaps the old fish may be caught that year, millions of spawn have been deposited on the banks of the river which in the following year will grow into salmon, and consequently are ready to be caught the following year, or in ye'ars afterwards. On the motion of Hon. J. D. Reid, Bill No. 29, to amend the Railway Act (Aid for Railway Crossings) was read a second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1-Grant continued for ten years.

This extends the time
so as to allow the Board of Railway Com-
missioners to pay a portion of the cost of removal of dangerous crossings for another ten years.
Does it apply to the Government railways?

No, I intend bringing
in a Bill later on to cover all the Government owned railways.
What does it apply to?
All railways under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners.
Does it apply to the Canadian Northern?

Oh, yes, to every Dominion incorporated railway. The sums expended from this fund from 1909 to 1919, do not appear to be very large. They are:
1909-4/910,	$70,00 ;	1910-1911,	$69,109.18;1911-1912,	$7,643.14;	1912-1913,	$20,807.38;1913-1914, $39,968.11;	1914-1915,	$92,099.48;1915-1916,	$47,079.99;	1916-1917,	$46,630.53;1917-1918, $13,740.85 ;	1918-1919	(to March
12th), $2,336.85.
We have not used a very large amount out of the fund voted each year, but we thought it was as well to continue the provision pending the enactment of the new Railway Bill.

It would .appear from the minister's statement that this Act is of no service to those parts of Canada served by the Government railways. On the Intercolonial Railway there are a great number of dangerous crossings, but so far as I know nothing has been done towards eliminating them. The hon. minister says that the Government railways may be brought under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and in that case I suppose the same law will apply as to other railways, but at the present time it is unsatisfactory. If that condition of affairs is going to continue, I would like the hon. minister to consider whether some arrangement could not be made by which the Government itself would take steps to eliminate these dangerous crossings, or unite with the municipalities in doing so.

There is no doubt that the Government railways in the lower provinces will be under the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners within a very short time, and of course this provision will apply there as well as to any other part of Canada. I have been over the Intercolonial, and I know there are some very dangerous crossings, but I sup-

pose the same condition applies to other railways. The difference is that in most of those cases on the Intercolonial they were urging the Government probably to do a greater proportion of the work than this section would cover. Under this section the railway, the municipality, and the Government each contribute a certain proportion of the cost of protection.

How
many people were killed last year at these dangerous crossings?
I have not that information.

I think the new Railway Bill as it left the Commons last session had a clause in it, with the consent of the then and the present Minister of Railways, placing the Government railways under the jurisdiction of the Railway Commission.
That is so.
Do the Board of Railway Commissioners order the replacement of dangerous level crossings by overhead crossings, or simply the protection of level crossings?
It is for the Board of Railway Commissioners to decide whether the removal shall be by subway or overhead.

A certain amount of money is paid out of the public exchequer to the agency that is constructing this work, because it is not Government work, and the aggregate amounts to a considerable sum of money. It would be well foT the House and the Committee to know under what system the parties to these crossings are entitled to get a contribution from the Treasury.

The department pays
out the money on the order of the Board of Railway Commissioners?
Yes.
Why do we not make the extension for two years instead of ten, so that in two years, when our railway policy is more clearly determined, we may decide what should be done?
If the new Consolidated Railway Bill is passed, it will probably supersede this Bill. The former Act was for ten years, and I prefer renewing the former Act as it stood.

I object to giving this
authorization for ten years, and I am going to move that the word "two" be substituted for the word "ten." If the Consolidated Railway Bill supersedes this, the change will not cause any great inconvenience to the Government. On the other hand, if the Consolidated Railway Bill does not supersede this, when that Bill is being discussed in committee, the same objection will probably be raised. I move, seconded by Mr. Duff:
That the word " ten " be replaced by the word " two " in the sixth line of section 1 of this Bill.

If the new Consolidated Railway Bill supersedes this one there will be in it a clause cancelling this measure. If the new Consolidated Railway Bill does not. supersede this one, and nothing else interferes, no better legislation could pass through the House than this to assist in doing away with level crossings. I see no reason why we should not continue this legislation for ten, or even twenty years.

We are now taking control of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and if we can judge from the announcements of the Government to the House we are also going to take control of the Grand Trunk. When this is done there will be in Canada only two railway systems, the Canadian Government Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, neither of which require this aid to carry out the changes in dangerous railway crossings. Surely the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are able to do this work without the help of the Government, and so far as the Canadian Government Railways are concerned, this means simply transferring the money from one department to another. It may be advisable for the next two years to retain this item in the Estimates and to vote it, because we have not as yet taken over the control of the Grand Trunk Pacific

and the Grand Trunk, but I do not see why we' should give this authorization for ten years. I do not believe it will be required for ten years, and I think we should economize and at the end of two years refrain from expending this sum of $200,000 a year.

There would not be any difficulty for the hon. member, if he so desires, to ask, at the end of two years, that this legislation be repealed. I think this is a good measure, and even if we take over those two roads, I will press that this law be continued, because I think we should remove these level crossings. If the hon. member's suggestion should prevail, there will be no authority to order that dangerous railway crossings be removed. I would rather that even the full amount of $200,000 a year be paid for ten years if the result will be the saving of lives at these crossings. As a rule, the crossings ordered to be removed are those where life has been lost. This legislation refers only to crossings built prior to 1909, and surely we should give assistance to have them removed wherever it is found necessary that they should be removed. If the new Consolidated Railway Bill supersedes this measure, this difficulty will cease to exist, but we have now been trying for three years to get that Bill passed.

The minister has not
answered my arguments at all. He says that in two years, if he thinks it advisable, he will have this law repealed.

I did not say that. I said
that if the hon. member finds after two years that, in his opinion, the Act should be repealed, it will be for him to make a motion to that effect. I do not want this legislation repealed until the end of ten years.

It would be much simpler
to make it two years, than make it ten, and repeal the Act after the end of the two years. The minister has not answered my other arguments at 'all. I am strongly in favour of dangerous crossings being done away with, but I contend that the expense in connection therewith should be borne by the railway companies and by the municipalities concerned, not by the public. It would be very easy when the Railway Act comes up for consideration so to amend it as to give authority to the Board of Railway Commissioners to order any changes that are required to make dangerous crossings safe, the expense to be borne by the municipalities and the railway companies, whether it be the Canadian National Rail-
[ M r. Vien.]
ways or the Canadian Pacific. It is not a question of not removing the danger; the question is, who shall bear the expense of removing it? I think the railway companies can well afford to pay the expense of making these crossings safe, and they are the ones who should be made to pay, together with the municipality concerned. Amendment negatived.

Section agreed to.
