lOGMiPENSATION TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES WHO ARE KILLED OR INJURED.
On the motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways and Canals) Bill No. 30, to amend an Act to provide compensation where employees of His Majesty are killed or suffer injuries while performing their duties, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
On section 1-Compensation payable out of Consolidated Revenue Fund as may be authorized:

When the resolution was under discussion, I suggested that the Provident Fund be devoted exclusively to pensions for retired employees of the road. I should like to hear from the minister with regard to that. Another point I made was that a certain class of employees on the Government railways does not appear to be provided for under this Act. If that is so, it is an important omission. The Act provides for all those who are employees according to the terms of the Provident Fund. Is it true that a certain class of employees on the Government railways are not provided for in this Act?

All permanent employees of the Government railways are supposed to be members of the Provident Fund, and all employees, whether permanent or temporary, come under either the Compensation Act or the Provident Fund.
Even temporary employees?

Yes, they come under one or the other.
In order to change the present Provident Fund Act the employees would have to approve of such change for the reason that they are subscribers to that fund. The largest part of it is subscribed by the members of that organization, and the Government could not undertake any change with-

out their consent. The present proposed changes are the result of a careful investigation of the whole matter by the solicitor of the Government railways, who has discussed the situation with the principals of the different organizations that subscribe to the Provident Fund. The employees of the Government railways have several organizations. They are union men, and the conductors, the engine drivers, the brakesmen, and others all have separate societies. In order that I might satisfy the House that this Bill, in the form in which it is, had received the approval of the employees, I brought into the House some days ago a memorandum signed by the heads of these different organizations in which there was a request that this legislation should be enacted. A number of employees who are superannuated and who availed themselves of this fund several years ago consider that the pension they are now receiving is far too small under present conditions. This matter has been brought to the attention of the organization, but so far no change has been agreed on. When I brought this matter up in the House a few days ago I expressed the opinion that there was a necessity for some arrangement whereby these different funds or benefits to the employees should be consolidated in one law in order to provide that employees in any part of the country might receive the same benefits as those elsewhere. I have made inquiries concerning the nature of the organization of the Canadian Northern Railway as regards the insurance fund-for this is really an insurance fund-and I find that it is entirely different from the Provident Fund of the Intercolonial Railway. The Grand Trunk Railway employees also have a different system, and if we could bring them all under one organization or under Government ownership a considerable advantage to all would acrue. When the 'Compensation Bill was discussed last year I stated that I had consulted the members of the Provident Fund who had expressed themselves at that time as being perfectly satisfied with the Bill, and I added that if the Act were found in practice to be unsatisfactory in any respect it could be amended at this session. Now the two main objects of this Bill are these: First, to provide for the payment to each province of its proportion of the cost of operation of the Compensation Act; and, second, in respect of cases in which employees were killed who had not elected, prior to the accident, what fund they would take advantage of. There was no way by which the dependents of such men could obtain the benefits of the Compensation Act or the Provident Fund. Two such cases were called to my attention by the hon. member for Kamouraska, and for that reason I have inserted the clause making it retroactive.

I do not want to be over critical of the Bill because I am heartily in favour of it, but I am still inclined to believe that there is a class of employees in the Government railways who are not provided for at all under this Bill. To say that they are provided for under the existing law is not strictly correct. Under the Provident Fund the only accident for which there is provision is permanent disablement. Am I correct in that statement?
I do not think so.

There is no provision in the Provident Fund Act for a man temporarily disabled. If a man loses a finger or has his leg broken, there is no provision for him under the Provident Fund which, as I understand it, provides for old age pensions and men permanently disabled. Men who are permanently incapacitated are put on the same basis as pensioners. That exhausts the Provident Fund. Now we come to this Compensation Bill. The minister tells us that the men who are provided for under this compensation are permanent employees of the railway. I do not think that is very satisfactory. To give an illustration. A man who was working in connection with a steam shovel gets injured while engaged in such work. If he is not a permanent employee of the railway he does not come under the Provident Fund, neither does he come under this fund. If I understood the minister correctly he said that permanent employees-

What I said was this: Any employee of the Intercolonial or the Government railways, even though he is a labourer and has been at work only a day, if he is employed on the Intercolonial railway at the time of the accident then he comes under the Compensation Act of last session. So that every employee of the Intercolonial railway or the Government railways will come under one Act or the other. I think I have made myself Clear. The Provident Fund applies only to permanent employees.

It is stated in this section what class of people this Act applies to. It will apply to any

one who is employed within the meaning of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees Provident Fund Act. The Minister says that that includes every person working for the Government railways, even a labourer.
I did not say that.

Well
then, this Aot does not apply because it specifies those who are employed within the meaning' of the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees Provident Fund Act.
That is right.
If the labourer I referred to in my illustration is not an employee in the sense of this Act, then this does not apply to him.
The Provident Fund Act does not apply.
There is no provision under this Act for any man unless he is a permanent employee.
The hon. member is quite right. A temporary employee would not receive any benefits from the Provident Fund. He would receive it under the Compensation Act.
If so that is quite satisfactory to me.

When the Act of 1918 was passed I raised an objection to the restriction which was inserted in the Bill limiting the responsibility of the Government railway to only one of these funds. The question now comes up again. It is declared in this Bill that the injured party must make election as to which fund he intends to draw from and if he is to draw anything under the Compensation Act he is not entitled to come under the Provident Fund. As the minister has just stated, a very large proportion of this Provident Fund is contributed by the employees themselves. It is nothing more or less than insurance. The employees pay for this. Although there have been clauses inserted in the Provident Fund Acts relating to railway companies, (not under the control of the Dominion) limiting the responsibility of the railways and declaring where a party becomes a member bf the provident society he renounces any claim to other damages, the Privy Council has decided that it is absolutely illegal and that the Provident Fund is an insurance fund. The employees pay for participation in that fund and they are entitled to its benefits irrespective of the re-

sponsibility of the company under the Compensation Act. Why should the Government attempt to restrict its responsibility to the Compensation Act or to the Provident Fund where the ordinary railways are responsible under both? That is isomething that the Government has attempted to enact by legislation which is denied to it under the common law. The Grand Trunk Railway 'Company to-day have a provident fund. It is declared that it is an insurance fund and the question of election or not does not cut any figure. Why will the Government insist upon putting itself in a better position than the ordinary railways of the country? It is quite wrong and the portion of the Bill which declares that the employee must elect which of the funds he is to draw from should be struck out. I would therefore move in amendment that the words:
11 Unless he elects to accept prior or subsequent to the injuries such compensation in lieu of the allowance payable under the provisions of the Provident Fund Act, section twelve, Class D, and gives notice in writing of such election."
That the words ** unless he elects to accept prior " be struck out.
In that way the employee will be entitled to participate in both funds. One is the Act under which he pays for insurance and the other is the Compensation Act, and which provides for the compensation to which he is entitled.
Is this Provident Fund composed altogether of contributions from the men, or does the Government also contribute?

The Government pay $100,000 a year towards this fund, and, therefore, if this amendment is carried, the Government will be paying twice. They will be paying the money that they are paying into this Provident Fund and they will also be paying under the Compensation Act.
Mr. McMfASTER: I think that a middle ground should be taken in regard to this matter. I think it is quite unjust and unfair to ask a man, in order to avail himself of a right which the law gives him, to waive his right to a fund to which he himself has contributed. It would seem that the proper attitude for the Government would be this: A man, if he is hurt should be entitled to have the proportion of the fund that his subscription would bear to the whole fund. The Government should not be obliged to pay twice, but I think a certain portion of the fund should be given a man as the insurance to which he has contributed and then he ought besides to have the right of

compensation that any other employee has from his employer.
That would put the railway employee in a different position from, every other class of employees in the country?

Because he pays for it?
Mr. M1ACLEAN (Halifax): He does not pay for it entirely because the Government contributes a certain amount annually. That was done because at that time there was no compensation law applicable to the railway employee.

I quite accede to the proposition that the Government should not be obliged to pay twice, but it seems to me that a man should not be obliged .to give up rights in a fund to which he has contributed in order to get his rights in another fund. There should be some allowance made for the man. He should receive something from the Provident Fund as well as getting the ordinary compensation under the law. You might express it in this way: A man who works for an ordinary employer is hurt. He has been carrying an accident insurance policy. He is entitled to certain payments under that accident insurance policy and he is also entitled to ask his employer to indemnify him for the loss he has suffered under the ordinary law of the land. In this case if the employee has contributed to a provident fund he should be entitled to withdraw a certain amount from that fund, and he should also be able to get compensation under the law of the land. Inasmuch as the insurer has also subscribed to the fund, in the case of the Government, the Government should not be obliged to pay twice, and it would be quite fair when a man is to take his compensation qua employee that he should not be paid full compensation from the Provident Fund. But he should not be obliged to waive all his rights to the Provident Fund in order to avail himself of his rights to compensation as against the Government who happens to be his employer.

With regard to the Provident Fund and Compensation Act, I have had these matters up with the employees and there has not been any question raised. * The employees are satisfied. We have been trying to make the Provident Fund Act and the Compensation Act satisfactory to them. This Bill is all that they have asked for or suggested. I would think
5	p.m. that it would be better to carry out the wishes of the employees.
I take the same position to-day that I did last year. Let this Bill go through, see how it works out and if it is found that the employees are not receiving the benefits that they should receive under either of these Acts, I have no hesitation in saying that I will come back again and ask that the Act be amended so that there will be no injustice to any employees and that they may receive all the benefits under these Acts. Then again, I think we will probably have to have a new Act to apply to the whole of the railways. I would not like to interfere with the Provident Fund Act at this particular time without again taking it up with the employees. As I have been trying for some time to make it satisfactory to them and to cover every point they raised, I would not like to amend the Bill now.

I pointed out to the minister last year that the law is directly against his contention. As to whether the employees are satisfied or not, that is not the question before us to-day. Sometimes the employees of a railway company are perforce obliged to be satisfied, or they may find themselves looking for a job. As I indicated to the minister last year, the decision of the Privy Council was to the effect that money paid out of a Provident Fund is no compensation at all to the employee; it is purely and simply an insurance. Why should this employee be obliged to pay into the Provident Fund, this insurance fund, and afterwards elect as to whether he is going to take the ordinary compensation which is provided for by the common law, or take this insurance for which he pays? Why should he pay a penny for this insurance if he is not going to get anything out of it? He could put his money into his pocket, he could buy two per cent, if he wishes, and fall back on the ordinary compensation law. But here he pays into the Provident Fund and gets nothing. He puts his penny into the slot and takes nothing from it. I say that if you take this money from this man as an insurance you are obliged to pay him the whole, or part of it, irrespective of the compensation to which he is entitled under the common law. As to being satisfied with it, is not a question for this House. This is a question of right and justice.
,1 take issue with the hon. gentleman. The House has voted $100,000, and we are putting up that amount each year as insurance under the Compensation Act.

The men have a right under the law of the land to get it. How much are the men paying into the fund?
Mr. 'REID: I admit it, but they are not paying one dollar into the compensation fund. They will receive greater benefits under the fund we are subscribing to as an insurance. I have not got the figures here, but I do not think they are paying any more.
The minister told us a few minutes ago, that a very large percentage of the Provident Fund is paid for by the employees.

They do pay a large percentage, there is no doubt about it at all. At all events, we are paying $100,000, and if the employees wish to take advantage of the Compensation Act there is no reason why they should not do so. However, I took this matter up with some of the employees and discussed it with them, and they think it is fair; I have never heard one of them complain yet. Now, until the matter is brought up and discussed with the employees and they say they are not satisfied, or until we get an opportunity of enacting a statute that will give the same treatment to an employee in Halifax as to an employee in Vancouver, I am in favour of continuing as we are. I want to do everything I can for the employees.
Then agree to my amendment.
Agree to your amendment?
Yes.

I will agree to any amendment that the employees and the management of the Government railways will say is fair and just, but so long as the employees themselves have not raised the question and say that the present plan is fair and just, I am going to accept their views and not those of the hon. gentleman.

Whan the minister says he has taken the matter up with the employees and discussed it with them, I assume that he is speaking generally. The hon. gentleman, does not, I assume, intend to convey to the committee that he has taken up and discussed with the employees the special clause covered by the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs).
What I have done is what any man would do. I have taken the matter up with representatives of the Provident Fund and with the employees.

Generally.
fMr. J. D. Reid.]

There was a representative here last year, and instead of taking it up with him I asked the solicitor of the department to go into the whole matter of the Provident Fund and deal with it, and then come back with a memorandum saying what the employees wanted, in order that I could assure the House that the employees were satisfied. He came back with this memorandum signed by eight or ten of the heads of the Provident Fund. Until I receive a complaint of some kind or another, some evidence of dissatisfaction, or some complaint such as was brought to my attention by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) last year to show that an injustice might be done to employees, I prefer to carry out their wish as they have submitted it to me. If this is so important a matter, why has there not been a complaint made to me by the employees? I have never heard of it from the time the hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) raised the question last year, and the hon. gentleman knows that every word he said then, and every word I said-indeed every word that has been said here to-day-is	taken cognizance of
by the committees of the Provident Fund. If the employees have any complaints, I am willing to come back to Parliament and apply for legislation to remedy their grievances, and make that legislation retroactive, until such time as the Compensation Act can be introduced. That is what I am trying to carry out, I do not think there could be anything fairer.

Does the minister wish the House to believe that he took up this question with the employees of the railway, and pointed out to them that this Provident Fund was an insurance, and that they would be entitled to that in any event, under the judgment of the Privy Council, irrespective of the Compensation Act, and did the employees who were interviewed say they were satisfied with one fund and not with the two funds?

The Provident Fund is not altogether an insurance scheme, because Section 12 of the Employees' Provident Fund Act provides as follows with respect to Class D:
Those who are permanently disabled from following their usual occupation in the service as a result of injuries received while on duty and actually at work in the service.
I assume that was to provide a scheme for workmen's compensation for injuries.
They pay for it.
That is what the Privy Council decided.
I am not quite satisfied that the point was ever before the Privy Council.
Look at the case of Miller and the Grand Trunk Eailway decided about ten years ago by the Privy Council.
I daresay some matters which involved the Provident Fund Act were before the Privy Council, but I am very doubtful whether the particular point we are discussing was ever before that tribunal.
I think so.

I think it is a matter for Parliament to say whether an employee of the Government railways is entitled to compensation from two separate funds,-that is, to be a beneficiary under the Act of last session and under the Provident Fund Act. I quite agree that he should not lose his rights under the other provisions of the Provident Fund Act. There is something in that contention.

The ease of Millqr and the Grand Trunk was an action for damages on behalf of an employee of the Grand Trunk who had been killed, and the Grand Trunk sought to evade its responsibility by pleading that the man was a member of such a fund as the Provident Fund (which has been created for the Government railways); that it was contributing to that fund every year, and that the employee agreed not to sue the company for any damages because of that contribution. The Grand Trunk succeeded before the courts of this country, but the Privy Council decided that the Provident Fund was to be considered as insurance, and that the agreement signed by this employee did not relieve the company from its liability.

In that case was the man killed?
Mr. LAPOINTE (Kamouraska!: Yes.
The Provident Fund does not apply in such a case, and the Compensation Act was brought in for that reason.

But the Privy Council decided that it was to be considered merely as insurance; that the employee was paying an amount every month to that insurance, and that the company was obliged to pay damages in addition to the amount of the insurance. This is the law in respect to the other railway companies. An employee of the Grand Trunk or the Canadian Pacific is a member of a railway provident fund, and if he is killed in a railway accident, and the company is responsible in damages, he receives the amount provided for by the Provident Fund as well as the compensation.
Might I ask if the Grand Trunk scheme provided for a system of compensation for injuries?
No; that is the common law.
Was it in anyway analogous to the amounts the Provident Fund provides?
No, the Grand Trunk was liable under the law of th#land.

I assume the Privy Council was perfectly right. All Compensation Acts strictly provide that no employee may contract himself out of his rights under the Act.
iMr. JACOBS:	The Government is contracting itself out of its obligations.

I think the
Eailway Employees Provident Fund Act was a step in the right direction, but since that Act was passed all the provinces have enacted Workmen's Compensation Acts. On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Marine and Fisheries) the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Fish Inspection Act, chapter forty-five of the statutes of 1914, and to provide that the said Act shall apply to pickled herring, alewives, mackerel, and salmon other than mild cured salmon, and the containers in which such fish are packed and marketed; that the Governor in Council may order that the provisions of the said Act shall extend and apply to any other kinds of fish, whether pickled or not, and the containers in which such fish are packed and marketed; excepting, however, fish packed in cans or other hermetically sealed containers, and fish packed by fishermen or others for their own use and not for sale or intended to he used for any other commercial purpose; that regulations may be made prescribing the size and make of such containers, and the manner in which and places where they shall be inspected and marked, and also prescribing how fish shall be graded, packed and inspected, and the place and manner and by whom fish are to be inspected, and other provisions relating thereto ; that no container shall be used unless inspected and marked in accordance with the regulations, and all fish shall be graded; that all fish imported into Canada from other countries shall be packed in containers of a similar character and equal quality to those required under the proposed legislation; and shall be clearly marked with the kind, grade and weight of fish they contain, and with the name of the country of origin, provided that when such fish are imported into Canada for exportation it shall only he necessary that the container in which such fish are packed be marked with the name of the country of origin; that with certain limitations an appeal to the minister may be made in case of disputes between an inspecting officer and the packer, owner or other person: that inspectors shall have the right to enter upon any premises, vessel or boat for the purpose of enforcing the provisions of the Act as amended ; that penalties may be imposed, and containers and fish forfeited and seized for violation of the Act or regulations ; and that the proposed legislation shall come into force with respect to fish caught on the Pacific coast on the first day of November, 1919, and with respect to fish caught on the Atlantic coast on the first day of April. 1920.

Substantially the proposal under this resolution is the compulsory inspection of fish. The subject of course will be controversial but I wish to promote the measure a stage so that it can be referred to the Fisheries Committee to be thoroughly inquired into. I assume that the committee will ascertain what public opinion is on the matter. I do not know if it has ever been discussed in the House before in the form of a resolution or a Bill.
There is a law now in connection with fish inspection, but it is not compulsory. This is compulsory inspection?

The proposal contained in the resolution is that the inspection shall be compulsory. The legislation now in existence was passed in 1914 and it provides for a system of inspection upon the request of any applicant. It is not compulsory. The results under this system of permissive inspection are as follows:

I represent a fishing constituency, and I do not object at all to this measure, although I have heard no expression of public opinion with respect to it. I learned last fall, however, that some fish were inspected at the Magdalen Islands by an inspector from Prince Edward Island, to which inspection my constituents objected very strenuously, contending that the inspection should be done by a man from their own district. On the whole I think this is a fair measure and that it will satisfy public opinion, but the minister will be expected to give full information with regard to it. For example, if the measure passes will there be a large number of inspectors appointed to carry out its provisions, or will the department utilize the good services of some of its present officials? In the-present financial state of the country I would not favour any wild expenditure for inspection purposes. The department should avail itself of the services of the present staff of inspectors or officers and thus avoid any additional expenditure.

The system of inspection to be adopted is the really important and serious feature of the Bill. If fish were to be inspected immediately they were put in the containers, it would mean employing- a tremendous army of inspectors, which would be undesirable and make the administration of the Act very expensive. I shall read a memorandum given me with respect to that by an officer of the department:
That with respect to the fish a system of inspection similar to that applied to fruit should be adopted, by which means the packers would be required to cuire, grade and pack their fish in accordance with the standards set; that they, not the inspectors; would be required to mark the packages with the kind, grade and weight of the fish contained, but that the inspectors would be empowered to thereafter examine the fish at any convenient time or place, in order to ascertain whether they are correctly designated by the marks on the package.
That appears to be about the only system of inspection that could be worked out, and it would not be necessary under it to have a large number of inspectors.
There are certain inspectors now.
Seven.

The
trouble is that every fisherman on the coast is also a packer. The blue-book tells us there are some eight thousand fishermen whose operations cover about five thousand miles

of coast, and the difficulties in connection with administering regulations of this kind would be very great on account of the scattered way in which the work is done.
If the packers of fish operated like the packers of fruit, and there were places where fish was handled in large quantities, as is done in the case of fruit in the Annapolis valley and other points, the task would be a much easier one. I understand that in many places fruit is sold on the trees, and the packer comes along with his crew of men, and the necessary boxes and barrels, and the fruit is picked and packed under inspection.
I think it is inspected at the warehouse largely.

That may be so, but the conditions under which fish is packed differ greatly from those under which the packing of fruit is carried on. A man may be living in a little harbour in an isolated place. He catches the mackerel and packs it himself in barrels, which are sometimes made by himself, and the difficulty of getting an officer to go to that man's place and inspect the fish after it is packed will be very great indeed. If the inspection work is done in that way it will require an army of officials and will prove very expensive.

I quite agree with my hon. friend. But ultimately these fish are forwarded to some centre; for instance, in my hon. friend's own constituency a great quaritity of pickled fish would reach Canso at one time or another, and would be inspected there.
Then the inspection would be in the interest of the dealer and not in the interest of the individual fisherman.

The Bill provides for regulations which will set up standards. The packer will assign the standard or grade of fish himself, and he will place that mark on the barrel. Later when the fish reach a certain place they will be inspected by the regular inspector.
Why should the proposed legislation come into force on the Pacific coast in November. 1919, and in the Maritime Provinces not until April, 1920?

On the Atlantic coast the fishing is over in September and October, and consequently there are no more fish to inspect until the following spring. Therefore, the ensuing April would suit Atlantic coast conditions.

I would suggest to the minister that this measure is capable of causing a great deal of hardship to fishermen. Take my own county. There is a large fishing establishment in the northern part of Victoria county which puts up five hundred barrels of what they call No. 1 Herring, and which they sell as such to Smith Brothers, or some other big fishing firm, in Halifax, at say $8 a barrel. The firm believe that they are selling No. 1 Herring, and they have so put it up. However we have not yet reached the millennium in commercial matters, nor the acme of perfection in square dealing. It is quite possible, therefore, that some person who desires to get cheap herring may have those herring examined in Halifax by an inspector who will say that they are not No. 1 Herring, and then the whole fat is in the fire. The people who sold those herring as No. 1 herring cannot get the price for that grade, although they acted quite honestly in the matter. I would say that the inspection must fake place before the fish is shipped, if it is to take place at all, and before delivery is taken, otherwise there will be no end of trouble, lawsuits and dissatisfaction, and much heartburning among the poor fishermen.
As the 'hon. minister is aware, deep-sea fishing is a very arduous occupation, entailing long hours and, sometimes in our part of the country, facing the full sweep of the Atlantic in all its terrors, and the fisherman has enough to contend with at present without inflicting , this inspection upon him, for it will make things worse than they are now. Therefore, in the interest of everybody concerned, I would enjoin upon the hon. minister the greatest possible caution in dealing with this matter to avoid creating unnecessary difficulties.
To-day a very excellent quality of fish is being sold in Nova Scotia, and it is in our own interest to sell good fish, for we have to compete with Newfoundland, Sweden, Norway and other countries. I hear very little complaint about the quality of fish sold in Canada brought either from the Pacific coast or from the Atlantic coast.
I would suggest to the hon. minister to do what he proposes to do about that small can and big Act of Parliament. He proposes to cut down the big Act of Parliament to suit the can. In this case, if there are too many officials and they have nothing to do I think it would be well to find something else for them to do or send them about their business. Do not try to legislate difficulties

in order to give them work; have greater care for the fishermen than furnishing unnecessary labour for too big an army of officials.

I quite agree with the point my hon. friend makes, and I apprehend there will be a great deal of criticism in reference to this Bill just upon the point to which he refers. However, if the Bill is eventually adopted, I hope it will not work an injury to the fishermen. If it results in placing upon the market a better fish it will also result, I think, in higher prices being secured by the fishermen.

That it is expedient to amend the Weights and Measures Act, Chapter fifty-two of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, and to define more clearly what officers are included under the term " inspector," and the ratio and proportion of the foot, French measure or Paris foot, to the Dominion standard measures; and also to provide for the appointment of a Superintendent of Weights and Measures, with prescribed duties, for the examination of inspectors and certificate of qualification required; and for the fixing of inspection divisions; and further to prescribe by regulation when and how often weights and measures and weighing and measuring machines are to he inspected, verified and stamped1; and that the Governor in Council may prescribe a fee to be charged for a specified period, not to exceed one year, instead of a fee for each inspection and verification ; and further, to prescribe penalties for selling or delivering anything by weight, measure or number short of the quantity ordered or purchased1; or for knowingly using any counterfeit weight, measure, weighing or measuring machine, or having, selling, or dealing in the same, except such as can, after adjustment, be admitted to verification.

The changes proposed in the Bill are not very numerous. The Weights and Measures Act heretofore was administered in the Department of Inland Revenue, but last year it was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce. One of the amendments is to substitute the name of the Minister of Inland Revenue in the Act for that of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There is a slight amendment in reference to the 
French measure or Paris foot. Iln the province of Quebec the French foot is used in land surveying, but only in such cases, I understand. The French foot is defined under the amending Bill as equal to 12.780 inches instead of 12.79, a correction of .001. I do not think you could get much of a lawsuit out of .001.

The Bill will also provide for an annual instead of biennial inspection, but there will be power in the Bill to make regulations to the effect that scales which are not used frequently need not be inspected so often. No, Quebec is the only province in which the French foot is the standard measure in land surveying.	t
You would not apply it in Ontario?
No.

Is it the intention to insert in the Bill this provision which is contained in the resolution:
-and further to prescribe by regulation when and how often weights and measures and weighing and measuring machines are to toe inspected, verified and stamped ; and that the Governor in Council may prescribe a fee to be charged for a specified period, not to exceed one year.
Does that apply to measures of all kinds? For instance, in the drygoods business yard measures made of brass are used. These
are and must be stamped by the Government at the time they are purchased and before they are put into use. Must they, under this Bill, be examined periodically in future? A yard stick made of metal cannot be stretched or varied, and as it has the Government stamp on it, why should it be necessary to have a periodical inspection of measures of that kind? There are no doubt other measures that are in the same class. Once a measuring article of that kind has been approved by the Government, it cannot vary unless a man deliberately cuts a piece off, and that would be absurd.
I do not think this would include a measure of that kind.

I think it would be wise to except measures of that kind in the Bill, because otherwise there would be no end of trouble to men using them. Inspectors would be coming along at irregular intervals and charging merchants fees for inspections that would not be necessary.
I do not think the Act applies to that at all.
The resolution says "measures."
The hon. member might bring that matter up on the second reading when the Bill is printed.

I do not know whether the measures of electric currents and the inspection of meters come under this department or not. They used to come under the Department of Inland Revenue and they likely come under this department now.
This is under the Department of Trade and Commerce, but I think a different set of officials inspect electrical measures.
When did that come under the Department of Trade and Commerce? It used to be under the Department of Inland Revenue.

If this is not in the minister's department. I hope whatever department has charge of the work will take note of what I have to say. In our pert of the country there is the greatest possible dissatisfaction in regard to these meters

and the calculating and reading of meters. It is believed there is a great deal of filching from the public by reason of defective meters, and there is no proper inspection at all. When you take into consideration that there are hundreds of thousands of these meters all over the country, on whose readings men are paying out large sums of money, it can be readily understood how important it is that they should be tested and kept in proper order. Are not electrical meters under provincial jurisdiction, just the same as the wiring of houses and buildings and all that sort of thing?

Civil Government-Department of Customs and Inland Revenue Service-salaries, including Commissioner and Chairman, Board of Customs at $6,000, Assistant Commissioner of Customs at $4,©00, Assistant Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue at $4,600 - Contingencies, $43,000, $4613,387.50.

Does not the minister think that is a large increase?
I do not think so.

It seems a large increase to me, especially in view of the finances of the country at the present time, faced as we are with a deficit.
