Have any changes been made in the staff? Have there been any deaths or additions to the staff?

The staff is exactly the same, with the exception of the addition of the minister's private secretary.

Customs.-Salaries and contingent expenses of the several ports in the Dominion including pay for overtime of officers, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, and temporary Customs buildings and rentals, $4,000,000.

There
is an increase of $110,000.

That is to provide for increases in salaries during the coming year. In the Inside Service there is an annual increase provided for under the statute, whereas increases to the Outside Service are given by the department, and there has always been each year a certain amount put in the Estimates to allow for these increases. Instead of $110,000 it has generally been $200,000 or $300,000, but this year it has been reduced to $110,000 in order to allow of increases to those who, it is considered, are entitled to them having been in the service for a number of years. When the re-organization of the Civil Service is effected and the Outside Service is put on the same basis as the Inside Service, the statute will give them an annual increase of $50 or $100, and there will of course be no necessity for a vote' such as this.

How
many officers are now in the Outside Service and how many were there a year ago?
The information will be available in a moment or two.

How much of this
$4,000,000 is applied to rentals and temporary buildings?

I am unable to say offhand how much the rentals amounted, but they are practically all made through the Public Works Department. We have not a record of them in the Customs Department. If we want an examining warehouse in the city of Montreal, the Public Works Department secures the premises on our information as to the number of surface feet that we require, and other specifications, and the rental is paid through that department. Only occasionally, and in the case of a very small building is this work done through the Customs Department.

What proportion of this $110,000 represents salaries? Does it embrace any increase in salaries for the coming year? The reason I ask is because on inquiry I was informed that the entire salaries of the Civil Servants must be adjusted to a general ratio of increase. I think we ought to be informed as to what
percentage is salaries, and what percentage rentals, and if the amount includes increases.

The increase of $110,000 is intended for increases to the officers of the Customs Department on the outside staff and not for any special salaries. The hon. member probably knows that during the present fiscal year ending March 31 salaries in the Outside Service were increased by way of bonuses out of the war vote put through last year. This $110,000 is not for that bonus, but for increases that are given every year. The departmental staff presents to the minister.a report showing what in their opinion each member of the staff should receive by way of increase. In the past we voted about $300,000 or $400,000 for increases, but as I have stated we have reduced it this year. In my opinion, however, it should be as much as it was last year, but the bonus is to be considered. If we were to give every member of the outside staff about $100 increase it would take at least $300,000 The hon. member asked for the number of employees last year and this year. On March 31, 1918, there were 3,351 in the Outside Service, and at the present time there are 3,283, or 70 fewer than there were a year ago.
Does the minister say that the war bonus is included in this amount?
No. Last year the Government gave the Outside Service a bonus which was taken out of the vote of $2,000,000.
The war bonus would have to be considered apart from this?
Yes.
I understand that a number of Civil Servants from various parts of Canada gathered recently and decided to ask for increases. Will these increases satisfy those men?

The matter will have to come up later on in the session. The Civil Service Commission are now classifying the Outside Service and will probably put it on the same basis as the Inside Service. Parliament will have to consider whether we are to continue bonuses or increase salaries under this classification that is being made. We are not in a position to decide this matter just at this mojnent and are making this vote the same as last year.
Did all the outside officers share in the bonus?
All up to $1,880, but not over.
Only the officers who are permanent and not those who have been employed for six or seven months?
All that were employed, both permanent and temporary, previous to April, 1918.
Do I understand the minister to say that those, such as messengers, who are employed in the House during the session received the bonus?
I am only talking about the Customs Department.

I understand that for some time there has been a staff of accountants from the United States e-mployed making a survey of the different departments so as to advise the Government on the increases that are demanded, and this at considerable expense, notwithstanding that the Government had a report three or four years ago from accountants from Great Britain. What I particularly desire to draw to the attention of the minister, and more especially to the attention of the hon. Acting Prime Minister (Sir Thomas White), is the fact that we are starting to-night to vote Supply to this Government. It seems to me that before the Government ask for Supply they should first give to the people of Canada a correct and complete statement of our financial position. We should have a statement of the debt of the country, the assets that would be deducted therefrom, temporary loans, treasury bills and all the outstanding and unsettled obligations and engagements in connection with pledging the credit of Canada, including railways, docks and steamships; in short Mr. Chairman, whatever engagements the people of Canada are pledged to. I think it is due, not to the Opposition, but to the country as a whole that we should have a complete, fair and honest statement before any considerable amount is voted.

The hon. member is perfectly right in saying that Parliament should have that information at the earliest possible date. I am glad the hon. gentleman mentioned it this evening and I shall draw the attention of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) to his remarks to-morrow morning. The Minister of Finance will take advantage of the opportunity, no doubt, when the House is in Committee 
of the Whole on the resolution by which he is asking for a vote of $350,000,000, to give a full Statement of the financial position of Canada.
Will tne minister give us any information in regard to the accountants who are employed?

The Civil Service Commission had in hand the reorganization of the Civil Service, and they employed a staff of accountants. I could not say where they are from, I never made any inquiries, but I would suggest that the matter might be brought up when the vote in connection with the Civil Service Commission is under consideration. If the information is wanted at an early date I will have it brought up in Supply again.

I wish to draw the attention of the minister to a request from my constituency for an additional custom house at Port Felix on the Atlantic coast. This is a fishing village with something like 1,500 inhabitants who are engaged in the inshore and deep-sea fisheries. A number of small vessels are going in and out of that port but there is no custom house nearer than five miles at White Head. It is not convenient for the inhabitants to go that distance to do their business with the custom house. They are also shipping fish to the United States, and some statements have to be filed and entries made in regard to these shipments. It is quite a cost and a burden to have to drive five miles to make these entries. These small customs offices on the coast are very inexpensive. The salary of the officer is a mere trifle, something like $200, and it would be very little compared with the convenience it would be to the people of that locality to have a customs office there. I would be obliged if the Minister would ask fhe inspector in that district to go into that matter and see if anything can be done to promote the convenience of the merchants, shipowners and others in that district.
I shall have our inspector make an investigation to see whether we should be justified in establishing an office there. Of course, every office -we open means more expense to us.
The salary would be very small.

Would the minister be able to tell me about the number of the customs warehouses in the province of Nova Scotia, or -what might be regarded as private warehouses? There is a great deal

of complaint about the improper use of customs warehouses in that province. It is said that liquors are stored in these warehouses and that in some manner they find their way out of them. The complaint is made that warehouse licenses are given to men who are engaged in the liquor business. There is absolute prohibition in Nova Scotia, and to find that large quantities of liquors are stored in Government warehouses, or in warehouses recognized by the Government, creates a great deal of adverse criticism. Last year I brought this matter to the notice of the Minister of Customs himself (Mr. Sifton) who is not present now, and he told me that no further recognition would be given to such warehouses. That you can find in Hansard. But they are still in existence and they are still a terrible nuisance particularly in that part of the country from 'which I come. I trust that the Government will not encourage the illicit sale of liquor by recognizing these warehouses. I would like to know how many such licenses there are, for what period they have been granted, and whether it is the intention of the Minister to cease granting them in territories where absolute prohibition prevails so far as it can be carried out by provincial enactment?

The policy adopted when I was Minister of Customs-and I think it is still carried out-was to grant no bonded warehouse licenses in any province without the consent of the provincial authorities. I remember cases where a private individual would apply for a bonded warehouse license-

That is what I am
complaining about.

-and our answer would be that it would only be granted -after getting permission from the local Government. In Nova Scotia there are no bonded warehouse licenses granted, . I venture to say, without such permission, and in that way we feel we are only giving effect to the provincial prohibition law. There may have been bonded warehouses where a person had a quantity of liquor stored when the Prohibition Act came into force, and possibly it may be a case of that kind to which the hon. gentleman refers. In that event we would allow the person to have a license until he sold the liquor on hand; but under no conditions would he be allowed to replenish the supply unless the necessary permission was forthcoming from the local Government. I can assure the hon. gentleman that no licenses have been
granted in the province of Nova Scotia since last session, unless through the instrumentality of the provincial license board, or whoever is entrusted with the enforcement of the provincial liquor law.
/Mr. McKENZIE:	I asked the minister
to state positively whether there are any bonded warehouses licenses outstanding today. I think there must be, and in that event I want the names of those who hold them. If there are no such licenses then the parties interested are imposing upon a credulous public, because they say they have the necessary authority. They certainly	have	such	places	and	thereare	liquors in	them. I	can
assure the minister that there is no such thing in Nova Scotia as a board, or a body of men, with authority to license anybody to sell liquor. Absolute prohibition exists there, except that medical men may sell liquor for sacramental purposes in accordance with the law. The municipal councils can also appoint a few vendors, as they are called, who are licensed to sell on a doctor's certificate. I believe that in the city of Halifax there is a board who have the power of appointing vendors within the city, but that is the extent of their jurisdiction. Apart from this, no body of men is authorized to grant licenses or deal in the liquor traffic in any way. The complaint of the good temperance people of Nova Scotia, particularly those of the county of Cape Breton, is that bonded warehouses or other places are loaded up at night with liquor brought in surreptiously in cars, under the pretext of being carloads of pressed hay. Upon complaining last session, the Minister of Customs assured me that these licenses would be cancelled altogether, but I find that that has not been done. I may tell the minister that in the county of Cape Breton there is a great deal of serious complaint about this matter.

There must be some mistake, because no licenses have been granted by the Customs Department except what we call Class 2 Bonded-Warehouse Licenses, which are endorsed " Storage of Liquors not Allowed." Now, as to the charge which the hon. gentleman makes, he knows that the bonded warehouse is in the custody of an officer of the department, who alone keeps the key, and if access to that bonded warehouse is desired it must be obtained in the presence of the officer. Under Dominion statute liquors cannot be shipped into the province of Nova Scotia, neither can any one in the

province import them. It is suggested that someone in the city of Montreal, or the province of Quebec, where the right exists to load and ship liquor, has consigned a carload of liquor, under the guise of being a carload of pressed hay, to someone in Sydney or North Sydney, and that the officer in charge of the bonded warehouse, the only man who has the key, is in league with the owner of the liquor, and permits it to be taken into the bonded warehouse, and afterwards smuggled out and sold to people in the locality. I cannot come to any other conclusion from the statements which the hon. gentleman has made.
I can hardly think that the officers of the Customs Department would allow anything of that kind to go on. The whole responsibility for the observance of the law is in the hands of the officer, the man who has the key of the bonded warehouse. My officers sitting beside me tell me that at the present time they do not know of any licenses that have been issued for bonded warehouses in Nova Scotia for the storage of liquor. It is possible that some person may have had a license prior to the Temperance Act coming into force, and was allowed to keep his liquor in bond until it could be disposed of, but if the law is that liquor cannot be sold in Nova iScotia, it. is still there, otherwise the officers of the department are not carrying out their duty. As a result of the statements made by the hon. member tonight, I shall at once instruct the officers of the department to see what bonded warehouses are still in existence where liquor can be stored, and if there are no such bonded warehouses, then they must ascertain whether there, is any possibility of liquors being stored in bond. Because I quite believe the hon. member has been informed-probably it may be from stories not founded on fact-that liquor is going in in that way, and of course if any officers are implicated they would not be entitled to remain in the service. But I can hardly believe they would do that. It is quite possible that liquor is being shipped into Nova Scotia in violation of our prohibition law, just the same as it is being shipped into every other province. There is no doubt that liquor is being shipped from the province of Quebec, where there is no prohibition, into all the other provinces in violation of the law, but I feel that when we investigate we will find that liquor is not going into any building under the control of the Customs Department.

I am informed that in the town of New Waterford, for instance,

there is a private bonded warehouse; that in the town of Glace Bay there is more than one bonded warehouse; and I think that in the town of North Sydney, from which I come, there is at least one bonded warehouse, if not more. When the owners got their licenses I do not know, but they have had them for a long time. The Temperance Act, with its prohibitive clauses, was passed in 1916, and, except for a certain period in the city of Halifax, there was no part of the province where licenses could be issued or where liquor could be legally handled. I do not think there is any good ground in a prohibited area to allow the continuance of these licenses for nearly nine years, and unless the minister can find that there is very good reason for it they should be cancelled altogether. Because I tell him on my responsibility as a member that these bonded warehouses are refuges for the illicit handling of liquor. I am not making any charge against any officers, because I have not any information, but this thing is going on under the eye of the officers Whether they have any complicity in it I am not saying for one moment; all I say is it is going on and it should be stopped.

My officials tell me that there can not be a bonded warehouse at New Waterford because it is not a customs port. They hand me this official report of March 31, 1918, and inform me that no licenses for bonded warehouses have been granted since. This report gives the receipts for the attendance of officers at bonded warehouses for the twelve months ending March 31st, 1918, and the number of bonded warehouses. Of class 2, where liquors are not allowed to be stored, I find that in Halifax there are 29, in Sheet Harbour 1, in Lunenburg 5, in La Have 2, in Sydney 1, in Yarmouth 1. These are licenses granted for the storage of goods other than liquors. At Halifax they have warehouses of class 3, that is, general warehouses where half a dozen merchants can store any goods in bond except liquor; at North Sydney there is 1.
Who has it?

I cannot give you that information; but whoever has that bonded warehouse has no right to have liquor in it, and if the officer in charge allows liquor to go into that bonded warehouse he should not only be dismissed, but he should be prosecuted for violating his office. In Sydney there are two bonded warehouses of class 3. Now, it may be possible that in North Sydney or Sydney some

official may be in league with the licensee of the warehouse. I have seen in the press, no doubt the hon. member has seen it too, that in some of the provinces-I do not mean Nova Scotia, but provinces west of Ontario, and probably in Ontario itself

charges have been made against Government officials that they were guilty of conniving with men engaged in the illicit handling of liquor. Possibly such a thing might happen with some of our officers in Nova Scotia, and in that way the information coming to the hon. member might be correct. As he has brought the matter before the House and shown that there may possibly be collusion on the part of our officers I shall make it a point to at once have a thorough inspection of all these warehouses in every province, and if there has been any such collusion in the past the officers should receive the treatment they deserve; but if we cannot find any dereliction of duty on their part, the very fact of the hon. member bringing the matter to the attention of the House, and our inspectors being instructed to investigate every bonded warehouse throughout the Dominion of Canada, will have the effect of stopping anything of that kind in the future.

I understand the minister to say then, that there are no bonded warehouses in the province of Nova Scotia where liquor can be stored. I am quite sure that there have been a good many such warehouses, but whether they exist to-day I do not know. I know a case in a certain town in Nova iScotia where the bonded warehouse was in the cellar of the hotel.
In some mysterious way the liquor seems to find its way from the cellar up to the bar where it is distributed to the customer. I do not think that is going on in that particular hotel at the present time, but it was certainly an abuse of the bonded warehouse system. The minister, I understand, read us a list of bonded warehouses, and he said that in not one of them can liquor legally be stored. The inference I take from that is that there is in Nova Scotia no place under the control of the Dominion Government where liquor can legally be stored. Am I right?

The information given to me by my officials is that in Nova Scotia there are no bonded- warehouses in which liquor may be stored by any private individual. The hon. member might catch me just a little if I said that there is no liquor stored in any of those bonded warehouses, because if a customs officer in Nova Scotia gets word of a carload of liquor that is there against the law, it would be his duty to seize it and put it into a bonded warehouse. There might, therefore accidentally be some liquor there that was seized and not yet disposed of, but unless it is there under a seizure or at the request of the local government or on their authority. I do not think there is any liquor stored in any bonded warehouse in Nova Scotia. At all events we are not granting and will not grant licenses for bonded warehouses in Nova Scotia without the consent of the local government. I remember cases where licenses have been requested from Western Canada for the purpose of storing liquor. I think one request came from Manitoba, the party stating in his letter: There is no license board here and no one has any authority. I replied that authority would have to be secured from the deputy minister or the minister of the department, and I think in one case the party was successful in getting that authority. Licenses may have been granted on the suggestion of the local government of Nova Scotia, but if the Government of Nova Scotia has not consented, then I do not think there is a license in that province.

I do not think the Government of Nova Scotia has, since 1910, consented to the granting of any license to any person in that province to keep a bonded warehouse for the purpose of storing liquor. I should like the minister, through his officials, to inquire into the matter. If there are any such licenses, or if the Government of Nova Scotia has consented to the granting of a license to any one for a bonded warehouse for storing liquor, I have a right to know it. I do not believe that such is the case.
Yes, the hon. member has that right.

I shall be very much surprised, because the Government of Nova Scotia has been strongly in favour of temperance and been passing strong temperance laws, particularly since 1910, if that Government or any member of it has given permission to, or helped directly or indirectly any person to get a license for the purpose of evading their own law. If there is such a case, we want to know it, and I want, if possible, to know if the Government of Nova Scotia or any official of the Governent is participating in any such transaction.

I agree with the hon. member that there should , not be any such licenses, and I will write him a letter to-morrow, stating just what the situation is in Nova Scotia. When the prohibition Order in Council came into force, the only licenses that I remember were granted were licenses in St. John and Halifax for ships' stores or for export, but as soon as we passed that Order in Council, those licenses were cancelled. I remember the matter coming up about St. John. There were in St. John some firms whose whole business had been the s'torage of liquor for selling to vessels entering the port and going out again, and they felt sore in regard to the matter. Their licenses were allowed to continue in force only until they got rid of their stock, and then their licenses were cancelled and they went out of business. I shall be very much surprised if there is a license for storing liquor in Nova Scotia. The official sitting beside me, who has charge of those licenses, says there is none.

If the minister will
see that a vigorous campaign is instituted against the existence of such warehouses he will be doing a great service to the cause of temperance in Nova Scotia and will win the gratitude of the good people who are putting forth great efforts to suppress the evil of intemperance in that province.

I will certainly
do that, and I will say further that I cannot understand how any one is going to get liquor into that province, because the Government railways cannot carry that liquor except in violation of the law. I gave orders that they were not to carry it, and that the officials were to have a vigorous compaign to see that no one was allowed to ship it in under the guise of some other article. No matter whether the liquor is being shipped to the province or in the province, it is in direct violation of the law, and I will again ask the officials to watch the matter very closely and to see that every possible precaution is taken to prevent violation of the law, either by transportation or importation.

As the
minister has mentioned the carriage of liquor by the railways, I want to point out to him that it is generally consumed by some person on the railway before it reaches its destination. I have noit the slightest doubt that nearly every train leaving Montreal for the Maritime Provinces con-

tains illegal packages. In 1916, the Government passed a law prohibiting the exportation of liquor from a province like Quebec, in which liquor can legally be sold, into a province like Nova Scotia which is a dry area. The law was made very positive that no liquor could legally be carried by the railway from one province to another in violation of the law of the province to which it was sent. At that time the question arose as to who was to prosecute, and a long discussion took place in the House as to how that should be dealt with. The attention of the Minister of Justice was drawn to the fact that the violations occur, let us say, in the city of Montreal, and the prosecutions in the Maritime Provinces are under the control of the municipalities, and it would be very difficult for a local municipality to prosecute a wholesale merchant in Montreal who had illegally shipped liquor into Nova Scotia. We, therefore, put into the Act a clause making it the duty of the Justice Department to carry on these prosecutions and to see to it that no violation of the law of 1916 took place.
That step was hailed with" great delight by the temperance people throughout the Maritime Provinces, and the clergymen thanked the Lord that we had a Government that not only passed a law prohibiting the carriage of liquor, but also gave us the Minister of Justice of Canada to enforce that law. It looked very good on the face of it. Ever since that Act was passed it was known by everybody down there that liquor was going into the Maritime provinces every day; there were two trains every day, and my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has told the committee that the liquor was packed in the centre of carloads of hay, and' that great quantities were shipped in that way. This has been going on for the last three years, and the other day I ventured to ask the Acting Minister of Justice how many prosecutions had been brought by the Minister of Justice since 1916, the year in which the Act was passed. And what do you think was the reply? The answer was, none. The Minister of Justice has done nothing, .although the railway has carried the liquor and the railway employees have been drinking it as it went along. The Minister of Justice has gone to sleep, and the good people who prayed for him and thanked the Lord we had such a minister have been deceived.

The accusation just made by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) is a very sweeping one, and if it is correct some recogni-

tion must be taken of it. I gather from what he says that information has been laid before the Justice Department by some responsible person, that violations of the law have taken place, and that the Justice Department has refused or failed to act. If that is the case, the House and the country should know it. If it is merely a case of hearsay, the House and the country should also know it. I do not think the hon. member would suggest that the Minister of Justice should go down to the province of Quebec or the province of New Brunswick or Nova iScotia and act as detective while the cars are being unloaded, but if any responsible citizen has laid an information, as the law provides for, and the Justice Department has failed to act, we should certainly know it.
Perhaps the hon. member for Guysborough will bring this matter up when the Estimates of the Justice Department are under consideration.

This talk of bonded warehouses and kindred matters is apt to make us rather dry. With regard to the item under discussion, I should like to know what percentage of the item is accounted for by the statutory increases in the Outside Service of the Customs Department.
Mr. REI'D (Grenville):	There are no
statutory increases in the Outside Service. In the Inside Service, there is a statutory increase of about fifty dollars a year until the maximum of the class is reached. In the Outside Service, the matter of salary increases has been left to the minister in the past, but now the Civil Service Commission are classifying the whole Service, Inside and Outside, and it is expected the Outside servants will get a regular statutory increase. The officer at a small port might start at a salary of $1,000 a year, and rise by annual increases of $50 up to $1,500, or whatever was the maximum for that port.

I understood the minister to say earlier in the evening that the increase of $110,000 was practically accounted for by salaries. That would be about twenty-nine per cent of $3,000,000. I do not think the increases should be as high as that.
There are 3,283 officers, and the increase would average about $35.

There is a vacancy in the staff at North Sydney caused by the death of an officer by the name of McLeod. I should like to know if anything is being
done to fill that office, and whether preference will be given to returned soldiers in making the appointment.

I understand that it is not necessary to fill that office, but if it is to be filled, the appointment will be made by the Civil Service Commission.
I understand that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Sifton) is carrying out the policy I insisted on when in charge of the Customs Department. During the last two years I was in charge, every vacancy was filled by a returned soldier who had served at the front, and I made about.380 appointments during that	time; I understand	that about 200 appointments
have since been made. I understand that the Civil Service Commission are giving preference to returned soldiers in every case, and they are certainly doing it in regard to my department, because I insist on it being done. I think every member of this House will agree that the men who have served at the front must get the positions if they can fill them, and they will get them.
I am very glad to hear that the minister has carried out that policy but certainly the Minister of Customs is not carrying it out, as I can prove by a case in my county last year.
All appointments are made by the Civil Service Commission, and they are carrying out the policy of giving returned soldiers the preference.
I called the attention of the Minister of Customs to this vacancy before the appointment was made.
Where was it?
At Riverport.

Last year a vacancy occurred in the Customs service at Port Hastings, in the county of Inverness. I called the attention of the Minister of Customs at the time to the fact that he had appointed an aged gentleman to the position without examination. The minister had assured me that whoever was chosen for the position would have to take the examination, but I do not think this old gentleman did take it; I do not think he could. What I want to ask the minister is this: In that case would it not be proper for him to have this position filled by a returned soldier? There are many of them who are well qualified for the position, and in making such appointment the minister would only be doing what was right.

I have just made inquiry and am informed by one of my officials that in March, 1918, a man named W. H. 'Skinner was appointed at a salary of about $300. He must surely have some other occupation, because he could not possibly live on $300. I do not know how the appointment was made, but I suppose it was by the Civil Service Commission.
Was the appointment permanent?

I shall have to ascertain why the appointment was made and just What the situation is. In some small places it has been found difficult up to the present time to get returned soldiers. Some of these places pay small amounts ranging from $50 to $300, and they could not get returned soldiers to take the positions owing to the smallness of the salary, while in many cases no returned soldiers were available. It is necessary to get a man living near who has some other occupation, and an appointment of that kind may have been made temporarily until a returned soldier could be found. You can hardly expect a returned soldier to go into a port and live on $300. You would have to secure a man who had some other means such as a pension, but there are positions of the kind which undoubtedly would offer great assistance to a returned soldier who had been seriously wounded and whose pension, being insufficient to support him, would be augmented by some $200 or $300.
I think that is being done; in fact, I know of one ease in which a returned soldier superseded a man who was willing to give way to and help the returned man, although the salary was not large.

I think this is nothing more nor less than a political appointment, because I understand that the regulations of the department call for an examination.
I had the assurance of the minister last year that there would be an examination, but it was never held, and this old gentleman was appointed. The man who filled the position previously-I think his name was Forbes-had held it for a number of years, and his son, the only support of a widowed mother, acted for three or four years before his father's death. One would expect that it would be only natural for the department to allow this young man to continue in the service, as he requested to be allowed to do, until he could have an opportunity of taking an examination. The department did not see their way clear to grant this request but appointed this particular friend who was [Hr. Chisholm.]
a very active politician in the district, I am not scrupulous enough to say that this was very reprehensible if the Government were pretending to be appointing men to office on account of their political persuasion. But when we have a Government who claim to have ,abolished patronage and who appoint men to positions of this kind although they have not fulfilled the regulations, I certainly must take exception to their action. They are not living up to the standard which they have set. Apart from this however, there are several soldiers there who have been home for some time and, if I mistake not, there was a returned man in the vicinity at the time the department made the appointment. I suppose the soldier did not care to make application for the position, but there are soldiers there now who would be glad to get it. It is not necessary that the soldier should be a cripple in order to get an appointment. If he is back from the service and is working on a farm I think it would be only a reasonable recognition of the part he has played in the war to give him an' opportunity of filling any of these positions if he cares to take it. Under these circumstances, therefore, I say that this position was filled for political purposes, and for no other reason. I corresponded with this young man and told him the examination would be held, and although I wrote the department requesting them to notify him when the examination would take place- I think it was to be held in Sydney-he never received a notice. However I understand my friend is permanently appointed.

I hardly believe the Minister of Customs would countenance political patronage. At all events the appointment was before the Civil Service Act came into force, and at that time it was necessary to fill the position by the minister. He had to take recommendations from the best source that was available to him, and no matter what means he took to obtain the best man he could, he would be open to criticism.

I desire to say a few words on this question. I think the whole country has gone crazy on this matter. If I had an enemy, or if I wanted to do the soldiers a dis-service, I would endeavour to get them into the Civil Service. If there is any calling in the country more degrading than another, it is the Civil Service. Put a man into the Civil Service, and, as a general rule, you spoil him for anything else. But apart from that, he is bereft of all ambition and his career

is destroyed. You might as well commit economic suicide as enter the Civil Service. There are soldiers coming across the seas who are persuaded by this propaganda -whether it is political or otherwise, I do not know,-that the Civil Service is a desirable thing to get into. But I would not put a dog into it.

There being no statutory increases for the outside service, by what method is it proposed to discover who are entitled to increases and who are not? What is the modus operandi by which increases are granted?

During the time I was Minister of Customs,-and I suppose the practice is the same at present and will continue unless we can get the classification through the present session,-the position was this: The officials of the department, that is, the commissioner, the assistant commissioner and the inspectors, knew those who were entitled to increases and made a list which they submitted to the minister, and I think in almost every case the recommendations were acted upon. Some one may ask: Why some and not others? In posts where men have reached their maximum their salaries remain stationary. Under the old Civil Service Act there were several classes. There was a maximum for inspectors, one for assistant inspectors, messengers, etc. That is why I say it would not probably apply to every officer in the outside service.
The minister has told us that all these appointments are to be made by the Civil Service Commission?
Yes.

I can understand how the Civil Service Commission can make an appointment after examination. If they want to fill a position they can examine the applicants and find out the one best qualified. But there is another class of cases where that cannot be done. In my own constituency the position of harbour master of Canso became vacant a few months ago.
That is in the Department of Marine.

I do not care where it is; I want to get at the principle upon which the commission act. To my knowledge there are three or four applicants for the position, all good men, but not one is known to the commission. How are the commission to decide between these
three or four applicants, a thousand miles away, men they never saw and know nothing about? Is it by some rule of thumb in the office here? It would not be proper to correspond with anybody down there; it would not -he proper, under the system which my hon. friend says is such a splendid one, to ask me who is the best man, and I would not venture to say anything about it. But how do they arrive at a decision in a case of that kind?
Again I must ask my hon. friend to bring that up on the Civil Service item. But there have been a good many appointments in the department I am administering.
Without examination?

I never ask them that at all. The only inquiry I make when a man is sent to me to fill a position is whether he is a returned soldier. If I get the answer "yes," T ask no questions as to what steps the commission have taken in examining him for the position. I know he is qualified in one way and I am willing to give him a six months' trial. If he does not prove himself to be qualified he must then make way. As long as they are carrying out that part of the law I feel satisfied that we have a proper system of examination.

My hon. friend has not dealt with my point. I think he will admit that there are a number of appointees in his department that are not subject to examination; for instance, those at small ports where there are salaries of $200 or $300. He must be satisfied that such appointments are made by the commission without knowing anything about how they are made. Let us put aside altogether the question of the returned soldier, because if a returned soldier is available for a position everybody will say, let him have it. The case that I mention is one with which a returned soldier is not concerned at all. None of these men is a returned soldier. Every one is well qualified for the position. Then, take a case in the department of my hon. friend where there is no clerical work to do and no examination. How do the commission arrive at a decision where there are two or three parties applying for the same position?

There is no
trouble about that. Take a small port in Nova Scotia. There are several applicants

for a $300 position. The commission suggests that the inspector go to the place, examine the applicants, take their papers and send them back to the commission. Then, the commission may decide which man they believe is the best. - In addition to that the inspector himself can examine the applicants after the Civil Service examination has taken place. It is no trouble for the Civil Service Commission to hold an examination in several places in Nova Scotia. In a small place where the salary is only a few hundred dollars they can depend on the inspector examining the applicants and making a report as to their qualifications.

In the case to which my hon. friend from Guysborough refers, the position of harbour master of Oanso, of which I have no knowledge, the Civil Service Commission would ask for applicants. An application form would give the age, previous occupation, and qualifications of each applicant and he would also be required to give three references. If they did not seek advice from any other source they would arbitrarily decide which of the applicants would seem to be the best qualified for the position. It may be a very arbitrary method of reaching a decision but that is what they do. In the case of appointments to the post office, particularly rural post office, the commission always seek the assistance of the inspector for the province. I imagine that in most cases the inspector would make some personal inquiry himself before advising the commission. In the case of a harbour master I do not think there would be any provincial official with whom Ithe commission could communicate.

Returning for a moment to the question of salary increases in the outside service, my hon. friend says they are made on the recommendation of the commissioner, the assistant commissioner and the inspector. In regard to the minor offices throughout the country the commissioner could not really know anything about them except by correspondence and the assistant commissioner would be no better off. The only official who would have any knowledge of the efficiency and the services rendered by these various officers would be the inspector. Can we assume that such increases are always made on the recommendation of the inspector?

The commissioner would have some knowledge of the amount

of work in connection with these offices from the reports sent to the department.
Of the volume of business.

I mean the volume of business. Returns are sent to the department of the clearances of vessels and the work performed in the different ports. You might have a case where an officer might probably have received $150 at the time he took the position and When there would be only a dozen clearances during the year. But the work would have increased very much at that particular port. We would have that information in addition to the report of the inspector himself.
Then, of course, the inspector would be better able to judge because there are places where, although the record did not show much business done, the person appointed as preventive officer might have to travel over a long piece of coast in order to prevent smuggling. In the gulf of St. Lawrence there are cases of that kind, and the inspector would know what work the man was performing and be able to make a report concerning it. The commissioner would have to depend a great deal on the information which he gets in this way, and upon his own knowledge of conditions when he placed an official at certain work. I do not know any other way in which an estimate could be arrived at. This is what has been depended upon in adjusting the salaries under the rule for the last twenty-five or thirty years. Now the Civil Service Commission are endeavouring to see whether they cannot introduce an improvement, under which the officials in the outside service throughout the Dominion would be placed on a more satisfactory basis.

I quite agree with my hon. friend when he says that the revenue is not to be the only measure of usefulness. There are many places throughout our coast line where the collection of revenue would be sipall, but the service is important because of its preventive character, and if you did not have these officers there the revenue would lose a great deal. But the point I was coming to is, how the minister and his officials, whose good purpose I am perfectly satisfied with, can obtain any knowledge of the operations on the coast except through the inspector, and I am leading up in my own mind to the question whether these things are done through the inspector or otherwise. If my hon. friend says it is done through the inspector, I think that is a fair answer.

We have a
report from the collector of the port as well as from the inspector. In the province of Nova Scotia, as in the other Maritime Provinces, all these officials in the out ports are under one particular collector who makes a report to the commissioner of the work performed by each. It is the only way that I can see whereby we can come to a conclusion as to what is fair.and right in the matter of remuneration. There may possibly be cases where there has not been absolutely fair treatment, but I think while I was administering the department the officials as a rule were satisfied that the staff was being fairly treated, and I believe that policy will be continued.
With respect to the vacancy in the port where I live, did I understand the minister to say it is not intended to fill it?

I remember having a communication from some person in North Sydney many months ago in respect to this position, and I was informed upon inquiry, I think by the Customs Department, that it was considered unnecessary to fill it.

This man McLeod was the customs officer at the railway station, and another officer may have been transferred to take his place. If that is so, I have nothing to say, but there should be an officer there.
Customs: - Miscellaneous - Printing and stationery, subscriptions to commercial papers, etc., 5200,000.
There is a large increase here. To what is it due?

It represents the regular increase based on the higher cost of materials and labour.
Customs :-To provide for expenses and maintenance of revenue cruisers and preventive service, 5105,000.
What is the reason for the increase here?

The Customs Department had a large Steamer, the Margaret. It was a new boat and had only arrived on this side of the Atlantic a few months before the war broke out. The Naval Department requisitioned the steamer and took it to Halifax where it was placed on service in adjacent waters. This vessel has now been brought back and re-commissioned for her regular route.

How many steamers are
there engaged in this service, and what work do they perform?

This vote covers other vessels besides the Margaret. If I remember aright, we bought a steamer for cruising operations around Sydney. I can recall a discussion which took place with reference to that vessel when I was Minister of Customs.
That was the Alert.
That was the Alert. There is no danger now of illicit operations because importations of liquor are prohibited.
Is the Alert still sailing the seas?
Yes.
How many of these revenue cruisers are there?
There are the Margaret, Alert, Winamac and Zaidee.
This item is also for preventive service. Are we to understand that the preventive service is carried on exclusively by the revenue cruisers, or is it done by other means?
This vote also provides for the salaries of the chief preventive officer, Mr. Wilson, and his staff, and their expenses.
Will the minister say if the vacancy created at Boyls-ton by the dismissal of an officer some time ago has been filled?
I cannot find the names of any Government officer at Boyls-ton.
I am told there was an officer there, but he was dismissed.
There is no officer there now.
Is there any intention of appointing one?
No.

Will the hon. minister inform me as to the duty of the preventive service in a case like the following: According to press reports a large cargo of whisky, or alcohol and white whisky, was wrecked on the coast of Nova Scotia and considerable quantities of it were taken inland and cached; some of it has since been discovered. Does the preventive service operate at sea to prevent smuggling; does the Customs Department get any

revenue out of this liquor when it is found; and are they taking any steps to find it, or are they going to leave it to Nova Scotia?

The vessels that I have just mentioned are employed in that service and it is the duty of officers in command to seize any such liquors. I noticed that item in the newspapers. The people who cached that whisky did so before the preventive officers arrived on the scene, otherwise they would not have had a chance to seize it.
Is it too late now to get the revenue from that cargo?
The whisky is gone; that is the trouble.
I suppose the preventive authorities will take care of that?
I am sure it is the intention of the hon. minister to have an efficient service from those boats.
Oh, yes.

II take it for granted that wherever he is paying out public money for the preventive service it is his intention to get value for it? I would like to find out something about the Alert- not thS old stories they used to tell about her, for I believe she has quite reformed and is leading a much better life, and far it be from me to remind her of her old sins. But suppose a steamer is attempting to smuggle liquor from St. Pierre, which is a little island only sixty miles from our coast where they have the right, under the law of France, to handle liquor, I presume the Alert is maintained for the purpose of preventing that smuggling, and is presumed to have sufficient speed to overhaul any steamer trying to get away from her. I would like to know the horse-power of the Alert, her age, tonnage, and particularly her speed, and also some information about her seaworthiness, because I am told that the Alert is not of much use beyond lying in harbour and cruising on fine days when the sea is very, very calm, and that when it comes to chasing she cannot chase herself very far. I think men who have very fast boats and know they can outsail the Alert go over to St. Pierre, load up with liquor and smuggle it into the locality. I would like the minister to make inquiry and see whether he is getting value for the money he is paying for the maintenance of this boat.

I will be very
glad to do that. Of course, it was difficult to get any steamer during the last two or

three years. The officials say the Alert has been doing good work in preventing smuggling in that locality.

If they are ready to
give me information I will be delighted to hear of one thing the Alert has done.
The hon. member will remember, when she did good work according to his statement. The hon. member will remember the trip which he discussed in this House.

Oh, yes. This is a new Parliament; perhaps they did not hear about that. The hon. member knows that she was in this service at that time and he was paying the salaries of the crew. Under his supervision she was permitted to load with rum at North Sydney, and it was used for corrupting the electorate in the northern part of Victoria county. That is the service she rendered.
Mr.'REID (Grenville): The ho'n. member said she did well. A few minutes ago the leader of the Opposition brought up a question as to whether there were any licensed bonded warehouses in Nova Scotia, and the statements I made in answer were what I had from the Customs Department, which were correct. However, I communicated with the Inland Revenue Department in order to see whether there might be any possibility of bonded warehouses under that department. I now have an official of the Inland Revenue Department beside me., Of course, the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) will understand that I know nothing of the Inland Revenue Department so far as its administration is concerned. The Assistant Commissioner of Inland Revenue tells me that in Nova Scotia there are the following bonded warehouse licenses issued by the Inland Revenue Department: John A. McKay, New Waterford; Pius Gannon, North Sydney; A. S. Taylor, Glace Bay; The P. Doherty Co., Ltd., Sydney; H. Con-ter, New Waterford; G. Martinello Co., Ltd., Sydney; Mayflower Bottling Co., Ltd., 'Sydney; King Bottling Co., Glace Bay; John A. McRae, Glace Bay; Michael Nolan, Glace Bay; Mendel Maganet, Glace Bay; Felix Dipenta, Sydney; G. Martinello Co., Ltd., Sydney. The Assistant Commissioner tells me that these parties had licenses issued to them prior to the passing of the Order in Council prohibiting the importation or sale of liquor throughout the Dominion of Canada.
They had a quantity of liquor in store, and the licenses were extended simply in order that they might hold the liquor in

store. Instructions were sent to the officials of the Inland Revenue Department that those people were not to be allowed to take in any more liquor than what was in store at the time the licenses were granted, and they were to hold it until they could export the liquor or dispose of it in accordance with the laws of Nova Scotia. The liquor had to be exported or sold or destroyed; it was not allowed to be disposed of in any other way. I think the hon. member will agree with me that the information I had from the Customs Department is correct, and if the information the hon. member has given to the House is correct, namely, that some of these bonded warehouses are allowing liquor to be put into them in violation of the law-because they cannot accept it in accordance with the law-then some official or officials in the Inland Revenue Department or some officers who have charge of the keys of the bonded warehouses must be in collusion with those who own the bonded warehouses. The statement of the hon. member in regard to the bonded warehouses is very serious, and it is the duty of the Inland Revenue Department to investigate every bonded warehouse in Nova Scotia and other places where there are bonded warehouses in order to find out whether there is any truth in his statement. If those bonded warehouses are in existence, some means should be taken to see that the liquor is exported or destroyed or disposed of in the province legally, and those bonded warehouses should be got rid of at the earliest possible moment.

The
bonded warehouses mentioned by the minister are all in the island of Cape Breton. Can he give us the names of owners of bonded warehouses on the mainland of Nova Scotia?

McCullough and Creelman, Truro; the National Drug and Chemical Company, Halifax. The latter have a bonded warehouse for medicine. No others appear on the list in Nova Scotia. Something may not be altogether right in the list I have given, but we shall have a thorough investigation into all those bonded warehouses. I promise the hon. member I will send one of our best officials to investigate the whole situation in the bonded warehouses in Nova Scotia, as well as in bonded warehouses in other parts of the Dominion.

I understand a reference was made to an extension of the licenses. Have they been extended, and if so, for what period of time? How
much intoxicating liquor was there in those warehouses at the time the prohibition Order in Council was passed and that extension was given, and how much is there now?

I cannot this
evening give the hon. member that information. Those licenses were granted a year ago, and the assistant commissioner of Inland Revenue tells me that the minister in charge of the department informed him that those licenses will not be renewed; that the parties who have those licenses must, prior to the expiry of them, dispose of the liquor, either by exporting it'or by disposing of it in the province legally. Otherwise the liquor will be destroyed .
When were those licenses issued?
The first of April a year ago.	,
Was not the Prohibition Order in Council passed a year ago?
I do not remember the date now. Even if it were passed about that time, if a large quantity of liquor was stored in those warehouses, the licenses would have- to be renewed.

I understood the minister''1 to say, at some period in this discussion, that the licenses were renewed. Are we to understand that they were new licenses that were given to those people within the year, or were they licenses that were renewed?

They were old licenses that had been in existence prior to April 1, 1918, and that were renewed. None of those was a new license issued either by the Minister of Customs or by myself within the last year.

When
will those licenses expire?	,
On the 31st of March, and they cannot and will not be renewed without the consent of the Government of Nova Scotia.
I suppose' the minister has, in his department, information as to the quantity of liquor that was stored in those bonded warehouses a year ago and also the quantity there now.

An officer of the department has a full record of what was

there at the time and what has been disposed of since, and he should be able to put his hand on it in five minutes.
Will the minister give that information to the House when his Estimates are taken up again?
Yes.

There is, in my part of the country, a general impression that liquor was put into those bonded warehouses for a purpose. Notice was given by the Government that on a certain date a certain Order in Council would be passed, and there was a most desperate rush to get hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of liquor into those bonded warehouses in Nova Scotia, although the people who shipped it in had a full knowledge that the Order in Council would be in force on a certain date. The impression is that, by some influence or another brought to bear upon the department, those licenses were either renewed or permitted to exist under those circumstances after those places were filled to the rafters improperly and illegally, and with the full knowledge that the Order in Council was to be passed. There is a feeling abroad amongst the temperance people in that part of the country that is not at all amicable to the department, because the officials of the department are blamed, justly or not, with being in league with those parties and helping them to move their liquor into those places from which it is being doled out. It cannot get out except when an officer is there. All those people who have those licenses are old-time rum sellers, and it is the most extraordinary thing that only such people have those licenses, when for the last ten years, indeed, for the last twenty years there has been no permission to sell liquor in that province. We had the Scott Act in 1910, and the minister knows how old the Scott Act is. For the last thirty years,
I might say, there have been no means of selling liquor in the county of Cape Breton except illegally.

I am glad of the discussion this evening. I am satisfied, from what the assistant commissioner tells me, that everything has been done to prevent illegalities in all the provinces. The prohibition order came into force about the middle of March last year, and I have no doubt that large quantities were shipped in immediately prior to that. People would import it in the hope of selling it to the local governments for medicinal purposes,

for instance. Of course, attempts are made in different parts of Canada to violate the law. The result of this discussion to-night will be vigorous efforts on the part of officers of the department to ascertain just what is going on and to take greater precautions, if that be possible. When the stocks in these bonded warehouses are disposed of, the licenses will be cancelled, and no more will be issued.
How many of these bonded warehouses are there in Prince Edward Island, and what are the names of the parties controlling them?
There are none in Prince Edward Island for liquor; only for tobacco.

I suppose these licenses and the renewals are in writing? When the minister brings down the information that has been asked for, I should also like to know what was the quantity of liquor stored in these warehouses at the time the licenses were issued, also the quantity on hand at the present time; and the form of license, so that we can see the conditions under which the sales are to be made.

I will bring down that information, and will also give it personally to my hon. friend and to the leader of the Opposition, because it is in that part of the country where a large number of these warehouses are. If we ascertain the quantity on hand when prohibition came into effect, and the quantity now on hand, we shall be able to find out whether there has been any collusion or not, so far as those figures will show; but it must be remembered that if there has been collusion the parties would probably try to cover it up. At all events, I shall bring down the information.
Excise-Travelling expenses, rent, fuel, stationery, etc., $100,000.
What accounts for this increase?

It is on account of the extra expense in travelling, hotel bills and so forth.
Excise-Stamps for imported and Canadian tobacco, $125,000.
What does this item for stamps mean?
It is for printing.
Is not all the printing done under contract with the Finance Department?
The Finance Department have a contract with the American Bank Note Company, but this department pays for its share of the stamps.

Has a settlement ever been made with the merchants in connection with the stamps on matches? There was a good deal of confusion in connection with the new law. It was not clearly understood when it was coming into effect, and the dealers were instructed to stamp all the matches they had in stock at a certain date. Some of them did so, at a considerable expense. Then they discovered that the Act was not to come into force until some weeks later, and that they had spent their money needlessly.
I understood that a refund was to be made. Has the department ever settled with these people?

The Assistant Commissioner tells me that all these cases have been settled satisfactorily.
Excise-Preventive service-Salaries, $110,-
000.
How does the minister account for this decrease?
Distilleries have been closed up, and not so many officers are employed.
Have many seizures of illicit stills been made by the department?
Since prohibition has come into force the seizures have increased by 1,100 per cent.
Has the department appointed any officers whose duty it is to look after these illicit stills?

Now that the illicit stills have increased by 1,110 per cent, the hon. gentleman can readily understand that it takes more officers to hunt them down than were required before prohibition came into effect. The department is doing everything it can to put an end to these illicit stills. If it were not for these illicit stills, we could get along with considerably fewer officers.
Where are these illicit stills located? How many seizures have been made?
In Ontario there are 37; in Quebec, 25; in New Brunswick, 1; in Nova Scotia, 3; in Manitoba, 6; in Alberta, 13; in Moosejaw, 7; in Vancouver, 11; in Victoria, 2.
Are there any in Prince Edward Island?

No. The seizures were ten last year, and this year 110.
Excise-To enable the department to supply methylated spirits to manufacturers, the cost of which will he recouped by the manufacturers to whom it is supplied and to pay rent, power, freight, salaries, etc., $400,000.
It is the desire to have this item of $400,000 stand.
Then the whole item will have to stand.

Is there any great
urgency about these votes for excise? We need not go over it all again. The Chairman will remember that we have discussed it all except this item of $400,000. I am willing that the next, $500, shall.be dealt with and carried.
What became of Mr. Vincent, Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue?

There is now only one deputy minister. Mr. Vincent was given his salary of $5,000 for this year and is receiving the salary of deputy minister as in the Estimates.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Reid, the House adjourned at 11.03 p.m.
Monday), March 31, 1919.
